Distinct from and never classified with election, foreknowledge, or predestination.

Chapter Five Hundred Seventy-Eight

Romans 9:10 — Rebecca, the Twin Sons, and the Spiritual Origin of Israel

Romans 9:10 “And not only so, but also when Rebecca had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac,” (ESV)
Corrected translation: And not only the previous case history, but also Rebecca, when she had become pregnant from one, Isaac our father.

Chapter 578 continues the exegesis of Romans 9:10, a verse that extends the case history of divine election begun with Abraham and his sons to the generation of Isaac and Rebecca. Paul's argument presses beyond the question of which mother produces the heir to the far more decisive question of regeneration. The doctrine of the divine decrees, omniscience, and the perfect plan of God provide the theological framework within which this verse must be read. The chapter concludes with a rich treatment of the six categories of blessing imputed from the justice of God to divine righteousness, and a preview of the doctrine of election to be developed beginning in verse 11.

I. The Plan of God: Three Brackets and Seven Imputations

The pattern Paul has been tracing through Romans 9 is rooted in the overarching structure of the plan of God. That plan can be outlined in three brackets corresponding to three adjustments and seven divine imputations.

A. The X-Bracket: Physical Birth and Condemnation

At physical birth, two imputations occur simultaneously. Human life is imputed to the human soul. Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. The result is that every person is physically alive and spiritually condemned from the moment of birth. Physical birth cannot transmit divine promises or qualify anyone for divine blessing. This is the first and most foundational point of the passage: physical descent from Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob is entirely incapable of making a racial Jew into a true Jew.

The X-bracket establishes the first potential: the potential for eternal salvation. The pertinent doctrine is the gospel. The first hope — absolute confidence — is that faith in Christ produces eternal life. That hope is replaced by reality at the moment anyone believes in the Lord Jesus Christ, which is salvation adjustment to the justice of God.

B. The Y-Bracket: Judicial Imputations and Divine Righteousness

The Y-bracket contains two judicial imputations. First, all personal sins were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there. This is why personal sins are not the basis for condemnation — they have already been dealt with judicially. Second, at the moment of faith in Christ, divine righteousness is imputed to the believer. This imputation is the indispensable prerequisite for every category of divine blessing. No human activity — giving, witnessing, prayer, or service — can bring blessing down the grace pipeline. Blessing flows only from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. Justice is the point of reference for man. What righteousness demands, justice executes.

The Y-bracket establishes the second potential: the potential of great blessing imputed from God in time. As the believer grows through daily intake of Bible doctrine, he advances toward maturity adjustment to the justice of God, at which point the six categories of blessing begin to flow. These six categories — spiritual blessings, temporal blessings, blessings by association, historical impact, undeserved suffering, and dying blessing — all move along the grace pipeline from the justice of God to the righteousness of God.

C. The Z-Bracket: Eternal Blessing and the Judgment Seat of Christ

The Z-bracket contains the third and fourth categories of imputation: eternal life imputed at salvation, and blessing imputed in time at maturity and thereafter. These establish the third potential: the potential of great blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ after the Rapture. Undeserved suffering serves a critical function here — it refocuses the believer on eternity when temporal blessings might otherwise become an end in themselves.

The logic of the a fortiori argument runs as follows: if the justice of God can provide the greater — blessing in time imputed to the mature believer — it follows that the justice of God can certainly provide the lesser, which is the imputation of eternal blessing to the resurrection body. Blessing in time is thus parlayed into blessing in eternity. This is the mechanism by which God is glorified, and it is the goal of the entire plan.

II. The Spiritual Origin of the Jewish Race

All Gentile races originate in the X-bracket — that is, in physical birth. All Gentiles descend from Shem, Ham, or Japheth following the flood. The Jewish race is categorically different, because its origin is in the Z-bracket. Abraham was a Gentile for the first ninety-nine years of his life — a Sumero-Akkadian, descended from Shem. After his maturity adjustment to the justice of God, God restored his physical capacity, and through Isaac the new race began. The Jewish race therefore has a spiritual origin in contrast to all other races, whose origin is purely physical.

This spiritual origin carries a decisive consequence: it is possible to possess the genes of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — to be a racial Jew in every biological sense — and still not be a true Jew. The true Jew must replicate the origin of the race: he must be born again. He must believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. This is the meaning of the statement Paul has already established: not all Israel is Israel.

Genesis 15:6 records that Abraham believed in the Lord — heʾĕmīn — and it was credited to him as righteousness. The Hebrew verb is the hiphil stem of אֱמַן (ʾāman), the causative active: his positive volition at God-consciousness led to gospel revelation, and his faith in Christ resulted in the imputation of divine righteousness. That imputation — dikaiosynē theou — qualified him immediately to become the beneficiary of divine blessing. Without divine righteousness as the target and home for blessing, no blessing can be imputed. God cannot bless sinful man or man performing human good without compromising His own attributes. Divine integrity demands an appropriate antecedent.

III. The Three Generations: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob

A. Abraham and His Sons

Abraham had three women who provided him with sons. Hagar, an Egyptian, produced Ishmael. Ketura, a Canaanite, produced six sons. Sarah, a Sumero-Akkadian, produced Isaac. Seven sons are set aside; one enters the line of promise. The superficial objection is that Isaac was Sarah's son and therefore the only legitimate birth. Paul anticipates and refutes this objection. The mother is not the issue. Legitimacy of birth is not the issue. The issue is regeneration. Isaac believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. Ishmael did not. The six sons of Ketura did not. The promise goes through the believer, not through the legitimate wife. Abraham's brother Nahor provides a parallel: Nahor remained an unbeliever and therefore remained a Gentile, while Abraham advanced through salvation adjustment and maturity adjustment to the justice of God and became the father of an entirely new race.

B. Isaac and His Sons

To eliminate any remaining appeal to motherhood, Paul moves to the generation of Isaac and Rebecca. Here there is one mother and two sons. The question of whose mother is superior cannot arise. The twins shared the same father, the same mother, the same womb, and were conceived in the same act. The case is constructed to isolate regeneration as the sole determining factor.

Jacob believed in the Lord Jesus Christ and received a new name — Israel, meaning prince of God — as he entered the Z-bracket, following the spiritual origin of the Jewish race. Esau remained an unbeliever and therefore remained a Gentile. He spent his life in the X-bracket. His later weeping was emotional repentance, not saving faith. Emotion cannot produce regeneration. Only faith in the Lord Jesus Christ saves. Esau's free will, functioning across the full range of his life, consistently rejected Christ. Jacob's free will, functioning from the same freedom and self-determination, believed.

IV. Omniscience and the Divine Decrees

Billions of years before space, time, or rational creatures existed — what may be called Alpha time, in reference to the eternal self-existence of the Godhead — God possessed complete and total knowledge of every thought, every decision, and every deed of every person who would ever live. This is divine omniscience, one of three systems of divine knowledge. God's omniscience encompasses not only what actually occurs but also all alternatives, probabilities, and possibilities. However, only realities — what actually happens — are fed into the computer of divine decrees. Alternatives that do not occur are known but not decreed.

God knew billions of years in advance that Esau would reject Christ from his own free will and self-determination. Esau's printout from the decrees is therefore condemnation, not predestination. God knew that Jacob would believe in Christ from his own free will. Jacob's printout is election, foreknowledge, and predestination. These terms — election, foreknowledge, predestination — apply exclusively to believers. No unbeliever is ever said in Scripture to be predestined. The unbeliever is condemned to the lake of fire because he has rejected Christ from his own volition, not because he has been foreordained to that end. Hyper-Calvinist double predestination is therefore exegetically and theologically untenable. John 3:18 states the principle precisely: the one who does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the uniquely born Son of God. That is the printout. Condemnation follows rejection; it is not imposed prior to it.

The omniscience of God fed into the decrees the reality that Jacob would believe and Esau would not. The resulting printouts are categorically different. Jacob: election, foreknown, predestined to eternal life and to the perpetuation of the Jewish race through his twelve sons, the patriarchs of Israel. Esau: fed into the decrees as an unbeliever; printout is condemnation in time and in eternity. The difference between the twins is not ethnic, not maternal, not the order of birth — it is salvation.

V. Exegesis of Romans 9:10

A. 'And Not Only' — The Adversative Conjunction

The verse opens with ἀλλὰ (alla), an adversative conjunction used here in its ascensive function to introduce an additional case history that intensifies the argument. The previous case histories — Abraham's sons by three different mothers — established that the mother is not the determining factor. Now Paul adds a case that eliminates even the variable of different mothers. The conjunction signals that further cases are coming: the hardening of Pharaoh and the contrast between Pharaoh and Moses will follow.

B. 'Also' — The Ascensive Kai

Alongside alla appears the ascensive use of καί (kai), functioning adverbially: 'also,' 'even.' In its ascensive use kai marks a point that heightens what precedes it and prepares for something still more definitive to follow. A point is made now, and an even more decisive point will emerge later in the chapter.

C. 'Rebecca' — The Subject

The nominative singular subject is the proper noun ῤεβέκκα (Rebekka), transliterated from the Hebrew. Rebecca is the wife of Isaac. Paul names the mother, not the father, at the outset — a deliberate rhetorical strategy. By foregrounding Rebecca and deferring Isaac, he leads the reader toward the assumption that the mother will again be the issue, only to demonstrate that she is not.

D. 'When She Had Become Pregnant' — The Participle

The present active participle of ἔχω (echō, to have) is used with a customary present, denoting what eventually occurs. It functions as a historical present, drawing a past event into the vividness of present experience for the reader. The active voice indicates Rebecca as the agent. The participle is temporal: 'when she had.' The direct object is the accusative singular κοίτην (koitēn), which denotes sexual intercourse. The standard English rendering 'when she became pregnant' is an acceptable condensation, though the literal meaning is more concrete. The grammatical construction reads: 'when she had conceived.'

E. 'From One' — The Exclusivity Phrase

The prepositional phrase ἐξ ἑνός (ex henos), 'from one,' is theologically significant. It excludes with precision any ambiguity about the paternity of the twins. Both children share one father. This eliminates the variable of different fathers, just as Paul's earlier case histories eliminated the variable of different mothers. With one father and one mother, the only remaining variable is the individual volition of each son.

F. 'Isaac Our Father' — The Identification

Isaac is identified by the indeclinable proper noun combined with the numeral ἑνός (henos, one) and the genitive of relationship πατρός (patros) with the possessive genitive of ἐγώ (egō), yielding 'our father.' The first-person plural 'our' encompasses both racial Jews who possess the genes of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and regenerate Jews who possess both the genes and the righteousness of God through faith in Christ. Paul includes himself and all Jewish readers in a shared heritage, precisely so that the distinction he is about to draw will carry its full force.

Corrected translation of Romans 9:10 in full: 'And not only the previous case history, but also Rebecca, when she had become pregnant from one, Isaac our father.'

VI. Israel as Client Nation and the Role of the Pivot

The theological argument of Romans 9:10 has direct implications for the doctrine of the client nation. The Jewish race was constituted as the first client nation to God precisely because its origin is spiritual rather than merely ethnic. A client nation requires freedom, the laws of divine establishment, evangelism, and the teaching of doctrine. Israel was given all of these through the Mosaic Law, the tabernacle, the covenants, and the prophetic ministry.

The tabernacle's articles of furniture encoded the gospel in visible form. The Ark of the Covenant contained items representing sin; the mercy seat above it represented propitiation. On one side of the mercy seat stood a cherub representing divine righteousness; on the other, a cherub representing divine justice — the two halves of divine integrity. Once a year the high priest entered the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement and sprinkled animal blood over the mercy seat. Righteousness was satisfied; justice was satisfied. Between the cherubim dwelt the Shekinah glory — the personal presence of the Lord Jesus Christ in pre-incarnate form, visible as a cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.

Many in Israel used their inability to see the Shekinah glory directly as a pretext for unbelief. The Shekinah glory therefore entered human history as true humanity — the virgin conception and birth of Jesus Christ, eternal God and true humanity in one person forever, the hypostatic union. He could now be seen, heard, and observed performing miracles. The response of the generation that witnessed this was identical to the response of every previous generation: rejection. Free will, volition, and self-determination are the determining factors, not the visibility or invisibility of the divine person.

As long as Israel maintained a pivot of mature believers, it functioned as a client nation. When the northern kingdom's pivot shrank below the critical threshold, Assyrian discipline followed in 722 BC. Judah continued until 586 BC, when the Babylonian captivity began. After seventy years of discipline, Judah was restored. The client nation continued through 586 BC to 70 AD, forty years into the Church Age, when the times of the Gentiles — of which Paul writes — commenced. From 70 AD through the Tribulation, Gentile nations serve as client nations. A Jewish client nation cannot be reconstituted until the Second Advent of Christ. The same principle that determined the survival of Israel as a client nation determines the survival of any Gentile client nation: the size and vitality of its pivot of mature believers.

VII. The Six Categories of Blessing from the Justice of God

When the justice of God imputes blessing to divine righteousness in the mature believer, that blessing falls into six categories. These are not rewards for human effort; they are sovereign imputations from the justice of God to the righteousness of God as the target and antecedent. No human activity initiates or earns them. Capacity precedes imputation: without capacity developed through doctrine, imputation of certain blessings would produce only misery.

The six categories are: (1) Spiritual blessings — the direct products of the believer's relationship with God in time. (2) Temporal blessings — material and circumstantial provision, including wealth, success, and promotion, when the believer has capacity for them. (3) Blessings by association — blessing extended to unbelievers and immature believers in proximity to the mature believer. (4) Historical impact — the mature believer's effect on the course of history through the pivot function. (5) Undeserved suffering — divinely permitted adversity that refocuses the believer on eternity and functions as the gateway to the Z-bracket blessings. (6) Dying blessing — the circumstances and quality of the believer's physical death, which serves as a final testimony to the grace of God.

Blessing in time is the guarantee, argued a fortiori, of blessing in eternity. If the justice of God can impute the greater — temporal blessing to the mature believer in a physical body subject to the old sin nature — it can certainly impute the lesser, eternal blessing to the resurrection body, which is no longer subject to the old sin nature. Righteousness demands righteousness; justice demands justice. What righteousness demands, justice executes.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Seventy-Eight

1. Physical descent is insufficient for divine blessing. No divine promise can be transmitted through physical birth alone. The racial Jew who possesses the genes of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob but has not believed in the Lord Jesus Christ remains outside the covenant promises. Physical descent can produce only condemnation — the inevitable result of the dual imputation at birth.

2. Only salvation adjustment to the justice of God qualifies the racial Jew as the elect Jew. Election, foreknowledge, and predestination are terms that apply exclusively to believers. They describe the printout of the divine decrees for those whom God knew would believe in Christ from their own free will. No unbeliever is predestined. The unbeliever is condemned from his own rejection, not foreordained to rejection.

3. The divine decrees contain only realities. Omniscience encompasses all alternatives, probabilities, and possibilities, but only what actually occurs is fed into the computer of divine decrees. The printout for each person is therefore a fact, not a probability. Jacob's printout: election, foreknowledge, predestination. Esau's printout: condemnation. Both are the result of their own self-determined volition, known to God before the creation of space and time.

4. The twin sons of Isaac and Rebecca isolate regeneration as the sole variable. Same father, same mother, same womb, same act of conception — yet one is a Jew and one is a Gentile. The only variable is faith in Christ. Jacob believed; Esau did not. Esau's emotional repentance later in life, complete with weeping, changed nothing. Emotion is not faith. Regeneration requires non-meritorious faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and nothing else.

5. The spiritual origin of the Jewish race defines what it means to be a true Jew. All Gentile races originate in physical birth. The Jewish race originated in regeneration — specifically in the salvation and maturity adjustment of Abraham, and the subsequent miraculous birth of Isaac. To be a true Jew is to replicate that origin: to be born again. The true Jew is the racial Jew who has believed in the Lord Jesus Christ and thereby received divine righteousness as the antecedent for covenant blessing.

6. Divine blessing flows exclusively along the grace pipeline from justice to righteousness. No human activity — giving, witnessing, prayer, church service — can initiate or sustain blessing from God. The grace pipeline is insulated against all human merit. Blessing is imputed from the justice of God to the righteousness of God in the mature believer. Capacity for blessing must precede its imputation; capacity is developed through daily intake and application of Bible doctrine.

7. The Shekinah glory is the pre-incarnate and incarnate Lord Jesus Christ. The divine presence between the cherubim on the mercy seat in the Holy of Holies was the personal presence of Christ. Righteousness and justice — the two halves of divine integrity — flank the mercy seat, satisfied by the blood of the animal sacrifice foreshadowing the cross. The Shekinah glory became incarnate in the hypostatic union: full deity and true humanity in one person forever. The generation that saw the incarnate Shekinah glory responded with the same rejection as every previous generation, demonstrating that the issue is always volition, never visibility.

8. The survival of a client nation depends on its pivot of mature believers. Israel's history as a client nation demonstrates the principle: the pivot sustains the nation under divine protection; when the pivot shrinks below the critical threshold, the cycles of national discipline advance. The same principle governs every Gentile client nation. The spiritual issue — the size and maturity of the pivot — determines the nation's historical trajectory, not its military capability, political structure, or economic strength.

9. Blessing in time is the a fortiori guarantee of blessing in eternity. If the justice of God can impute the greater — temporal blessing to the mature believer in a physical body subject to the old sin nature — it follows necessarily that the justice of God can impute the lesser — eternal blessing to the resurrection body freed from the old sin nature. Temporal blessing is thus parlayed into eternal blessing. This is the mechanism of divine glorification and the goal of the entire plan of God.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
alla ἀλλὰ alla — but, yet, however Strong adversative conjunction. In Romans 9:10, used in its ascensive function to introduce an additional case that intensifies and extends the preceding argument. Signals that further illustrations are forthcoming.
kai (ascensive) καί kai — also, even Conjunction functioning adverbially in its ascensive use. Marks a point that heightens the preceding statement and prepares the reader for a more decisive development. Rendered 'also' in the corrected translation.
echō ἔχω echō — to have, to hold Present active participle in Romans 9:10; customary present used as a historical present. Temporal participle: 'when she had.' The participle governs the action of conception.
koitē κοίτη koitē — bed, sexual intercourse Accusative singular direct object of the participle in Romans 9:10. Literally denotes sexual intercourse; translated in context as 'became pregnant.' The term underscores the physical, natural character of the conception — the point being that what is merely natural cannot produce spiritual standing.
ex henos ἐξ ἑνός ex henos — from one Prepositional phrase combining ek (from, out of) with the genitive of the numeral heis (one). Establishes with precision that both twins share one father, eliminating paternity as a variable and isolating regeneration as the sole determining factor between Jacob and Esau.
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The central organizing concept of Romans. Divine righteousness is imputed to the believer at salvation adjustment to the justice of God and serves as the antecedent and target for all divine blessing in time and eternity. No blessing can be imputed apart from this righteousness as its home.
Shekinah glory שְכִינָה shəkīnāh — divine dwelling, presence The personal presence of the Lord Jesus Christ dwelling between the cherubim on the mercy seat in the Holy of Holies. Visible as a cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night over the tabernacle. The Shekinah glory became incarnate in the hypostatic union, uniting full deity and true humanity in one person forever.
hiphil of ʾāman אֱמַן ʾāman — to believe, to trust Hebrew verb used in Genesis 15:6 of Abraham's faith. The hiphil (causative active) stem indicates that his volition produced the action of believing. The result was the imputation of divine righteousness — credited to him as righteousness — establishing the pattern for all subsequent salvation adjustment to the justice of God.
pivot The body of mature believers within a national entity whose adjustment to the justice of God sustains divine blessing and protection on that nation. As long as a sufficient pivot exists, the nation continues to function as a client nation. When the pivot shrinks below the critical threshold, the cycles of national divine discipline advance.
client nation A national entity chosen by God to fulfill specific functions in a given dispensation: maintaining freedom, upholding the laws of divine establishment, evangelizing, and teaching Bible doctrine. Israel served as the first client nation. During the Church Age and Tribulation, Gentile nations serve in this capacity. A Jewish client nation will not be reconstituted until the Second Advent of Christ.
hypostatic union The union of full deity and true humanity in the one person of Jesus Christ, beginning at the virgin conception and continuing forever. In the hypostatic union, the Shekinah glory became visible and audible in human history. The two natures are united without mixture, confusion, or loss of the attributes of either.
propitiation ἱλασμός hilasmos — propitiation, satisfaction The satisfaction of divine righteousness and justice by the work of Christ on the cross. Foreshadowed in the tabernacle by the sprinkling of animal blood on the mercy seat on the Day of Atonement. Divine righteousness sees the blood and is satisfied; divine justice sees the blood and is satisfied. Propitiation is the basis for all subsequent imputation of divine blessing.

Chapter Five Hundred Seventy-Nine

Romans 9:11 — Election, Divine Decrees, and the Omniscience of God

Romans 9:11 “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For though the twins, Esau and Jacob, had not yet been born, and though they had not accomplished anything, good or evil, in order that the predetermined plan of God might remain in status quo in relationship to election.

Romans 9 continues Paul's extended argument that the word of God has not failed with respect to Israel (v. 6). Having established that the line of promise runs through Isaac rather than Ishmael (vv. 7–9), Paul now introduces a second case history — the twin sons of Isaac and Rebecca — to press the same point at even closer range. Verse 11 is a parenthetical statement, grammatically a genitive absolute in the Greek, inserted to explain why the divine selection of Jacob over Esau cannot be grounded in human merit. The verse introduces the doctrine of election, which Paul will develop through the remainder of the chapter. This chapter examines the grammatical structure of verse 11, the theological framework of the divine decrees, the nature of omniscience as the ground of election, and the first two major divisions of the doctrine of election.

I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 9:11

The verse opens with the explanatory, post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), marking a parenthesis inserted to explain the second case history of the twins. The understood subject of the parenthesis — Esau and Jacob — is drawn from the preceding verse.

The Genitive Absolute: 'Not Yet Having Been Born'

The first genitive absolute consists of the negative adverb mēpō (μήπω), meaning not yet, followed by an aorist passive participle from the verb gennaō (γεννάω), meaning to be born. The twins, Esau and Jacob, are the implied subject of this participial phrase. Although the subject of a genitive absolute is ordinarily in the genitive case and is set apart from the main clause, it is here supplied from context. The aorist passive participle represents a momentary action — the point-in-time event of birth — which had not yet occurred. The participle is concessive in force, requiring the translation: though not yet having been born. Corrected rendering: For though the twins, Esau and Jacob, had not yet been born.

Before birth, neither twin had received the imputation of human life. Human life is imputed by God to the soul at the moment of physical birth, not at conception. The blastocyst, embryo, and fetus are genetically human but do not yet possess imputed human life. Accordingly, before birth there can be no function of the old sin nature, no exercise of volition, and no accumulation of either merit or demerit.

The Second Genitive Absolute: 'Having Accomplished Nothing Good or Evil'

The second genitive absolute is introduced by the negative disjunctive particle mēde (μηδέ), meaning and not / nor. With it comes an aorist active participle from the verb prassō (πράσσω), meaning to accomplish, to practice — a verb that emphasizes ongoing practice or attained result, as distinct from the simpler poieō (ποιέω), meaning merely to do. The culminative aorist views the action in its entirety from the standpoint of existing results: absolutely nothing had been accomplished. The participle is again concessive. The object is expressed by two accusative adjectives: agathon (ἀγαθόν) and phaulon (φαῦλον). Agathon here denotes divine good — accomplishment within the plan of God. Phaulon denotes evil — the inevitable reversion resulting from the rejection of Christ as Savior. Sin is conspicuously absent from this pair.

Why Sin Is Not Mentioned Here

The old sin nature produces three categories of output that are contrary to God: sin, human good, and evil. Sin and human good can both be channeled into evil through intensification. Of these three, only sin has already been adjudicated. Every personal sin of every human being — past, present, and future — was imputed to the Lord Jesus Christ at the cross and judged there. This is the saving work of Christ, documented by His cry of dereliction: 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken Me?' (Matthew 27:46). God the Father and God the Holy Spirit withdrew from God the Son at that moment precisely because He was bearing the imputed sins of the human race and receiving their judgment. Because all personal sin has been judged, it is not at issue in the angelic conflict. Human good and evil remain unjudged and are therefore the operative categories in the conflict between the kingdom of God and the kingdom of darkness.

The restoration of the sinning believer to fellowship operates on the same principle. When a believer names a known sin to God (1 John 1:9), that sin is already judged at the cross. The naming does not produce the forgiveness; it acknowledges the already-accomplished judicial fact. Restoration to fellowship is never on the basis of sincerity, remorse, penance, or any human work. Such additions constitute arrogance — the imposition of human energy upon a divine transaction that is already complete.

The Purpose Clause: 'In Order That the Predetermined Plan of God Might Remain in Status Quo'

A final (purpose) clause follows, introduced by the conjunction hina (ἵνα) with a verb in the subjunctive mood, indicating future purpose. The subject is the nominative singular of prothesis (πρόθεσις), the predetermined plan, with a possessive genitive of theos (θεός): the predetermined plan of God. This same term appears in Ephesians 1:11 in connection with the verb proorizō (προορίζω), meaning to foreordain, establishing that the divine decrees constitute the content of this predetermined plan.

The prepositional phrase kata eklogēn (κατὰ ἐκλογήν) follows. The preposition kata with the accusative here denotes relationship: in relationship to election. The noun eklogē (ἐκλογή) means election. The verb is the present active subjunctive of menō (μένω), meaning to remain, to abide. The static present tense represents a perpetually existing condition: might remain in status quo. The active voice indicates that the predetermined plan of God — the divine decrees — produces this action of perpetual stability.

Corrected translation of the full verse: 'For though the twins, Esau and Jacob, had not yet been born, and though they had not accomplished anything, good or evil, in order that the predetermined plan of God might remain in status quo in relationship to election.'

II. The Old Sin Nature, the Divine Decrees, and the Twin Case History

The point of the genitive absolute construction is theological precision. Before birth, before the imputation of human life, and therefore before any function of the old sin nature, the omniscience of God had already known for billions of years that Jacob would believe in the Lord Jesus Christ and that Esau would reject Him. That eternal foreknowledge was entered into the computer of the divine decrees as historical fact.

The result for Jacob: foreknowledge, election, and predestination — the three printout categories for the believer in the divine computer. The result for Esau: condemnation and rejection from the genealogical line of Israel — the printout categories for the unbeliever. Esau, as the firstborn twin, would ordinarily have been the heir under the order of primogeniture. That order of physical birth was set aside. The younger twin became the line through which the nation of Israel would be constituted. The Jewish race was formed by regeneration rather than by natural generation — a principle that governs the entire argument of Romans 9.

The verb prasso is selected deliberately. Its semantic force — to practice, to attain by sustained effort — applies to both agathon (divine good, the accumulated product of spiritual advance) and phaulon (evil, the accumulated product of rejecting Christ and operating on the old sin nature). Neither category had any application to the twins in the womb. This eliminates human achievement as the basis of the divine selection in either direction.

Long before Jacob received the imputation of human life at birth, long before his salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ, and long before his maturity adjustment to the justice of God through maximum doctrine resident in his soul — the omniscience of God knew these things and entered them into the computer of the divine decrees. The printout is election. Long before Esau existed in any biological stage, the omniscience of God knew that he would reject the Lord Jesus Christ, sell his birthright for a bowl of lentil stew, and pursue a life pattern of reversionism. The printout for Esau is condemnation.

III. Doctrine of Election — Part 1: Election Orientation

Before election can be defined, it must be oriented to the divine attribute from which it proceeds. Election orientation begins with the omniscience of God.

Omniscience as the Ground of Election

Election simply means that God knows eternally, perfectly, and simultaneously all that is knowable, whether actual or possible. God possesses three distinct categories of knowledge.

First, self-knowledge: God knows Himself — His attributes, His essence, the equality of those attributes across all three members of the Godhead. This knowledge is eternal and unvarying.

Second, omniscience: God's knowledge of all that pertains to creatures. He knows every thought, decision, and action of every person — eternally (there was never a time when He did not know), perfectly (without approximation or error), and simultaneously (all facts of human history were known at once, not sequentially). This omniscience encompasses both the actual — what will in fact occur — and the possible — what could have occurred under different decisions. Only the actual is entered into the divine decrees.

Third, foreknowledge: This is not a separate cognitive faculty but rather the divine acknowledgment of what is already in the decrees. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain and creates nothing; it merely recognizes what omniscience has already entered into the computer. This distinction is critical: nothing could be foreknown until it was first decreed, and nothing was decreed apart from what omniscience supplied as actual historical fact.

Biblical Support for Divine Omniscience

Psalm 139:1–6 provides the fullest poetic exposition of this attribute. 'O LORD, you have searched me and known me' (v. 1) — the search existed in eternity past, billions of years before the psalmist existed. 'You know when I sit down and when I rise up' (v. 2) — every posture, every movement, known before the fact. 'You have computed my path and my lying down' (v. 3) — God has assigned to each person a defined quantity of time and space, and every detail of how that time and space is occupied was known in eternity past. 'Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether' (v. 4) — every word, formed before it is uttered, was known billions of years before the speaker existed. 'Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high; I cannot attain it' (v. 6) — the psalmist's honest acknowledgment that omniscience transcends human comprehension while remaining fully credible.

Hebrews 4:13: 'No creature is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.' The 'eyes' here are an anthropomorphism for the perception inherent in omniscience. Acts 15:8: 'God, who knows the heart, bore witness.' Acts 15:18: 'the Lord, who makes these things known from of old' — from eternity past. Matthew 6:8: 'your Father knows what you need before you ask him.'

Five Principles of Election Orientation

1. Every minute detail of thought, every decision, and every action is completely known and perfectly understood by God at all times — eternally, simultaneously with all other thoughts and actions of all other persons.

2. Every detail of life is in the mind of God at all times. Therefore, to God the future is as clearly perceived as the past.

3. God's perfect and eternal knowledge is not subject to development, reasoning, regretting, or foreboding. It is immutable.

4. The divine decrees are the giant computer that illustrates this principle. God knew all actual facts and entered them simultaneously into the decrees. The omniscience of God knows everything that has ever happened or ever will happen, and He knew them simultaneously in eternity past.

5. Only the actual was entered into the computer — not the probable, the possible, or the alternative. Isaiah 46:9–10 states: 'I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, “My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose.”' The end of time was known at the beginning. The decrees of God will be established and His good pleasure accomplished.

Two Categories of Printout from the Divine Computer

The facts entered into the divine decrees fall into two broad classifications: facts concerning believers and facts concerning unbelievers. For the believer, the computer produces at least three categories of printout: election, foreknowledge, and predestination. For the unbeliever, the computer produces condemnation and judgment. Predestination, election, and foreknowledge are never applied to the unbeliever in Scripture. The unbeliever is not predestined to the lake of fire; he arrives there by the self-determination of his own negative volition toward Christ. His condemnation is the printout of what his own free will chose. This is the point at which a certain tradition of Calvinist inference goes beyond the biblical data: reasoning from the predestination of the elect to a symmetrical predestination of the reprobate imports a logical schema (thesis/antithesis/synthesis) that the text does not support and that Scripture explicitly contradicts.

IV. Doctrine of Election — Part 2: Definition and Description

Definition

Election is the plan of God for believers only. More specifically, election is that part of the divine decrees which relates the believer to the plan of God in a specific period of history. It is a categorical concept: different elections apply to different dispensations. Those who live during the dispensation of Israel fall under the election of Israel. Those who live in the Church Age fall under the election of the royal family of God. Tribulational believers — Jewish elect and Gentile elect — fall under their respective dispensational categories. The Lord Jesus Christ Himself is designated an elect in Isaiah 42:1.

Biblical Attestation

2 Thessalonians 2:13: 'We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth.' Election always relates to those who are believers.

1 Peter 1:1–2: 'To those who are elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood.' Here election is explicitly coordinated with foreknowledge (prognōsis, πρόγνωσις) and with the sanctifying work of the Spirit (baptism of the Spirit at salvation) and the atoning work of the Son.

Ephesians 1:4–5 coordinates election with predestination: 'He chose us in him before the foundation of the world... he predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ.' The verb behind predestined is proorizō (προορίζω), meaning to foreordain. Ephesians 1:11 uses the same verb alongside prothesis (πρόθεσις), the predetermined plan — the identical term used in Romans 9:11.

Twelve Structural Propositions on Election

1. Election is the plan of God for believers only; it is never applied to unbelievers.

2. Election is that part of the divine decrees which relates the believer to the plan of God in a specific historical dispensation.

3. Election always relates to those who have trusted in Christ as Savior (2 Thessalonians 2:13).

4. Election is related to foreknowledge (1 Peter 1:1–2).

5. Election is related to predestination (Ephesians 1:4–5).

6. Election, foreknowledge, and predestination are three of the categories in the divine computer that deal with the believer.

7. Election emphasizes the plan of God for the believer.

8. Foreknowledge emphasizes the divine cognizance of what is in the computer.

9. Predestination establishes certainty — what is in the computer must come out.

10. The divine decrees, or predestination, alone establish certainty. Therefore nothing could be foreknown until it was first decreed.

11. Omniscience places the facts into the computer; foreknowledge merely acknowledges what is in the computer regarding the elect.

12. Election, foreknowledge, and predestination deal with the same facts — the content of the decrees regarding believers — but from different viewpoints. Election: the plan. Foreknowledge: divine cognizance. Predestination: certainty of outcome.

Vocabulary of Election

Hebrew: bāchîr — used in Isaiah 42:1; 45:4; 65:9, 22.

Greek nouns: eklektos (ἐκλεκτός) — Matthew 24:22, 24, 31; Romans 8:33; Colossians 3:12; 1 Timothy 5:21; 1 Peter 1:2. Eklogē (ἐκλογή) — Romans 9:11; 11:5, 7, 28; 1 Thessalonians 1:4. Compound: suneklektos (συνεκλεκτός) — 1 Peter 5:13.

Greek verb: kaleō (καλέω), to call or elect; related noun klēsis (κλῆσις), calling.

Note: elect angels are mentioned in 1 Timothy 5:21, indicating that election as a principle applies beyond humanity to angelic creatures who remained faithful in the angelic conflict.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Seventy-Nine

1. The genitive absolute construction in Romans 9:11 carries the weight of the argument. Paul is not making a casual aside; he is erecting a formal grammatical barrier against any merit-based interpretation of the divine election of Jacob. The concessive force — 'though not yet having been born, though having accomplished nothing' — eliminates human achievement as the basis for either the selection of Jacob or the rejection of Esau.

2. Sin is absent from the pair in Romans 9:11 for a precise theological reason. All personal sin has been adjudicated at the cross. The two categories that remain unjudged — human good and evil — are the operative issues in the angelic conflict. Human good (agathon achieved apart from the plan of God) and evil (the pattern of life built on rejection of Christ) are the categories Paul places before the reader to indicate that neither twin had established any such pattern before birth.

3. The divine decrees are best understood as a computer that receives input only from omniscience. Omniscience supplies historical facts — what will actually occur — not probabilities or alternatives. The alternatives were known to God but not entered into the decrees. Only the actual is decreed. This prevents any charge that the decrees impose on free will: the decrees record what free will will do; they do not cause it.

4. Predestination, election, and foreknowledge are exclusively categories for believers. The unbeliever is never predestined to condemnation in any biblical passage. The unbeliever's condemnation is the printout of his own negative volition — a self-determined outcome. Importing a symmetrical double predestination from logical inference rather than exegesis produces a conclusion the text never makes and that contradicts the biblical emphasis on the universal offer of salvation and the genuine freedom of human volition.

5. Foreknowledge is not causative. Foreknowledge is the divine acknowledgment of what is in the decrees; it makes nothing certain. Certainty belongs to predestination and to the decrees themselves. Nothing could be foreknown until it was first decreed, and nothing was decreed apart from actual historical fact supplied by omniscience. The three categories — election, foreknowledge, predestination — cover the same facts from three different theological vantage points: the plan (election), the cognizance (foreknowledge), and the certainty of outcome (predestination).

6. Election is dispensationally specific. Different elections apply to different historical periods. The election of Israel governs the Old Testament era and the tribulation. The election of the royal family of God governs the Church Age. Believers in each dispensation are related to the plan of God through the election appropriate to their age. Jesus Christ is Himself designated an elect — the unique elect of the Father — from whom all other elections derive their meaning.

7. The case of the twins demonstrates that the origin of the nation of Israel was not biological but theological. The Jewish race was constituted through regeneration rather than natural generation. The order of primogeniture — the firstborn as heir — was set aside. Esau, the firstborn, remained outside the covenant line. Jacob, the younger, became the origin of Israel. Physical descent from Abraham through Isaac does not constitute membership in the true Israel; membership in the true Israel requires the faith response that the decrees acknowledge under the category of election.

8. The maturity adjustment to the justice of God is the long-term goal of the believer's election. Election does not end at salvation adjustment. The predetermined plan of God (prothesis) encompasses the full trajectory from salvation through rebound adjustment to maturity adjustment — the progressive intake of Bible doctrine that advances the believer through the maturity barrier to supergrace and ultra-supergrace. Jacob's election looked forward not only to his faith in Christ but to his advance in doctrine.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
gar γάρ gar — for, because (explanatory/causal particle) Post-positive conjunctive particle used here in an explanatory sense to introduce a parenthetical statement that unpacks the second case history in Paul's argument. Its position after the first word of the clause marks it as subordinate and explanatory.
mēpō μήπω mēpō — not yet Negative adverb used with the aorist passive participle of gennaō to form the first genitive absolute of Romans 9:11. It denies the occurrence of birth up to the point in view.
gennaō γεννάω gennaō — to beget, to bear, to be born Used here as an aorist passive participle in the genitive absolute: 'not yet having been born.' The aorist marks a momentary action — the point-in-time event of birth. The passive voice indicates the twins receive the action; birth is something done to them, not by them.
mēde μηδέ mēde — and not, nor Negative disjunctive particle introducing the second genitive absolute. It coordinates with mēpō to establish a double negation: neither had the twins been born, nor had they accomplished anything.
prassō πράσσω prassō — to accomplish, to practice, to attain by sustained effort Distinguished from poieō (to do) by its connotation of ongoing practice or attained result. The culminative aorist here views the totality of non-accomplishment as an existing fact. The Holy Spirit's selection of this verb over poieō emphasizes that no sustained pattern of either divine good or evil had been established by the twins.
agathon ἀγαθόν agathon — divine good Accusative neuter singular of agathos. In this context refers to divine good — accomplishment within the plan of God, the product of the believer's advance in doctrine. Contrasted with phaulon to establish the complete absence of any basis for differentiation between the twins before birth.
phaulon φαῦλον phaulon — evil, worthless, base Accusative neuter singular of phaulos. In this context refers to evil in the pattern of the old sin nature operating under rejection of Christ — the inevitable reversion that follows sustained unbelief. Not a synonym for personal sin, which has already been judged at the cross.
prothesis πρόθεσις prothesis — predetermined plan, purpose Literally 'a setting before,' used for the divine plan set forth in eternity past. In Romans 9:11 it designates the divine decrees as God's predetermined plan. The same term appears in Ephesians 1:11 in direct connection with proorizō (to foreordain), confirming that prothesis and the divine decrees are equivalent concepts.
eklogē ἐκλογή eklogē — election Noun from eklegō (to choose out). In Paul's usage, election is the printout from the divine decrees that relates the believer to the plan of God in a specific dispensation. Never applied to unbelievers. Distinct from the related noun eklektos (the elect person) and the compound suneklektos (fellow-elect).
menō μένω menō — to remain, to abide, to continue in status quo Present active subjunctive in the purpose clause of Romans 9:11. The static present tense represents a condition as perpetually existing: the predetermined plan of God remains in permanent status quo in relationship to election. The subjunctive is required by the hina purpose clause.
proorizō προορίζω proorizō — to foreordain, to predestinate Compound verb: pro (before) + horizō (to set a boundary, to determine). Used in Ephesians 1:5, 11; Romans 8:29–30; Acts 4:28; 1 Corinthians 2:7. Predestination establishes certainty — what is in the divine computer must come out. It is applied exclusively to believers and operates as a printout coordinate with election and foreknowledge.
prognōsis πρόγνωσις prognōsis — foreknowledge From pro (before) + ginōskō (to know). Divine foreknowledge is not a separate cognitive act but the acknowledgment of what is already in the divine decrees. It makes nothing certain and causes nothing. Nothing could be foreknown until it was first decreed. Used in 1 Peter 1:2 in coordination with election.
bāchîr בָּחִיר bāchîr — chosen one, elect Hebrew adjective from bāchar (to choose, to select). Used of the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah 42:1 and of Israel in Isaiah 45:4 and 65:9, 22. The Old Testament vocabulary of election corresponds directly to the Greek eklektos and provides the background for Paul's argument in Romans 9.

Chapter Five Hundred Eighty

Romans 9:11 — The Doctrine of Election, Points 3–5: The Election of Christ, the Royal Family, and Israel

Romans 9:11 “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—” (ESV)
Corrected translation: for though the twins, Esau and Jacob, had not yet been born, and though they had not accomplished anything good or evil, in order that the predetermined plan of God, the divine decrees, might remain in status quo in relationship to election — not of works but of Him who calls —

Romans 9 continues the apostle's defense of the faithfulness of God's word in the face of Israel's apparent rejection. Verse 11 introduces the doctrine of election as the explanatory framework: the divine decrees, rooted in omniscience and executed through foreordination, are the ground on which God's purposes rest — not human merit, heritage, or performance. The previous session established election orientation (Point 1) and the definition and description of election (Point 2). This chapter continues with Points 3 through 5: the election of the Lord Jesus Christ as the foundation of all elections, the election of the royal family of God in the Church Age, and the election of Israel.

I. Review: Election Orientation and Definition (Points 1–2)

Point 1 established that election orientation begins with the divine attribute of omniscience. God knows eternally, perfectly, and simultaneously all that is knowable, whether actual or possible (Psalm 139:1–6; Hebrews 4:13; Acts 15:8, 18; Matthew 6:8). From this foundation, several orienting principles were drawn.

First, every minute detail of thought, decision, and action is completely known and perfectly understood by God at all times. Second, every detail is in the mind of God at all times; to God the future is as clearly perceived as the past. Third, God's perfect and eternal knowledge is not subject to development, revision, regret, or foreboding. Fourth, the decrees of God function as a vast repository: the omniscience of God knows everything that ever happened or ever will happen. Only the actual — not the merely probable — was fed into the decrees. The facts so decreed fall into two classifications: facts concerning the believer, and facts concerning the unbeliever. The computer of divine decrees prints out, for believers: election, foreknowledge, predestination. For unbelievers: condemnation, retribution, judgment.

Point 2 defined and described election. Election is the plan of God for believers related to a specific category and period of history. Election always relates to those who are saved (2 Thessalonians 2:13). Election is related to foreknowledge (1 Peter 1:1–2) and to predestination (Ephesians 1:4–5). Election, foreknowledge, and predestination are three categories of the divine decrees regarding believers, each emphasizing a distinct aspect: election emphasizes God's plan, foreknowledge emphasizes divine cognizance of what is in the decrees, and predestination establishes certainty. Nothing can be foreknown until it was first decreed. Omniscience places the facts into the decrees; foreknowledge merely acknowledges what is already there. All three deal with the same content: the decrees regarding believers only. Predestination is never applied to the unbeliever.

The Hebrew term

The vocabulary of election spans both Testaments. The Hebrew term bachar (בָּחַר) — to choose, to select — underlies the Old Testament election texts. The Greek terms include eklogē (ἐκλογή) — election, selection; eklektos (ἐκλεκτός) — elect, chosen; kaleō (καλέω) — to call; and cognate terms. These vocabulary items establish the breadth of the doctrine across both dispensations.

II. Point 3: The Election of the Lord Jesus Christ

In eternity past, the omniscience of God fed into the decrees not only facts about believers and unbelievers, but also facts about the unique person of all human history: the Lord Jesus Christ, the incarnate Son of God. The central factor of human history is not any political or economic development but the incarnation — the first advent of Jesus Christ. The omniscience of God fed all facts concerning both advents into the divine decrees.

Isaiah 42:1 identifies Christ as the elect servant: "Behold My servant, whom I uphold; My elected one in whom My soul delights; I have put My Spirit upon Him." The term rendered 'elected one' is bachar (בָּחַר). The Lord Jesus Christ is Himself called an election.

Acts 2:23 connects the election of Christ directly to the cross: "This one, delivered up by the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God, you nailed to the cross." The cross was fed into the decrees by omniscience; foreknowledge merely acknowledges what is already there.

1 Peter 2:4 calls Christ "a living stone rejected by men, but elected and precious in the sight of God." 1 Peter 2:6, citing Isaiah 28:16, adds: "Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, elected, held in honor; and he who believes in Him will not be put to shame" — the underlying Hebrew reading: he will not panic.

Three conclusions follow. First, the election of the Lord Jesus Christ is the foundation for all other elections. All other elections are composed of believers only; Christ's election is unique in that it involves one person who is not Himself a believer — Christ does not believe in Himself. He is the object of faith, the ground on which every other election rests.

Second, faith in the Lord Jesus Christ — a free-will function, non-meritorious self-determination — is the key to every election. It is the key to the election of Israel, the key to the election of the Church, the key to every dispensational election.

Third, the Lord Jesus Christ is the elect one, and the key to all elections is faith in Christ as He was and is revealed. He always has been and always will be the foundation of all elections.

III. The Dispensational Structure of Elections

Each dispensation has its own election, and every election includes believers only — with the single exception of Christ Himself. The dispensational framework proceeds as follows.

The Age of the Gentiles spans roughly two thousand years, encompassing the periods of innocence, conscience, and government. Only one category of race existed: Gentile. Believers in this age formed the election of the Gentiles. The basis for election was faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, even though Christ had not yet died. He was revealed as the only Savior and the only object of faith prior to the cross.

The Age of Israel adds a new race: the Jewish people. Beginning with the patriarchal period (Abraham to Moses), continuing through the priest-nation period under the Mosaic economy, and extending to the death, burial, resurrection, and ascension of Christ — the election of Israel is made up of Jewish believers. The Jewish Age is currently interrupted by the Church Age and will resume with the Tribulation and the Millennium.

The Church Age is divided into two sections: the pre-canon period (approximately AD 30 to 96), during which temporary spiritual gifts operated, and the post-canon period, during which only the permanent gifts function. The Church Age election is called the royal family of God. The Church Age ends with the rapture, at which point Israel's program resumes in the Tribulation.

The Millennial Age lasts one thousand years. Believers gathered into the millennium form their own election, consistent with the pattern of every preceding dispensation.

The duration of the Church Age is unknown. No one knows when the royal family will be completed. But in every dispensation, the principle holds: the election consists of believers only, and the election is grounded in the person and work of Jesus Christ.

IV. Point 4: The Election of the Royal Family of God

The election specific to the Church Age is the royal family of God. Several foundational truths define this election.

A. Basis: The Baptism of the Holy Spirit

The basis for the election of the Church — the royal family of God — is the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which occurs at the moment of faith in Christ. At salvation, God the Holy Spirit enters the believer into union with Christ as He is seated at the right hand of the Father (current positional truth) and also into union with Christ as He died on the cross (retroactive positional truth — the great divorce from the old sin nature). This Spirit baptism is the mechanism by which the royal family is formed.

B. Command to Know One's Election

1 Thessalonians 1:4 reads: "knowing, brethren beloved of God, His election for you." The participle rendered 'knowing' in standard translations is better understood as an imperative participle: "you know" — a command to learn one's election. No Church Age believer can understand the plan of God for his life, or the significance of his royal status, without understanding the election of the Church. Election is the doctrinal orientation to the entire Christian way of life.

C. Supporting Passages

2 Thessalonians 2:13: "But we are obligated to give thanks to God for you, beloved of the Lord, because God has elected you from the beginning — from alpha time, eternity past — to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and faith in doctrine." The baptism of the Spirit forms the royal family; doctrine sustains and advances it.

1 Corinthians 1:2: "To the church of God which is at Corinth, to those who have been sanctified in Christ Jesus" — the baptism of the Spirit — "saints, royal family, by election, with all who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours." One must be a believer to be elected. Election is a printout of the divine decrees for believers only, just as predestination and foreknowledge are printouts for believers only.

Colossians 3:12: "As elected ones of God, holy and beloved, put on the affections of grace, compassion" — the royal family honor code in summary form. Compassion, flexibility, impersonal love, personal love: all the components of the honor code are gathered into this command.

2 Timothy 1:9: "The one having saved us and having elected us into a holy station of life — royal family — not according to our works, but according to His predetermined plan, even grace, the name of the plan, which has been given to us in Christ Jesus before human history" — before the dispensations began.

D. Ephesians 1:3–6, 11

Ephesians 1:3–6 brings together the full range of election terminology in a single doxology. Corrected translation: "Worthy of praise and glorification is the God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the one having provided us benefits by every spiritual blessing in the heavenlies in Christ — even as He has elected us for Himself in Him before the world began. In love having foreordained us to the adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will, resulting in recognition of glory from the source of His grace, from which He has pursued us in grace in the beloved one." Election, foreordination, predestination, foreknowledge, and adoption are all present in this passage.

Ephesians 1:11 continues: "In Christ, we have received an inheritance, a destiny — having been foreordained according to a predetermined plan, from the one putting into operation all things according to the decree from His own will." This is among the most comprehensive summaries of the doctrine of election in the New Testament.

E. Romans 8:28–34

Romans 8:28: "We know, in fact, that to those who love God — those who have attained spiritual maturity — all things work together for the purpose of the good, to those who are the elected ones, according to a predetermined plan." The predetermined plan takes cognizance of human volition: only the actual decisions of believers — not the probable — were fed into the decrees.

Romans 8:29–30: "Whom He foreknew, He also foreordained as conformed ones to the image of His Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brethren" — the royal family of God. "Whom He foreordained, the same ones He also elected. Whom He elected, the same ones He also justified. Whom He justified, the same ones He also glorified." Glorification is the imputation of divine blessing to imputed righteousness (dikaiosynē, δικαιοσύνη). The justice of God imputes blessing in time to the divine righteousness that has been credited to the believer.

Romans 8:31–34: "Therefore, face to face with these things, to what conclusion are we forced? If the God is for us, who is against us? The God who did not even spare His own Son, but on behalf of us all delivered Him over to judgment — how shall He not with Him in grace give to us all things? Who will bring accusation against the elect of God? God is the one who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is the one having died — yes, rather, having been raised — who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us."

The application of the doctrine of election to the royal family of God is the motive for advancing to spiritual maturity. Motivation becomes momentum. Ephesians 4:1 commands: "Therefore I, the prisoner of the Lord, continue to encourage you to walk in a manner worthy of your station of life — to which station you have been elected." Titus 1:1 grounds the apostolic ministry itself in "the doctrine of God's elected ones and the full knowledge of doctrine according to the norm of godliness."

V. Point 5: The Election of Israel

Israel is also an election. The election of Israel is distinct from the election of the Church but operates on the same principle: it is composed of Jewish believers only. The election of Israel must be related to regeneration.

Romans 9:4–8 catalogs the privileges of Israel: adoption, the Shekinah glory, the unconditional covenants, the Mosaic Law, the Temple worship, the promises, and the patriarchs. Paul then clarifies: "Not all who are descended from Israel are really Israel; neither because they are Abraham's physical seed are all the children. But — quoting Genesis 21:12 — 'in Isaac your posterity shall be elected.'" The election of Israel is the election of believing Jews, not of ethnic descent as such.

Romans 11:1–7 returns to the same theme: "I say therefore, God has not rejected His people, has He? Definitely not. For I too am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected His people, whom He foreknew." Every believing Jew who is in the divine decrees as a believer is also elected. Paul cites the example of Elijah and the divine response: "I have left behind for Myself 7,000 men who have not bowed the knee to Baal. In the same way, therefore, there has also come to be at the present time a pivot, a remnant, according to the election of grace." Israel as a corporate entity has an election; that election is a remnant of grace — it is never the totality of the ethnic group but the subset of believing Jews in any generation.

Isaiah 44–45:4 reinforces this: "I, the Lord God of Israel, who call you by your name, for the sake of Jacob My servant, even Israel My elected one." Isaiah 65:9: "I will bring forth from Jacob a seed, the elect of Israel out of Judah, an inheritor of My mountains; even My elected ones will inherit it, and My servants will dwell there." The believing remnant of Israel has a guaranteed future in the millennium.

A. The Function of the Jewish Pivot

The election of Israel has always been the basis for divine blessing upon the Jewish nation. When Israel functioned as a priest nation, the believing Jews who advanced to spiritual maturity formed the pivot that sustained the nation's prosperity. Since Israel's client-nation status was interrupted in AD 70, the Jewish believers who reach maturity in each generation — wherever they are scattered during the Church Age and Tribulation — determine the measure of divine preservation extended to the Jewish people during those periods.

Matthew 24:21–22 applies this principle to the Tribulation: "For at that time there will be great tribulation such as never occurred since the beginning of history until the present time, nor ever will occur. And unless those days had been cut short, no human life would have been delivered — but because of the elected ones" — the mature Jewish believers — "those days will be cut short." The pivot of mature Jewish believers in the Tribulation determines blessing and safety for the Jewish people scattered throughout the earth. The principle is identical to the one operating in every dispensation: as goes the elect, so goes the client nation to which that elect is attached.

VI. Election Excludes Human Works as the Basis of Blessing

Returning to the text of Romans 9:11, the phrase translated 'not of works' is a prepositional phrase in Greek:

The preposition is ek (ἐκ) followed by the genitive plural of ergon (ἔργων): ek ergōn. As an ablative of source, it reads 'not from works'; as an instrumental ablative, 'not by works.' Either rendering communicates the same theological point: election excludes all human works as the source or means of divine blessing.

Election forms a circle around the believer and excludes human personality, human performance, human talent, and human effort as the basis for receiving anything from God. This is the negative side of grace. The believer cannot be blessed because of improved character, moral uprightness, religious activity, philanthropic effort, or any combination thereof. God does not respond to human merit.

Legitimate activities are commanded — prayer, witnessing, giving, functioning in one's spiritual gift, assembling with other believers. But these commanded activities are not the mechanism of blessing. They are the result of blessing already received and capacity already developed. The direction of causation is critical: because the believer is blessed through the intake of doctrine, he functions in his commanded duties — not the reverse.

The only basis on which the justice of God imputes blessing is imputed divine righteousness. At the moment of salvation, the righteousness of God is credited to the believer's account. Simultaneously, a printout of the divine decrees occurs: the believer is elected. Election then protects the pipeline of grace blessing by insulating it completely from any human contribution. The justice of God imputes blessing exclusively to the divine righteousness that has been credited to the believer. Election is the doctrinal declaration that this pipeline is sealed.

The mechanism of blessing in the Christian life is the non-meritorious perception of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). When sufficient doctrine is resident in the soul to produce capacity for life, capacity for love, and occupation with Christ, the justice of God imputes the corresponding level of temporal blessing. Election declares that no shortcut exists and no substitute is accepted.

VII. Conclusion: The Summary Principle

Election is the content of the divine decrees related to believers in the Lord Jesus Christ, assigned to their various dispensations. Election is the category of divine decrees that explains the omniscient viewpoint of God in relation to His people across all of human history.

Each dispensation has its own election, related to the divine policy for that dispensation. The election of the Gentiles, the election of Israel, the election of the Church, and the election of the millennial saints are all grounded in the same foundation: the election of the Lord Jesus Christ. Faith in Him is the key that unlocks every election in every age.

As goes the elect in any dispensation, so goes the client nation to which that election is attached. For Church Age believers in any national entity, spiritual momentum — consistent intake and application of Bible doctrine leading to spiritual maturity — is the decisive factor in the corporate blessing or discipline of that nation. The pivot of mature believers functions as the preservative of the nation, just as the Jewish remnant preserved Israel.

Romans 9:11 establishes that the divine decrees regarding election stand apart from any human works — good or evil — accomplished before or after birth. The predetermined plan of God maintains its integrity precisely because it is grounded in divine omniscience, executed through the cross of Christ, and insulated from human merit by the doctrine of election itself. The verse continues with 'but of Him who calls' — a phrase that will be examined in the following session.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty

1. Election is grounded in divine omniscience. Only the actual — not the merely probable — was fed into the decrees of God. Omniscience places the facts of every believer's existence into the divine computer; foreknowledge acknowledges what is already there; predestination establishes the certainty of the outcome. The three categories — election, foreknowledge, predestination — are printouts of the same facts regarding believers only.

2. The election of Christ is the foundation of all other elections. Every dispensational election rests on the person and work of Jesus Christ. He is the elect one (Isaiah 42:1; 1 Peter 2:4, 6), and faith in Him — non-meritorious self-determination — is the key that opens every election in every age.

3. Each dispensation has its own election, composed of believers only. The election of the Gentiles, the election of Israel, the election of the Church (royal family of God), and the election of millennial believers all follow the same pattern: the elect are those who believed in Christ as He was revealed in their dispensation.

4. The election of the royal family of God is based on the baptism of the Holy Spirit. At the moment of faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit enters the believer into union with Christ — both current positional truth (at the right hand of the Father) and retroactive positional truth (identified with His death). This Spirit baptism forms and defines the Church Age election.

5. No Church Age believer can understand the plan of God without understanding election. First Thessalonians 1:4 issues an imperative: learn your election. The royal family honor code, the Christian way of life, and the entire framework of the believer's purpose on earth become intelligible only when election is understood as the doctrinal orientation to all of it.

6. The election of Israel is a remnant of grace, not an ethnic totality. Not all descended from Israel are the Israel of election. The election of Israel consists of believing Jews in every generation — those in the divine decrees as believers. This remnant has always formed the pivot that sustained divine blessing on the Jewish people, and will continue to do so through the Tribulation and into the Millennium.

7. As goes the elect, so goes the client nation. The mature believers in any national entity — forming the pivot — determine the measure of divine blessing or discipline extended to that nation. This principle operates identically across all dispensations and applies with full force to Church Age believers in the present era.

8. Election absolutely excludes human works as the basis of divine blessing. The phrase ek ergōn — 'not from works, not by works' — in Romans 9:11 is an ablative of source and means. Election insulates the pipeline of grace blessing from every form of human merit: personality improvement, moral achievement, religious performance, talent, or effort. The only mechanism of blessing is the non-meritorious intake of Bible doctrine through GAP, which produces the capacity for the justice of God to impute temporal blessing to imputed divine righteousness.

9. Election is the doctrinal declaration that grace is absolute. The believer was elected not because of anything he did or would do, but because of what Christ did. He will be blessed not because of anything he does, but because of what the integrity of God does with the righteousness credited to him at salvation. Election is the other side of grace: it knocks out the notion that anything human can earn anything divine.

10. Glorification is the imputation of divine blessing to imputed righteousness. Romans 8:30 uses 'glorified' in the aorist — a settled certainty. The justice of God imputes blessing to the divine righteousness credited to every believer. This is the goal toward which election, foreknowledge, predestination, and justification all point: the complete execution of the plan of God for each member of the royal family.
