Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Four

Romans 9:13 — Divine Decrees, Omniscience, and the Blessing of Man

Romans 9:13 “As it is written, 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Just as it is written: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.

This chapter continues the preparatory doctrinal groundwork for Paul's exegesis of Romans 9:13 — the divine hatred of Esau and the hardening of Pharaoh's heart. Before those passages can be rightly interpreted, the doctrine of divine decrees must be thoroughly understood. What does it mean that God knew every thought, every decision, and every action of every creature before history began? How do election, foreknowledge, and predestination function within the decree structure? And how does the imputation of divine blessing — not human works — constitute the organizing principle of God's plan? These questions are addressed in the extended doctrinal treatment that follows.

I. The Will of God and the Divine Decrees

The doctrine of divine decrees has been under study for several sessions. Having examined its definition, its mechanics, and its characteristics, we turn now to the relationship between the will of God and the decrees.

A. Unity and Scope of the Divine Will

There is one all-inclusive will and purpose of God concerning all that ever was or ever will be, from the beginning of human history through the last day of the Millennium. Because God knew every thought, every action, and every decision that has ever occurred or ever will occur, all of it resides within one comprehensive decree. Many things are printed out of that computer, but they are all contained within it from the outset.

This will and purpose of God originates from within Himself — long before any creature of any category ever existed, whether angelic or human. It is therefore designed entirely for the glory, pleasure, and satisfaction of God. All creatures have been placed into space and time, and all events related to space and time were simultaneously decreed.

These events resolved themselves in divine action in two categories. First, divine action within the Godhead — the actions of the members of the Trinity — which are immanent, intrinsic, and subjective in the proper sense. Second, actions related to creation, which are extrinsic (taking cognizance of angelic and human volition), transient (chronological in their execution), and objective. This second category constitutes the function of divine justice as the point of reference for the human race.

B. The Formation of the Jewish Race

From the Gentile races descending from Noah through Shem, Ham, and Japheth, God formed the unique Jewish race so that He might have a client nation — a priest nation — in the Dispensation of Israel. The omniscience of God knew, before history began, every decision every person would ever make, and only facts were fed into the computer of divine decrees.

Abraham was by birth a Gentile of the Semitic branch. At approximately age 100 he became the first Jew — this was inseparable from his maturity adjustment to the justice of God and the resulting imputation of divine blessing from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in him. His older brother Nahor remained a Gentile, maintaining a posture of negative volition throughout his life and never departing from the Gentile racial category. Accordingly, Abraham's printout from the computer of divine decrees reads: election, foreknowledge, predestination. Nahor's printout reads: condemnation. These are entirely distinct categories.

The terms foreknowledge, election, and predestination are never used in Scripture for the unbeliever. They are printouts for the believer only. God's omniscience knew billions of years ago that Isaac would believe and eventually crack the maturity barrier, distinguishing him from his half-brother Ishmael, who remained negative and whose printout is condemnation. Isaac remained in the line of the Jewish race, and at the moment of faith the righteousness of God was imputed to him — establishing the target for all subsequent divine blessing. The same is true for Jacob, the believing twin, whose printout reads election; and Esau, the unbelieving twin, whose printout reads condemnation. These are the individuals at the center of Romans 9:13.

No Jew is truly a Jew in the deepest sense until he believes in the Lord Jesus Christ and is born again. The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is the Lord Jesus Christ — the Shekinah glory. This is the origin of the Jewish race and the key to understanding its historical problems.

C. Foreknowledge Distinguished from Omniscience and the Decrees

Three types of divine knowledge must be carefully distinguished: self-knowledge, omniscience, and foreknowledge. They are not synonymous and must not be conflated.

Self-knowledge — God's eternal knowledge of Himself and the other members of the Trinity, who are co-equal and co-eternal in essence while distinct in personality.

Omniscience — God's knowledge of all actual and potential facts in all of history. Omniscience feeds only actual facts — not wishes, not possibilities apart from reality — into the computer of divine decrees.

Foreknowledge — not the source of the decrees, but a printout from the computer. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain. It merely perceives and acknowledges what is already decreed. Nothing can be foreknown until it was first decreed. Foreknowledge is cognizance of what is decreed.

This sequence is logically precise: omniscience feeds information into the computer; the decrees are the all-inclusive plan; foreknowledge acknowledges what the decrees contain. Conflating omniscience with foreknowledge produces theological confusion and leads to misreadings of passages such as Romans 8:29 and 9:13.

II. Characteristics and Synonyms of the Divine Decrees

Several further characteristics of the divine decrees require careful definition before the doctrinal application can be made.

The decrees are efficacious, determining all that ever was or will be, including the directive, permissive, and overruling will of God. All things depend on God's will, and nothing is certain apart from His will. At the point where theology requires it, the will of God and the decrees must be understood as synonymous. Synonymous terms include: foreordination, predetermination, the decrees, and the sovereign will of God.

The decrees originate from God's omniscience in eternity past, separating fact from fiction. Therefore a clear distinction must be maintained between the omniscience of God and the foreknowledge of God: the former feeds facts into the computer; the latter reads out what is already there. Nothing can be foreknown until it was first decreed. Accordingly, the decrees — not foreknowledge — are what make events certain.

A further distinction must be made between the decrees of God and the desires of God. The decrees contain all the facts of history — every sin, every act of human good, every act of evil — because they record the actual exercise of human and angelic free will. Many of those facts are contrary to what God desires. God desires that every person be saved; yet the person who says no at God-consciousness and no at gospel hearing is decreed accordingly. The decrees contain both what pleases God and what violates His desires — but both are included under one all-comprehensive plan.

Sin, human good, and evil are not the desires of God, but they are in the decrees because people sin, perform human good, and commit evil from their own free will. God did not desire the consignment of conscious creatures to the lake of fire forever, but it is decreed under the printout of retribution for all who express negative volition at God-consciousness and at gospel hearing. Similarly, God does not desire the discipline of believers, but divine discipline is decreed for all carnality and reversionism, because human beings are responsible for their own decisions as free agents.

A final distinction must be made between the decrees of God in eternity past and God's actions in time. The action of God in time is the execution of the decrees established in eternity past. The execution is not the decree, but logically follows it. This also requires a distinction between God's decrees and God's laws: the decrees constitute the plan and action of God, while God's laws regulate human conduct in space and time. The laws of God are completely revealed in Scripture, while the decrees are only partially revealed in eschatological passages.

God did not decree Himself to be. God eternally existed before and outside of the divine decrees, so that the divine decrees do not act upon God, but God acts upon the decrees.

III. The Divine Decrees and the Blessing of Man

The relationship between the divine decrees and the blessing of man is organized around seven imputations that together constitute the plan of God. These imputations are the structural backbone of everything Paul is arguing in Romans 9.

A. The Seven Imputations

Five of the seven imputations are real imputations — meaning they have an antecedent home, a natural target to which the imputed element belongs. Two are judicial imputations, meaning they have no natural antecedent target; they are acts of the justice of God in which something is placed where it does not naturally reside.

The plan is organized into three categories, which we may designate as the X, Y, and Z equations.

B. The X Equation: Birth to Regeneration

Imputation 1 — Human life imputed to the soul at birth. There is no life in the womb in the Biblical sense; there is reflex motility, but not the divinely imputed human life. At birth, God imputes human life to the human soul, and that life is permanent. No sin, no deed, no action can ever separate human life from the soul. Those who never reach God-consciousness — due to mental incapacity or death in infancy — are automatically saved, because their volition is not implicated in the angelic conflict.

Imputation 2 — Adam's original sin imputed to the old sin nature. This is a real imputation: Adam's original sin has a genetically formed home — the old sin nature (OSN) — transmitted through the male line. This imputation occurs simultaneously with the imputation of human life, producing immediate condemnation. Condemnation must precede salvation. This arrangement also ensures that personal sins are reserved for a later, judicial imputation at the cross. No one is ever condemned on the basis of his first personal sin — only Adam was. The second imputation creates the first potential: the potential for salvation.

The X equation therefore reads: human life imputed at birth, plus Adam's original sin imputed to the old sin nature, equals the first potential — salvation through faith in Christ. The pertinent doctrine of the gospel, when received, produces the first hope: absolute confidence that faith in Christ means eternal salvation. When that faith is exercised, the hope becomes reality — eternal salvation.

C. The Y Equation: Salvation and the Imputation of Righteousness

Judicial Imputation 1 — All personal sins imputed to Christ on the cross. At the cross, every personal sin of every human being who would ever live was imputed to the Lord Jesus Christ and judged. This is the basis of salvation.

Judicial Imputation 2 — Divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation. This is a judicial imputation because it has no natural antecedent: the sinner has no home for God's righteousness. But once imputed, that righteousness becomes the target — the potential home — for all subsequent divine blessing. Justice demands that God impute blessing only to His own righteousness resident in the believer. This is why no amount of human works, talent, or merit can ever obtain one unit of divine blessing. The second imputation creates the second potential: blessing.

Imputation 3 — Eternal life imputed to the human spirit. God the Holy Spirit simultaneously creates a human spirit at salvation — this is regeneration, being born again. Eternal life is then imputed as a real imputation to that newly created human spirit. It is permanent. No sin, no action, no reversionism can ever remove eternal life from the human spirit. This is the basis of eternal security.

The Y equation: judicial imputation of all personal sins to Christ, plus judicial imputation of divine righteousness to the believer, equals the second potential — blessing in time. The pertinent doctrine of the Christian life, consistently learned and applied, produces the second hope: absolute confidence that maturity adjustment to the justice of God will result in the imputation of divine blessing. When the maturity barrier is cracked through maximum doctrine resident in the soul, that hope becomes reality.

D. The Z Equation: Maturity, Blessing, and Eternal Glory

The Z equation takes cognizance of the two imputations from the Y equation as its foundation: eternal life at salvation (first plus) and blessing in time (second plus). The imputation of blessing in time is the potential for the imputation of blessing in eternity. If no blessing is imputed in time, there is no basis for eternal blessing at the judgment seat of Christ.

The logical structure here is the argument from the greater to the lesser — what Romans 5 establishes as the a fortiori principle. If the justice of God can impute the greater blessing — temporal blessing to divine righteousness at the point of maturity — it certainly follows that the justice of God can impute the lesser: eternal blessing to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. The imputation of eternal blessing at the judgment seat is secured precisely because blessing in time was first imputed.

This is the complete plan of God as structured through the seven imputations. It explains in systematic form what election, foreknowledge, and predestination mean for the believer — and why those terms are never applied to the unbeliever. It also explains the story of the Jewish race in Romans 9: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob received the righteousness of God at the moment of faith, establishing them as the bearers of the covenant promises. Their unbelieving counterparts — Nahor, Ishmael, Esau — received no such imputation and remain in the printout of condemnation.

E. Summary Principles

The omniscience of God, taking cognizance of the fall of mankind in the garden, graciously provided a plan based on imputations from divine justice. This plan involves seven imputations feeding maximum blessing to mankind in time and in eternity.

Non-meritorious human volition can fall short of any potential within God's plan. To what extent every human being advances in this plan was known to the omniscience of God in eternity past and fed into the computer of divine decrees as fact. In too many cases the potential exceeds the reality. But only the reality was decreed — because only facts are fed into the computer.

From this emerges the governing principle: the attainment of divine blessing through imputation is the means God has chosen to glorify Himself and to give Himself pleasure. The imputation of divine blessing to the mature believer emphasizes His grace and excludes human talent and human works. Blessing flows exclusively from the priesthood side — doctrine received, believed, and applied — never from production, witnessing, giving, or any other function of the ambassadorship.

IV. The Decrees and the Glory of God

Every point in the doctrine of divine decrees converges on this: the decrees unite in one all-inclusive and final objective — the glory of God. This principle appears in Proverbs 16:4, Romans 11:36, Hebrews 2:10, and Revelation 4:11.

Before all creation, the decrees of God concerned no one but the members of the Trinity and their eternal glory. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possessed perfect, eternal, and infinite glory in eternity past and will possess it in eternity future. Nothing any creature does can promote or diminish that glory. A believer can glorify God — but cannot promote God's glory, which is already infinite. A believer's failure cannot reduce it.

This means that the plan of God moves forward independently of any individual's success or failure. If a believer fails, the plan keeps moving. Divine discipline follows the failure, but the plan itself is not interrupted. It began in glory and ends in glory. The believer who advances in doctrine participates in that glory; the believer in reversionism is left behind under discipline.

Since the manifestation of God's declarative glory also secures the highest blessing for His creatures, it is inevitable that the imputation of blessing to the mature believer will glorify God — emphasizing His grace and categorically excluding human talent and human works. The decrees include every detail of every creature's experience: every thought, every decision, every seemingly minute circumstance.

As the origin and subject of the divine decrees, God is glorified in everything that history produces — both the decisions that give Him pleasure and those that violate His desires. The believer in Supergrace A, Supergrace B, or Ultra-supergrace represents the highest positive expression of this glory in the human realm.

The decrees, though appearing many to the finite mind, are one plan to God — embracing both cause and effect, both means and end. God is glorified and pleased in the momentum and advance of believers within His plan. The omniscience of God knew in eternity past what thoughts, motivations, decisions, and actions would carry one believer to maturity and another into reversionism. God has prepared magnificent blessing by imputation for the mature believer, and He has prepared concentrated divine discipline for the believer in reversionism. Since there is no lake of fire and no eternal suffering for the believer, all discipline is concentrated in time.

V. The Decrees and Human Freedom

The plan of God and the decrees of God are entirely consistent with human freedom and volition. God does not limit, coerce, or violate human self-determination. This is a categorical statement that must be understood before Paul's argument in Romans 9 can be followed.

A distinction must be maintained between what God causes directly — such as the cross — and what God permits indirectly — such as sin, human good, and evil. God created man with free will, that is, volition resident in the soul. He therefore permits human volition to function in self-determination. Without that permission, there would have been no fall of man. The permissive will is just as much a part of the decrees, and therefore just as glorifying to God, as the directive will.

God is not the author of sin or human evil in any form. Free will and self-determination are the origin and source of sin, human good, and evil. Both sin and the cross are fed into the computer of divine decrees by the omniscience of God — one as the direct will of God, the other as the permissive will. The divine decrees are simply the facts of human history in the mind of God in eternity past.

Since the decrees are the sum total of God's plan and indicate His purpose designed in eternity past, they inevitably center around the unique person of the Lord Jesus Christ. It is at the cross that the sovereignty of God met the free will of man — for the glory of God and the momentum of the plan of God. Under the divine policy of grace, the work of salvation is accomplished by God; man benefits entirely apart from his own human merit or works.

God's plan was so designed in eternity past as to include all events and all actions related to their causes and conditions as parts of one indivisible system, every link being part of the integrity of the whole. This is why all things work together for good (Romans 8:28). Without violating human volition, God has provided a plan so perfect that it includes directive provision, preservation, function, cause and effect for all believers.

God has decreed to accomplish some things directly, some through secondary agencies such as Israel and the Church, and some through individuals such as the Apostle Paul. Primary, secondary, and tertiary functions all constitute one all-comprehensive plan — perfect, eternal, unchangeable, and without any compromise of divine integrity. The only revelation of the divine decrees is found in the content of the Bible. This is why the perception of doctrine is the highest priority of the Christian life and the only adequate preparation for historical pressure.

All of this doctrinal framework — the structure of the decrees, the three types of divine knowledge, the seven imputations, the relationship between the will of God and human self-determination — is the necessary preparation for the exegesis of Romans 9:13: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” That passage will be addressed in the following chapter.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Four

1. Three types of divine knowledge must be distinguished: self-knowledge, omniscience, and foreknowledge. Omniscience feeds only actual facts into the computer of divine decrees. Foreknowledge is a printout of what is already decreed — it makes nothing certain. Only the decrees make events certain.

2. The decrees of God are the facts of all human history in the mind of God in eternity past. They precede history entirely. They contain everything that every creature would ever think, decide, or do — including sin, human good, and evil — without God being the author of any of them.

3. The decrees and the will of God are synonymous with foreordination, predetermination, and the sovereign will of God: these are not competing concepts but synonymous terms for the one all-inclusive plan. Directive, permissive, and overruling will are all contained within the decrees.

4. Foreknowledge, election, and predestination are printout terms for believers only. They are never applied to unbelievers in Scripture. The unbeliever's printout is condemnation, reprobation, and judgment — the result of negative volition at God-consciousness and at gospel hearing, which the omniscience of God knew in eternity past and fed into the computer as fact.

5. The plan of God is organized around seven imputations. Five are real imputations (having natural antecedent homes); two are judicial imputations (having no natural antecedent). The second imputation in each equation establishes the potential: condemnation creates the potential for salvation; divine righteousness creates the potential for blessing; blessing in time creates the potential for eternal blessing.

6. Divine blessing is imputed exclusively from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the mature believer. No human work, production, witnessing, giving, or talent contributes one unit of blessing. Blessing flows entirely from the priesthood side through the intake and application of Bible doctrine. Works are the result of advance, never its cause.

7. The decrees are fully consistent with human freedom. God does not coerce, limit, or violate human self-determination. The fall of man was permitted, not caused. The unbeliever's rejection of Christ is decreed as fact — not as God's desire, but as the exercise of free will, which the omniscience of God incorporated into the decrees in eternity past.

8. God's glory is infinite, eternal, and independent of any creature. God possessed perfect glory in eternity past and will possess it in eternity future. No creature promotes or diminishes it. The believer glorifies God by advancing to maturity and receiving the imputation of divine blessing — not by human production. The plan of God moves forward with or without any individual's participation.

9. The doctrine of divine decrees is not abstract theology — it is essential preparation for historical pressure. The believer who understands how the decrees function, how divine blessing is imputed, and how human volition relates to God's plan will be able to apply doctrine under personal disaster, collective pressure, and historical crisis. The believer in reversionism, lacking this framework, will panic, accuse God of injustice, and fail.

10. The only revelation of the divine decrees is found in Scripture. Therefore, consistent, systematic perception of Bible doctrine is the highest priority of the Christian life. It is the sole means of advancing through the X, Y, and Z equations of the plan of God and the only adequate preparation for the coming exegesis of Romans 9:13.

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition

The decrees are the facts of all human history in the mind of God in eternity past.
Omniscience One of the three categories of divine knowledge. God's knowledge of all actual and potential facts in all of history. It is distinguished from self-knowledge (God's eternal knowledge of Himself) and from foreknowledge (a printout of what is already decreed).
Foreknowledge πρόγνωσις prognōsis — foreknowledge Not the source or cause of the decrees, but a printout of what the omniscience of God fed into the computer of divine decrees. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain; it merely perceives and acknowledges what is already certain by decree. Nothing can be foreknown until it was first decreed.
Election ἐκλογή eklogē — election, selection A printout term for the believer only. The divine selection of the believer, known in eternity past through the omniscience of God, based on the factual reality of that person's faith in Christ. Never applied to unbelievers in Scripture.
Predestination προορίζω proorizō — to predetermine, to foreordain A printout term for the believer only. The divine foreordination of all that the believer will become and receive in Christ — including election, adoption, and ultimate glorification. Synonymous with foreordination and predetermination as applied to the plan of God.
Real imputation An imputation in which the thing imputed has a natural antecedent home — a target for which there is an affinity. Five of the seven imputations in God's plan are real imputations: human life to the soul, Adam's original sin to the old sin nature, eternal life to the human spirit, blessing in time to divine righteousness, and blessing in eternity to the resurrection body.
Judicial imputation An imputation in which the thing imputed has no natural antecedent home. Two of the seven imputations are judicial: all personal sins imputed to Christ on the cross, and divine righteousness imputed to the believing sinner at salvation. Both are acts of divine justice without natural affinity between the imputed element and its recipient.
Old sin nature (OSN) The sin capacity inherited at birth through the male genetic line. The natural antecedent home for the imputation of Adam's original sin. The OSN is the source of personal sin, human good, and evil in the believer's experience throughout the Christian life.
Maturity adjustment to the justice of God δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The progressive stage of adjustment in which the believer, through sustained daily intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit, cracks the maturity barrier and becomes the target for the imputation of divine blessing in time. Distinguished from salvation adjustment (instantaneous, at faith in Christ) and rebound adjustment (instantaneous, repeated; restores fellowship per 1 John 1:9).
Reversionism Retroactive spiritual regression — the believer's return to the thinking, values, and motivations of the old sin nature. The reversionistic believer falls short of every potential in the plan of God and becomes the object of concentrated divine discipline in time.
Supergrace / Ultra-supergrace Stages of spiritual maturity beyond the maturity barrier. Supergrace A denotes the initial breakthrough of the maturity barrier through maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Supergrace B and ultra-supergrace represent continued advance to higher levels of blessing imputed in time, with corresponding eternal blessing at the judgment seat of Christ.
A fortiori a fortiori — from the greater to the lesser A logical argument establishing that if God can accomplish the greater, He certainly can accomplish the lesser. Applied in Romans 5 and in the imputation framework: if the justice of God can impute temporal blessing to divine righteousness at maturity, it certainly follows that He can impute eternal blessing to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ.
Logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence and continued function in the plan of God. Logistical grace is sustained by the justice of God and is independent of the believer's merit, works, or spiritual condition.
Pivot The body of mature believers within a national entity whose adjustment to the justice of God sustains divine blessing on that nation. The pivot is the invisible spiritual infrastructure that determines a client nation's historical prosperity or discipline.

Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Five

Romans 9:13 — Anthropopathisms: Divine Love and Hate as Language of Accommodation

Romans 9:13 “As it is written, 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Just as it stands written: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.

Romans 9 continues Paul's extended demonstration that the word of God has not failed with respect to Israel. The argument has moved through the doctrine of divine election, the sovereignty of God's choice among the twins Jacob and Esau, and the role of the divine decrees in ordering all of human history. Verse 13 introduces the quotation from Malachi 1:2–3 — 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' — which requires a careful distinction between the divine attribute of love and the anthropopathism of love, and between the divine attribute of hatred and the anthropopathism of hatred. The resolution of this exegetical problem unlocks the governing principle of the entire epistle: the justice of God, not the love of God, is the direct source of all divine blessing to mankind.

I. The Text and Its Source: Malachi 1:2–3 Quoted by Paul

The verse opens with the comparative conjunction καθάπερ (​kathaph​er), rendered 'just as' or 'even as,' introducing an analogy drawn from the Old Testament canon. The verb that follows is the perfect passive indicative of γράφω (​graphŋ), 'it stands written.' The perfect tense is the dramatic or resultative perfect: the action of inscription is complete and its results remain permanently in force. The passive voice identifies the human author — the prophet who called himself מלאכי (​Malʼākhī, 'my messenger') — as the one receiving the action, while the ultimate author is the Spirit of God. The indicative mood declares the historical reality of the citation.

Paul quotes from Malachi 1:2–3. The Hebrew of verse 2 reads: אהבתי אתכם אמר יי — ʾāhab̥tī ʾĕṭkĕm ʾāmar YHWH, 'I have loved you, says the LORD.' Israel's reply is immediate: 'How have you loved us?' The LORD answers by contrasting the two sons of Isaac. The love-verb in verse 2 is the Qal perfect of אהב (ʾāhab̥), and the hate-verb in verse 3 is the Qal perfect of שנא (sānĕʾ), 'I have hated.' Both verbs are categorical statements of divine policy, not emotional reactions. The Qal active participle of ʾāhab̥ also appears in verse 2 to indicate the continuity of that policy across all generations of Israel despite the nation's persistent apostasy.

Paul cites this passage — sometimes directly from the Hebrew, sometimes from the Septuagint, sometimes in paraphrase — always under the superintendence of the Holy Spirit, so that the divine intention of the original context is faithfully preserved. The quotation applies the election of Jacob over Esau established in the divine decrees before the twins were born (9:11–12) to the broader question of Israel's standing before God. One twin represents the believing line; the other the unbelieving. One is a Jew; the other becomes the progenitor of Edom and, through the Edomites, is associated with the Gentile nations. The contrast between them is the contrast between salvation adjustment and maladjustment to the justice of God.

II. The Doctrine of Anthropopathisms

A. Definition and Description

An anthropopathism is a figure of speech that ascribes to God a human characteristic which God does not actually possess and which is not a genuine divine attribute. The purpose of the anthropopathism is to explain a divine policy to mankind in terms of man's own frame of reference. Anthropopathisms become language of accommodation: human affections, human emotions, and even human sins are ascribed to God so that finite persons can understand infinite divine policy and divine attitude.

The term itself is derived from two Greek elements: ἄνθρωπος (anthrŋpos, 'man, human being') and πάθος (pathos, 'a function of the soul with outward manifestation'). An anthropopathism, therefore, is a human-soul-function ascribed to God for communicative purposes only.

B. Classification of Anthropopathisms in Scripture

Scripture employs anthropopathisms across a broad range of human experiences. The principal categories are as follows.

1. Love. God is said to love in John 3:16; Romans 5:8; Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:13; 2 Corinthians 9:7. As will be demonstrated below, this is not the divine attribute of love but an anthropopathism explaining divine motivation and policy in human terms.

2. Hatred. God is said to hate in Psalm 5:4–6; Malachi 1:3; Romans 9:13. Hatred is a sin when it functions in a fallen human being. It is obviously impossible for God to sin. These references therefore ascribe to God a human characteristic to explain a divine policy of judgment or condemnation in language that any human being can immediately grasp.

3. Anger or Wrath. God is said to be wrathful or angry in Psalm 88:16; Romans 1:18; Romans 9:22; Ephesians 2:3; Revelation 19:15; Psalm 7:11; Psalm 90:11; Psalm 103:8. Human anger is the frame of reference through which divine judgment is communicated.

4. Repentance. God is said to repent or change His mind in Genesis 6:6; Exodus 32:14; 1 Samuel 15:35; Psalm 90:11–13; Jeremiah 15:6; Jeremiah 26:3, 13; Ezekiel 24:14; Amos 7:3, 6; Jonah 3:9–10; Zechariah 8:14. The doctrine of divine immutability established in the study of the divine decrees makes plain that God never changes His mind. These passages use the language of repentance to describe, in terms accessible to finite readers, divine judgments and adjustments in the outworking of history. The Authorized Version renders the idiom awkwardly as 'it repented the LORD' in an attempt to soften what is in fact a straightforward anthropopathism: the LORD repented.

5. Scorn. God is said to scorn or mock in Proverbs 1:26; Psalm 2:4; Psalm 37:13; Psalm 59:8. Scorn involves mental-attitude sins when exercised by fallen human beings. Ascribed to God, it explains in vivid human terms a divine policy of judgment against the arrogant.

6. Compassion. God is said to have compassion in Psalm 119:71, 75; Lamentations 3:33; 2 Corinthians 4:17; Colossians 1:24; 2 Timothy 1:8. These references illuminate divine grace policy through the most sympathetic of human characteristics.

7. Long-suffering. God is said to be long-suffering in Exodus 34:6; Numbers 14:18; Psalm 86:15; 2 Peter 3:9. This anthropopathism explains the patience of divine forbearance in terms of a human virtue extended across time.

III. Divine Love as Attribute and as Anthropopathism

A. The Divine Attribute of Love

To rightly divide the word of truth, the believer must distinguish between the divine attribute of love and the anthropopathism of love. This distinction is as important as distinguishing between the dispensations of Israel and the Church.

1. The divine attribute of love is complete and total from all of eternity past as part of God's infinite being. There never was a moment in alpha time — eternity past — when God did not possess love as an attribute, and there never will be a moment in omega time when He ceases to do so.

2. God does not fall in love, nor does He maintain love through emotion. God is absolutely without emotion. Emotion is a human faculty, necessary and appropriate for finite beings whose love requires sustaining by feeling. God's love requires no such sustaining mechanism. It is infinite and perfect, incapable of increase or decrease, unmoved by tears, entreaty, or performance.

3. Like all divine attributes, God's love belongs to God's essential being. God is love (1 John 4:8) regardless of whether any object of love exists. In eternity past, before any creature existed, God possessed love without any external object.

4. There are two objects of divine love in eternity past, and the same two objects persist in time. First, God loves His own holiness — His own integrity, which is constituted by His perfect righteousness and His perfect justice. God's love for His own righteousness has always existed and will always exist. Second, within the Trinity, the Father loves the Son, the Son loves the Holy Spirit, the Spirit loves the Father and the Son, and so on. These are the eternal objects of divine love in its attribute form.

5. All creatures are excluded from the divine attribute of love except where divine righteousness has been imputed. At the moment of salvation adjustment to the justice of God — faith in Christ — the righteousness of God is imputed to the believer. Because God loves His own righteousness with a perfect and eternal love, wherever His righteousness is imputed, there the attribute of divine love is directed. The believer thus becomes in time what the other members of the Trinity were in eternity past: the object of God's eternal and infinite love. But it is the justice of God that imputes the righteousness, and it is the justice of God that therefore remains the point of reference — not love.

6. Because the love of God is perfect, it is totally devoid of human emotion (Jeremiah 31:3; Romans 8:39). Emotion is a sustaining factor for imperfect persons. God's love is an absolute, not a progressive or conditional state.

7. The divine attribute of love is therefore not the subject when Scripture says 'God loved Jacob' or 'God so loved the world.' The problem in reading God as the subject of love in Scripture arises not from His attribute but from the anthropopathism — the human characteristic of love ascribed to God for communicative purposes.

B. The Anthropopathism of Divine Love

1. The anthropopathism of love ascribes to God the human characteristic of love — which God does not actually possess in the emotional, relational sense — in order to explain His policy in terms of human frame of reference. Human love gives. Human love responds. Human love is immediately intelligible to every person.

2. The classical illustration is John 3:16: 'God so loved the world that He gave His uniquely born Son.' The Greek reads μονογενής (​monogenēs), 'uniquely born,' not merely 'only begotten.' God the Father made the decision to impute human life to the fetus born of the virgin, knowing that the full weight of the sins of the world would be imputed to that Son at the cross and that divine justice would judge those sins. To communicate the magnitude of that decision in terms accessible to finite minds, Scripture employs the language of love: 'God so loved the world that He gave.' That is human love ascribed to God — not divine love as attribute — because the divine attribute of love cannot have as its object a world full of sin, human good, and evil.

3. Romans 5:8 — 'God demonstrates His love toward us in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us' — likewise employs the anthropopathism. God cannot direct His attribute of love toward sinners as such. But God can, and does, explain through the language of accommodation that the same divine action that sent Christ to the cross can be understood by analogy to the noblest act of human love: giving up the most precious thing one possesses for the sake of another.

4. The anthropopathism of love explains in human frame of reference the fact of Jacob's salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ. The omniscience of God, in eternity past, knew that Jacob would believe. That fact was fed into the divine decrees, and the readout for Jacob is election, foreknowledge, predestination, and foreordination. To communicate that cluster of doctrines in a single vivid phrase accessible to every reader, Scripture says: 'Jacob I loved.'

5. The anthropopathism of hate explains in human frame of reference the fact of Esau's rejection of Christ as Savior — maladjustment to the justice of God — and the consequent judgment and condemnation that is his readout from the divine decrees. Even Esau's emotional, tearful human repentance after the loss of the birthright had no effect because human repentance — changing one's feelings — is not adjustment to the justice of God. Only faith in Christ constitutes that adjustment. To communicate the stark difference in divine policy between the two twins, Scripture says: 'Esau I hated.'

6. Neither the love nor the hate represents God functioning in a human emotional mode. God is neither humanly noble in His love nor sinfully vindictive in His hatred. Both are language of accommodation to explain a divine policy that, stated in full technical precision, requires mastery of the doctrines of omniscience, divine decrees, election, foreknowledge, and predestination. The anthropopathism compresses all of that into two words any person can understand: love and hate.

IV. Justice as the Point of Reference, Not Love

The anthropopathism of divine love is frequently misread as establishing love as the governing attribute of God's relationship to mankind. This misreading has been the source of numerous theological errors, including the reduction of the gospel to a message of divine sentiment and the rise of social movements that mistake sentimentality for biblical doctrine. The correction is straightforward.

Love as an anthropopathism explains divine motivation in terms of human frame of reference. Love is not, and never has been since the fall of Adam, the direct source of blessing from God. The direct source of blessing from God is divine justice — one half of divine integrity, the other half being divine righteousness. Righteousness demands righteousness; justice demands justice. What righteousness demands, justice executes. This is the basis of divine blessing to man.

God does not bless mankind from human sentimentality or emotional attraction. Man errs when he concludes that he must do something or say something to please God and thereby receive blessing. The justice of God imputes blessing in six categories in time to the mature believer. The justice of God imputes blessing in eternity at the judgment seat of Christ. It is justice that imputes blessing to the resurrection body, just as justice imputes blessing in time to the believer who has advanced to maturity adjustment. Love is never the point of reference; justice always is.

The key is justification, which is a function of divine justice, never a function of divine love. Because it is justice that justifies — because the most unlovely, the most untalented, the most outwardly repulsive member of the human race stands before the same standard as the most admirable — only God is genuinely impartial. The point of reference is divine justice, and divine justice is blind to human merit. God found a way to bring sinful man into eternal relationship with Himself and to bless mankind without compromising any divine attribute, including love. Through justification, God is free to bring sinful man into eternal relationship with Himself and to impute blessing to him both in time and in eternity.

Perfect God produces a perfect plan for imperfect persons. God loves His own perfect righteousness with an infinite and perfect love. In that love for His own righteousness and holiness, the entire economy of grace is revealed: righteousness demands righteousness, justice demands justice, and what righteousness demands justice executes. To explain this to finite, fallen persons, language of accommodation ascribes to God human love as an anthropopathism — but it is always and only divine justice that is the operative mechanism.

V. The Twins as a Case Study in the Divine Decrees

The contrast between Jacob and Esau in Romans 9:13 recapitulates the argument of verses 11–12. The divine decrees are based entirely on the omniscience of God. Omniscience — distinct from self-knowledge and knowledge of the possible — encompasses every thought, every decision, and every deed of every person in all of human history. Into the divine decrees only the actual is fed: the actual decisions that persons actually make. The possible — what could have occurred under different decisions — informs divine omniscience but does not enter the decree itself.

For the twins: the omniscience of God knew in eternity past that Jacob would believe in the Lord — salvation adjustment to the justice of God — and that Esau would reject Christ as Savior. Those facts, actual facts eternally known, were entered into the divine decrees. Jacob's readout is election, foreknowledge, predestination, and foreordination. Esau's readout is condemnation and judgment. Foreknowledge does not precede the decrees; foreknowledge acknowledges what is in the decrees. Omniscience feeds the decree; foreknowledge reads out from it.

Esau's emotional response — weeping, seeking the blessing with tears — changed nothing because tears and emotion are not the mechanism of adjustment to the justice of God. Faith in Christ is. Esau never exercised that faith, and no amount of human repentance, however intense or tearful, altered the divine decree. The decree was based not on foreseen works, whether good or evil (9:11), but on the actual volitional response of each person to the person and work of Christ.

One twin emerges as a Jew in the line of promise; the other as the progenitor of Edom and the Gentile nations. The simplest way to communicate the absolute difference in divine policy between them — a difference rooted in the deepest mysteries of omniscience and decree — is the language of human relationship at its most unambiguous: 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.' Almost any person, regardless of theological background, grasps the difference in status conveyed by those two phrases. That is the purpose and the power of the anthropopathism.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Five

1. Romans 9:13 cites Malachi 1:2–3 with the resultative perfect of γράφω (graphŋ), 'it stands written,' indicating that the inspired record is permanently in force. Paul's quotation — whether from the Hebrew, the Septuagint, or in paraphrase — is always governed by the ministry of the Holy Spirit, preserving the divine intention of the original context.

2. An anthropopathism ascribes to God a human characteristic He does not actually possess, for the purpose of explaining divine policy in terms of human frame of reference. Scripture's major anthropopathisms include love, hatred, anger, repentance, scorn, compassion, and long-suffering. None of these imply that God is humanly emotional, humanly sinful, or humanly mutable.

3. The divine attribute of love is complete and total from eternity past as part of God's infinite being. God does not fall in love, does not maintain love through emotion, and does not need an external object for love. In eternity past, the two objects of divine love were God's own righteousness and the other persons of the Trinity.

4. All creatures are excluded from the divine attribute of love except where divine righteousness has been imputed. At the moment of salvation adjustment to the justice of God, the righteousness of God is imputed to the believer. Because God loves His own righteousness with a perfect and eternal love, wherever His righteousness is imputed, there the attribute of love is directed. The believer becomes in time the object of God's eternal and infinite love.

5. Because the love of God as an attribute is perfect, it is totally devoid of human emotion. Emotion is a sustaining mechanism for imperfect beings. God's love requires no such sustaining. Tears, entreaty, and performance have no effect on the divine attribute of love. Doctrine resident in the soul, not emotional appeal, is the mechanism of blessing.

6. The anthropopathism of love in Romans 9:13 explains Jacob's salvation adjustment to the justice of God. The omniscience of God knew in eternity past that Jacob would believe in Christ. That fact was entered into the divine decrees, and the readout for Jacob is election, foreknowledge, predestination, and foreordination. The single phrase 'Jacob I loved' communicates that entire complex of doctrine in language accessible to all.

7. The anthropopathism of hate in Romans 9:13 explains Esau's maladjustment to the justice of God. The omniscience of God knew in eternity past that Esau would reject Christ. Esau's emotional, tearful response to the loss of the birthright was human repentance — a change of feeling — not adjustment to the justice of God. His printout from the divine decrees is condemnation and judgment, expressed in the phrase 'Esau I hated.'

8. Love as an anthropopathism explains divine motivation; it is never the direct source of divine blessing. Not since the fall of Adam has love been the point of reference for God's relationship to mankind. The direct source of blessing from God is divine justice — one half of divine integrity. Righteousness demands righteousness; justice demands justice; what righteousness demands, justice executes.

9. Justification is a function of divine justice, never a function of divine love. Because the point of reference is divine justice, God is genuinely impartial: the most unlovely and the most admirable member of the human race stand before the same standard. God found a way to bring sinful man into eternal relationship with Himself and to impute blessing without compromising any divine attribute, including love. Perfect God produces a perfect plan for imperfect persons.

10. The entire economy of grace is revealed in the integrity of God: God loves His own perfect righteousness with an infinite and perfect love. Righteousness demands righteousness; justice demands justice. What righteousness demands, justice executes. To explain this to finite, fallen persons, language of accommodation employs the anthropopathism of love — but divine justice is always and only the operative mechanism by which blessing flows from God to man.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
kathapher καθάπερ kathaphēr — just as, even as Comparative conjunction used to introduce an analogy or citation from Scripture. In Romans 9:13 it introduces the quotation from Malachi 1:2–3.
graphŋ γράφω graphŋ — to write; perfect: it stands written Used here in the perfect passive indicative (resultative perfect): the act of writing is complete and its results remain permanently in force. The dramatic perfect emphasizes the abiding authority of the inscripturated word.
ʾāhab̥ אהב ʾāhab̥ — to love (Hebrew, Qal perfect/participle) The primary Hebrew verb for love. In Malachi 1:2–3, the Qal perfect states the completed act of divine favor toward Jacob, and the Qal active participle indicates the continuing policy of that favor across generations. As quoted in Romans 9:13, this is an anthropopathism, not the divine attribute of love.
sānĕʾ שנא sānĕʾ — to hate (Hebrew, Qal perfect) The Hebrew verb for hatred. In Malachi 1:3 and Romans 9:13, it is used as an anthropopathism to describe divine policy of judgment and condemnation toward Esau, who rejected Christ. God does not hate in the sinful human sense; the term is language of accommodation.
anthropopathism ἄνθρωπος + πάθος anthrŋpos + pathos — human + soul-function A figure of speech that ascribes to God a human characteristic He does not actually possess, for the purpose of explaining divine policy in terms of human frame of reference. Language of accommodation. The major biblical anthropopathisms include love, hatred, anger, repentance, scorn, compassion, and long-suffering.
monogenēs μονογενής monogenēs — uniquely born, one of a kind Compound adjective: monos (only, alone) + genos (kind, class). Used in John 3:16 of the Son of God. More precisely rendered 'uniquely born' than 'only begotten,' pointing to the singular nature of the incarnation.
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — the righteousness/justice of God The central organizing concept of the Epistle to the Romans. The integrity of God consists of His perfect righteousness and His perfect justice. Righteousness demands righteousness; justice demands justice; what righteousness demands, justice executes. All divine blessing to mankind flows through divine justice, not through divine love as attribute.
Malʼākhī מלאכי Malʼākhī — my messenger The name of the prophet whose book supplies the quotation in Romans 9:13. The name is itself a title meaning 'my messenger' or 'messenger of the LORD.' Malachi 1:2–3 contains both the Qal perfect of ʾāhab̥ (love) and the Qal perfect of sānĕʾ (hate) applied to Jacob and Esau respectively.

Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Six

Romans 9:14 — Divine Decrees, Omniscience, and Human Volition: Jacob and Esau

Romans 9:14 “What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God's part? By no means!” (ESV)
Corrected translation: What therefore shall we say? Is there unrighteousness with God? Absolutely not!

Romans 9 continues Paul's sustained argument concerning the elective purpose of God in human history. Having established in the preceding verses that divine election operates through grace rather than works — citing God's word to Rebekah that 'the older will serve the younger' before the twins Jacob and Esau had done anything good or evil — Paul now anticipates the objection that such sovereign differentiation constitutes injustice on God's part. His response, grounded in the Old Testament quotation from Malachi 1:2–3, requires a careful analysis of the divine decrees, the relationship between omniscience and foreknowledge, and the reality of human volition operating freely within the framework of God's comprehensive plan.

I. Exegesis of Romans 9:13 — The Malachi Quotation

The phrase 'as it stands written' signals a formal Old Testament citation, drawn from Malachi 1:2–3. The grammatical structure of this citation in the Greek text rewards close attention.

The Direct Object Construction

The clause opens with an accusative singular definite article followed by the indeclinable proper noun Iakōb (Ἰακώβ). Because the definite article appears in the accusative case, Jacob functions as the direct object of the sentence, with God as the implied subject. The definite article here functions as a demonstrative pronoun — 'that Jacob' — calling special attention to the person and investing the statement with pointed particularity. Corrected translation: that Jacob.

The Verb agapaō — Love as Anthropopathism

The main verb is an aorist active indicative of agapaō (ἀγαπάω), rendered 'I loved.' The aorist tense here functions as a constative aorist, contemplating the action in its entirety and referring to a condition that has obtained over an extended span of time — from the moment Jacob believed in the Lord and received the imputation of divine righteousness. The divine righteousness and the divine justice together constitute the holiness or integrity of God. The justice of God imputed to Jacob at salvation the very righteousness of God; the love of God, which in eternity past always loved His own righteousness, now loves Jacob as the possessor of that righteousness. This is technically an anthropopathism — language of accommodation that describes divine policy in terms the finite human mind can grasp. God does not literally 'love' in the emotional sense of human experience; rather, 'love' here communicates divine approbation, which includes propitiation. The active voice indicates God as the source of the action. The indicative mood is declarative, presenting the reality of the anthropopathism. This verb translates the Qal active participle of the Hebrew ʾāhab (אָהַב), the verb for love in its continuous aspect.

The Adversative Particle de and the Esau Clause

The postpositive conjunctive particle de (δέ) functions here as an adversative conjunction, marking the contrast between the divine attitude toward Jacob and the divine attitude toward Esau. The direct object Esau (Ἠσαῦ) is positioned first for emphasis, highlighting the person and the contrast. The verb is an aorist active indicative of miseō (μισέω), a mental-attitude term denoting hatred. The constative aorist again contemplates the action in its entirety. Corrected translation: but I hated that Esau.

This 'hatred' is equally an anthropopathism. Hatred is a sin; God is perfect and cannot sin. The term communicates the divine policy of disapprobation toward the unbeliever — not an emotional attitude of malice, but the just outworking of divine policy toward one who remained throughout his life in a state of unbelief. The indicative mood is declarative, presenting the language of accommodation as a statement of divine reality expressed in finite terms.

The Contrast Between Jacob and Esau

Jacob and Esau were twins with identical genetic heritage, born within moments of each other. Both entered the world under the same condition of spiritual death inherited through the imputation of Adam's original sin. The difference between them is not biological, cultural, or moral in the conventional sense — it is soteriological. Esau remained throughout his life in a state of unbelief, never exercising saving faith. Jacob, born under the same condition, eventually believed in the Lord Jesus Christ and advanced from salvation to spiritual maturity. The distinction between them is the origin of the Jewish race: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are the founding line of Israel through regeneration. Esau, the unbeliever, represents the origin of the Gentile nations from his line.

II. The Divine Decrees and Human Volition — Doctrinal Framework

The Malachi quotation raises the question Paul addresses directly in verse 14: is there unrighteousness with God? The answer requires a thorough analysis of the relationship between the omniscience of God, the divine decrees, foreknowledge, and the freedom of human volition. The following doctrinal framework addresses these issues in sequence.

Omniscience, Foreknowledge, and the Computer of Divine Decrees

The omniscience of God is the faculty by which God knows all reality — actual and probable — simultaneously, without sequence, without acquisition, and without limitation. The omniscience of God never gains in knowledge. Foreknowledge, by contrast, is the printout of what omniscience has already known from eternity. Foreknowledge does not precede omniscience; it is merely the expression of it in relation to time and history.

The divine decrees are the eternal determinations of God with respect to all events in history. The omniscience of God fed only facts — not possibilities, not hypothetical outcomes — into the register of the divine decrees. Those facts include every act of every free will across all of human history. The omniscience of God knew that Esau would reject Christ and Jacob would believe in Christ. These facts, fed simultaneously into the divine decrees, produced for Jacob the decree of election, foreordination, and predestination, and for Esau the decree of reprobation, condemnation, and just retribution.

A critical error in much systematic theology is to place foreknowledge before or on a par with omniscience, or to allow foreknowledge to function as the source of the decrees. This confusion generates a cascade of theological errors that eventually distorts the entire framework of the Christian life. Foreknowledge does not make anything certain. It merely perceives what is certain — namely, that every human being possesses free will, and that free will will make a determinate number of decisions across the course of a lifetime. God knew those decisions from eternity; He did not cause them.

The Decrees Do Not Coerce Human Volition

The divine decrees determine the certain future of events but do not directly cause any event. Cause and effect in history is the interrelationship of innumerable acts of human volition operating freely within the structures of divine establishment and human authority. The decree itself provides, in every case, that the event shall be brought about by its own proper causes — causes acting in a manner consistent with the nature of the event in question. When God decreed that Jacob would believe and Esau would not, He did not coerce either man's will. He recorded, from eternity, the free decisions those men would freely make.

In the case of every free act of a moral agent — that is, a responsible person operating within the authority structures of divine establishment — the decree itself provides that the agent shall remain a free agent. All the antecedents of the act, all present conditions bearing on it, and the act itself shall be spontaneous and free on the part of the agent. No divine decree functions as a constraint on human self-determination.

Ends, Means, and the Comprehensiveness of the Decrees

God has decreed ends as well as means, and means as well as ends — causes as well as effects, conditions and instrumentalities as well as the events that depend on them. A human being has no free will choice with respect to his parentage, his genetic heritage, or his historical era. God knew from eternity who each person's parents and grandparents would be. But once a person enters the world, his own volition begins to function, and God knew from eternity the full course of that volition as well.

God's purpose relating to all events of every kind constitutes one single, all-comprehensive intention. This divine intention comprehends all events — the free operating as free, the necessary operating as necessary — together with all their causes, conditions, relations, and interdependencies as one indivisible system. Every link of the chain of history is essential to the whole.

The Certainty of the Decrees versus the Freedom of the Agent

The decrees do not oppose human freedom; they guarantee certainty. No decree causes human volition. Even as the foreknowledge of God does not cause human self-determination, neither do the decrees. The decrees have to do only with the certainty of the action — the fact that it will occur — not with the mechanism of its occurrence, which remains the free exercise of the human will. Human freedom exists in the sphere and on the plane of human experience. No human being ever acted outside of the divine decrees; to claim otherwise would be to deny the omniscience of God.

What God Causes and What God Permits

A further distinction is essential: between what God causes and what God permits. God does not decree men to sin. He decrees that man may have a free choice to sin. While God permits sin, He does not sponsor sin, endorse it, or approve it. The omniscience of God fed the fact of sin into the register of the divine decrees; sin is thus anticipated, provided for, and incorporated into the decrees — but God is not the author of sin. By the same token, God decreed that human good and evil would occur as results of human freedom operating under conditions of thought, decision, and action. None of these are actions God causes; all are actions God knows, permits, and has comprehensively incorporated into His plan.

Omniscience and the Atonement

The centrality of divine omniscience to the doctrine of salvation deserves particular emphasis. The entire provision of the atonement rests upon the omniscience of God. Every sin committed by every human being from Adam's original transgression to the last sin of history — including all sins committed after the cross — was known to the omniscience of God in eternity past. That omniscience fed every one of those sins into the register of the decrees, and they were collected and imputed to the Lord Jesus Christ on the cross, where the justice of the Father judged them all. Without the omniscience of God, the atonement as a provision for post-cross sins would be impossible. The gospel offer — 'believe in the Lord Jesus Christ and you will be saved' — is credible and complete precisely because every sin of every potential believer was already judged at the cross.

Jacob and Esau illustrate this with precision. Both committed sins across their lifetimes. All of those sins — whether we number them as more or fewer — were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged by the justice of God. The message to both was identical: believe in the Lord Jesus Christ and receive eternal life. Esau declined. Jacob believed. The quantitative difference in their respective sins was irrelevant to the offer or to its acceptance. What determined the outcome was volition — the free exercise of the human will with respect to the person and work of Jesus Christ.

The Origin of Israel and the Purpose of Divine Election

The line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob establishes the origin of the Jewish race through regeneration, not merely through physical descent. Jacob became the father of Israel not because of biological priority but because he believed in the Lord. The divine election of Israel as a nation had a defined purpose in the Protocol Plan of God: to provide a national entity that would receive and preserve divine revelation, serve as a missionary nation to the Gentile world, demonstrate the principles of divine establishment in national life, and provide the human lineage through which the Messiah would enter history.

This purpose was operative throughout the dispensation of Israel. With the ascension and session of Jesus Christ, the Church Age began, and the royal family of God — Church Age believers — became the new agency of God's purpose in history. Forty years after the Church Age commenced, Israel went out under the fifth cycle of discipline in 70 AD. From that point, Gentile nations became the potential client nations to God during what the New Testament identifies as the times of the Gentiles — the period extending from 70 AD until the Second Advent of Christ.

A client nation to God must provide a stable environment for the proclamation of the gospel, the advance of believers to spiritual maturity, and the protection of the Jewish people dispersed throughout the world. Anti-Semitism represents not merely a moral failure but a structural threat to any nation's standing as a client nation. The provision of safety and equal protection for the Jewish people within a host nation is a measurable index of that nation's alignment with the principles of divine establishment and its qualification to receive logistical grace at the national level.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Six

1. The omniscience of God fed only facts into the register of the divine decrees. God knows the actual and the probable simultaneously, but only the actual was recorded in the decrees. The actual established Esau as an unbeliever and Jacob as a believer. The omniscience of God never gains in knowledge; there was never a moment when these facts were not known.

2. The printout for Jacob was election, foreordination, and predestination. The printout for Esau was reprobation, condemnation, and just retribution. These different outcomes reflect the different free-will decisions of the two men, recorded by omniscience and decreed by God.

3. Both Jacob and Esau had the same free will and the same opportunity for salvation. Their identical genetic heritage, simultaneous birth, and shared historical setting meant that no external factor created inequality between them. The difference was entirely soteriological.

4. The sins of both Jacob and Esau were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged by the justice of God. The atonement was equally available to both. The offer of eternal life through faith in Christ was extended to both. The outcome was determined by volition alone.

5. It was the direct will of God that both Jacob and Esau be saved. The fact that only one was saved demonstrates that the direct will of God does not override or coerce human volition. God's antecedent will for universal salvation is not the same as His decretive will, which records the actual choices of free agents.

6. The fact that Jacob believed and Esau rejected Christ demonstrates the reality of human volition acting independently of the sovereignty of God. Divine sovereignty and human freedom are not in competition. They operate on different planes, and the divine decrees accommodate both simultaneously.

7. The divine decrees do not coerce or tamper with human volition. The decrees record what will happen in history before it happens. They do not cause it to happen. Cause and effect in history is the interrelationship of free volitions operating within the structures of divine establishment.

8. The divine decree of foreordination establishes certainty, not compulsion. Certainty with respect to the believer means that God's knowledge of the outcome is infallible, not that the agent's freedom was suspended.

9. God's decrees do not originate from His foreknowledge but from His omniscience. Foreknowledge and omniscience are both functions of God, but they are not equivalent. Omniscience feeds the facts; foreknowledge is the printout of what omniscience has always known. To place foreknowledge before or equal to omniscience produces a sequence of theological errors that eventually distorts the framework of the Christian life.

10. The foreknowledge of God makes nothing certain — it merely perceives what is certain. What is certain is that human beings possess free will, that their free will will produce a determinate sequence of decisions, and that God has known those decisions from eternity. He does not coerce them.

11. God's decrees determine only the certain future of events; they do not directly cause any event. The decrees do not function as a causal mechanism. Cause and effect in history is the interrelationship of volitions, not the operation of divine compulsion.

12. The decree itself provides that in every case an event shall be brought about by its own proper causes, acting in a manner consistent with the nature of the event. God's knowledge of the outcome does not alter the mechanism by which the outcome is produced. The mechanism remains the free exercise of human volition.

13. In the case of every free act of a moral agent, the decree provides that the agent shall remain free. All antecedents of the act, all present conditions, and the act itself are spontaneous and free on the part of the agent. The decree guarantees certainty without eliminating freedom.

14. God foreknows all events as certainly future because He has decreed them. Foreknowledge is not the basis of the decrees; it is the expression of what the decrees contain. The decrees themselves are grounded in the omniscience of God.

15. God's decrees relate equally to all future events of every kind. To the free actions of moral agents and to the actions of necessary agents. To sinful as well as honorable actions. No category of event lies outside the comprehensive scope of the divine decrees.

16. God has decreed ends as well as means, and means as well as ends. Causes as well as effects; conditions and instrumentalities as well as the events that depend on them. No human being had free will with respect to parentage or historical placement. But once placed in history, every act of volition is both free and foreknown.

17. God's purpose relating to all events constitutes one single, all-comprehensive intention. This intention comprehends all events — the free operating as free, the necessary as necessary — together with all their causes, conditions, and relations as one indivisible system. Every link of the chain of history is essential to the whole.

18. The decrees do not oppose human freedom — they guarantee certainty. The function of the divine decrees is to establish the certain future of events, not to eliminate the freedom of the agents who produce those events.

19. No decree opposes human freedom; decrees do not cause human volition. Even as the foreknowledge of God does not cause human self-determination, neither do the divine decrees. The agent remains self-determining within the sphere of human experience.

20. The decrees have to do only with the certainty of the action, not with its mechanism. They guarantee that the action will occur; they do not supply the energy or motivation by which it occurs. That energy and motivation come from the free agent operating within the conditions of his own existence.

21. Human freedom exists in the sphere and on the plane of human experience. The divine decrees exist on the plane of divine omniscience. These are not competing planes; they are complementary dimensions of the one divine plan.

22. No human being ever acted outside of the divine decrees. To assert that any human act could fall outside the divine decrees would be to deny the omniscience of God. Every decision, every volition, every act of acceptance or rejection is comprehended within the decrees.

23. God does not decree men to sin, but He decrees that man may have free choice to sin. God permits sin without sponsoring it, endorsing it, or approving it. Sin is a reality anticipated by divine omniscience, provided for in the decrees, and judged at the cross — but God is never its author.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
agapaō ἀγαπάω agapaō — to love; divine love or approbation Verb used in Romans 9:13 of God's love for Jacob. In this context an anthropopathism — language of accommodation expressing divine approbation toward the believer who possesses imputed divine righteousness. Aorist constative contemplates the action in its entirety.
miseō μισέω miseō — to hate; mental-attitude antagonism Verb used in Romans 9:13 of God's attitude toward Esau. An anthropopathism communicating the divine policy of disapprobation toward the unbeliever — not an emotional malice but a just outworking of divine holiness against persistent rejection of salvation.
anthropopathism ἀνθρωποπάθεια anthrōpopatheia — attribution of human emotions to God A figure of speech in which human emotions or attitudes are ascribed to God for the purpose of communicating divine policy in terms comprehensible to finite human minds. God does not actually experience emotion in the human sense; anthropopathisms describe divine policy, not divine psychology.
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The perfect righteousness that constitutes one pole of the divine integrity (holiness), the other being the justice of God. At salvation, the justice of God imputes divine righteousness to the believer. The love of God, which always loved its own righteousness, now loves the believer as the possessor of that righteousness.
omniscience The divine attribute by which God knows all reality — actual and probable — simultaneously, without sequence or acquisition. The omniscience of God feeds all historical facts, including every act of every free will, into the register of the divine decrees. It never gains in knowledge and is never surprised by any event.
foreknowledge πρόγνωσις prognōsis — foreknowledge, prior knowing The expression of divine omniscience in relation to time and history. Foreknowledge is the printout of what omniscience has always known; it is not the source of the divine decrees and does not cause any event. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain; it perceives what is already certain by virtue of the divine decrees grounded in omniscience.
divine decrees The eternal determinations of God with respect to all events in history. The decrees record only facts fed into them by divine omniscience. They establish the certain future of events without causing those events or coercing the volitions that produce them. Every link of the chain of history — free and necessary, sinful and honorable — is comprehended within the one indivisible system of the divine decrees.
election / predestination ἐκλογή / προορισμός eklogē / proorismos — election / foreordination Election is God's eternal choice of believers for blessing, based on His foreknowledge of their faith. Predestination is the determination of the destiny of those chosen — conformity to Christ and all the blessings of that status. Both are grounded in the omniscience of God and the divine decrees, not in the suppression of human volition.
reprobation The judicial determination of God with respect to the persistent unbeliever. Not an arbitrary exclusion but the just consequence of the free decision to reject salvation. Esau's reprobation was the divine decree recording his free refusal of faith in Christ.
constative aorist A use of the Greek aorist tense in which the action of the verb is contemplated in its entirety without regard to its internal development or duration. Used in Romans 9:13 of both agapaō and miseō to express the comprehensive divine attitude toward Jacob and Esau respectively.
client nation A national entity qualified by the presence of a believing pivot, functioning freedom, and alignment with the principles of divine establishment, to serve as an instrument of divine purpose in a given dispensation — providing for evangelism, spiritual growth, missionary activity, and the protection of the Jewish people.
fifth cycle of discipline The terminal stage of national divine discipline described in Leviticus 26:27–33, involving military conquest, destruction of the capital, and dispersion of the population. Applied to Israel in 70 AD with the Roman destruction of Jerusalem under Titus, ending the function of Israel as a client nation to God for the duration of the times of the Gentiles.
times of the Gentiles The period from the fall of Jerusalem in 70 AD until the Second Advent of Christ, during which no Jewish nation is or can be a client nation to God. During this period, Gentile nations serve as the potential client nations through which the Protocol Plan of God operates in history.

Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Seven

Romans 9:14 — Adikia, Anthropopathisms, and the Justice of God

Romans 9:14 “What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God's part? By no means!” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Therefore to what conclusion are we forced? There is no injustice with God, is there? Emphatically no.

Paul has established that God loved Jacob and hated Esau before either had done good or evil — a statement drawn from Malachi 1:2–3 and grounded in the divine decrees. That statement now draws the inevitable objection: if God distributes blessing and judgment on such grounds, is He not arbitrary? Is there injustice with God? Romans 9:14 introduces this objection in the form of a debater's rhetorical question, and this chapter works through the exegesis of that verse together with the doctrinal principles that resolve it — principles concerning the divine decrees, the nature of anthropopathisms, and the justice of God as the sole pipeline of blessing and condemnation.

I. The Divine Decrees and the Content of Divine Omniscience

Before any creature existed, the triune God — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — existed alone in eternity past.
