Chapter Five Hundred Ninety-Three

Romans 9:17 — Exodus 9:16 Quoted: God's Preservation of Pharaoh and the Worldwide Purpose of Negative Volition

Romans 9:17 “For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, 'For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, 'For this very purpose I have caused you to continue in history, in order that I might demonstrate my power through you, and in order that my name might be celebrated in all the earth.'

Romans 9:17 continues Paul's extended quotation from Exodus 9:16, applied to the hardening of Pharaoh Amenhotep II in 1441 BC. The verse stands at the center of Paul's argument that the justice of God is neither arbitrary nor capricious: divine blessing flows to Moses through maturity adjustment, while Pharaoh's sustained negative volition is itself taken up into the plan of God and made to serve worldwide evangelism. This chapter completes the exegesis of the opening clause of Romans 9:17 — the quotation formula and the verb of divine preservation — and draws out the doctrinal principles latent in that clause.

I. Review: The Thirty-Point Doctrine of the Hardening of Pharaoh's Heart

The following summary consolidates the analysis developed across the preceding sessions. It is provided here as a structured reference because its application to subsequent verses in Romans 9 — and to the believer's response to national and personal crisis — depends on command of the whole argument.

1. It was not until the sixth plague that Pharaoh hardened his own heart through negative self-determination. Pharaoh was a free agent with enormous authority, and he exercised that authority in sustained rejection of the divine command.

2. At that point God hardened Pharaoh's right lobe — not by mechanically altering his volition, but by keeping him alive and granting him greater opportunity to express negative volition than any human being had previously received.

3. The 'heart' in this context is the right lobe of the soul — the thinking, evaluating, deciding center of the human person. The hardening of Pharaoh's heart is the hardening of his right lobe through accumulated scar tissue produced by repeated acts of negative volition.

4. The doctrine of scar tissue of the soul, developed within the broader doctrine of reversionism, is the key to understanding the hardening process. Each 'no' to God added scar tissue to the right lobe, which in turn strengthened the capacity for the next refusal.

5. The hardening of Pharaoh Amenhotep II's right lobe in 1441 BC was the means by which God evangelized not only Egypt but the entire world of that generation.

6. This is illustrated by Rahab the prostitute, who was saved forty-five years later through knowledge of the very events surrounding the hardening of Pharaoh's heart (Joshua 2:10–11). The evangelistic ripple extended across decades and nations.

7. The justice of God gave Pharaoh numerous opportunities to believe in Jehovah Elohim — Jesus Christ — before and throughout the plague sequence.

8. Pharaoh witnessed repeated demonstrations of divine power specifically designed to evangelize him, yet refused consistently, as the pattern of Exodus 7:13 records: 'Yet Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them.'

9. When Christ was crucified, Pharaoh's sins were imputed to Him and judged. Christ died for Pharaoh's sins. The barrier to Pharaoh's salvation was never on God's side.

10. God was not willing that Pharaoh should perish (2 Peter 3:9). This was the will of God. Pharaoh overruled it by his own negative volition.

11. Pharaoh had multiple opportunities for positive volition at God-consciousness and at gospel hearing, as illustrated in Exodus 7:22; 8:15; 8:32; 9:34–35.

12. With each refusal, Pharaoh's free will added further scar tissue to his soul, which in turn provided him more volitional momentum to refuse the next time.

13. As Pharaoh's scar tissue deepened, God intensified the manifestations of divine power, so that while Pharaoh was saying no, large segments of his kingdom were saying yes. The world was being evangelized through the escalating confrontation.

14. The divine hardening of Pharaoh's right lobe, beginning in Exodus 9:12, is the context in which plagues seven through ten must be interpreted.

15. Pharaoh's unbeliever reversionism had resulted in scar tissue of the soul and maximum maladjustment to the justice of God.

16. Beginning at Exodus 9:12, the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart — that is, He removed restraint from the expression of Pharaoh's already-entrenched negative volition.

17. The justice of God gave Pharaoh maximum opportunity to express that negative volition by keeping him alive and exposing him to plagues seven, eight, nine, and ten.

18. This divine act is recorded under the heading 'the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart' in Exodus 9:12; 10:1; 10:20; 10:27; 11:10; 14:8.

19. God hardened Pharaoh's heart by granting Amenhotep II more opportunities to say no than any human being had previously been permitted — and this is a correct, just function of divine omniscience and sovereignty.

20. God preserved Amenhotep II, alive and in great human power, to demonstrate that divine power is infinitely greater than the greatest human authority.

21. By keeping Pharaoh alive to multiply his refusals, God impressed upon the entire world the greatness of His power: both to condemn one of the most powerful men of that age and to save the believer in Jehovah Elohim.

22. The hardening of Pharaoh's right lobe — the extension and expression of his accumulated scar tissue — was the means by which God evangelized the world for two generations.

23. While others were being impressed by the power of God, Pharaoh was being impressed by his own will. Each expression of his arrogance revealed to the watching world the omnipotence of the God he refused.

24. In Egypt, Egyptians, Ethiopians, and Jews responded in faith. When Israel departed, a mixed multitude departed with them — those who had believed in Jehovah Elohim through the evangelistic pressure of the plague sequence.

25. Pharaoh therefore fulfills the pattern described in Romans 2:5: 'But because of your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up and accumulate wrath for yourself against the day of wrath, even the manifestation of the just judgment from the justice of God.'

26. It was not until the sixth plague that God hardened Pharaoh's right lobe by removing all restraint from the expression of his negative volition.

27. Even after the hardening, Pharaoh retained opportunity for repentance — a change of mind toward Christ — as illustrated in Exodus 9:27; 10:16–17.

28. The divine purpose in the hardening of Pharaoh's right lobe is stated in Exodus 7:3–5: the evangelization of Egypt.

29. A second divine purpose is revealed in Exodus 9:16: the evangelization of the entire world.

30. This second purpose is reiterated in Paul's quotation of Exodus 9:16 in Romans 9:17, which opens with the formula: 'For the Scripture says to Pharaoh' — and then states the purpose directly.

II. Exegesis of Romans 9:17a — The Quotation Formula and the Verb of Preservation

A. The Quotation Conjunction

Paul introduces the Exodus quotation with the conjunction hoti (ὅτι). This particle most commonly introduces a purpose or result clause, but here it functions as a quotation marker — the Greek equivalent of an opening quotation mark. In this usage it need not be translated, or may be rendered simply as 'quote.' The quotation that follows is from Exodus 9:16.

B. The Purpose Phrase

Before the verb, Paul includes a short prepositional purpose phrase: eis auto touto (εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο). The preposition eis (εἰς) with the accusative is used here to express a brief purpose clause. The neuter singular accusative auto (αὐτό) derives from the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός) in its attributive function — a relatively rare usage — where it carries the force of 'same' rather than the ordinary third-person personal pronoun. Combined with the immediate demonstrative pronoun touto (τοῦτο), the phrase reads: 'for this same purpose' or 'for this very purpose.' The phrase establishes that what follows is not incidental but the direct declaration of divine intentionality.

C. The Verb: exegeirō

The central verb is the aorist active indicative of exegeirō (ἐξεγείρω). In classical Attic Greek this verb meant 'to raise up' or 'to bring into being.' In Koine usage, it bears the more specific sense of causing someone to appear in history or calling a person into continued existence within the historical framework. The correct translation here is therefore: 'I have caused you to continue in history,' not the softer 'I have raised you up' of many English versions.

The aorist tense is culminative: it views the entire historical existence of Amenhotep II as a completed whole, but regards it from the standpoint of its existing results — namely, the glorification of God accomplished through and despite Pharaoh's deceitfulness, arrogance, and sustained refusal of divine commands. The active voice indicates that Jesus Christ produces the action of the verb: it is the sovereign preservation of God that kept Pharaoh in power. The indicative mood is declarative, asserting this as historical reality. The direct object is the second-person singular accusative pronoun se (σέ): 'you' — Pharaoh, addressed personally through the word of God delivered by Moses.

III. The Theological Import of Divine Preservation

A. God's Preservation as an Act of Justice, Not Favoritism

The statement 'I have caused you to continue in history' carries a double force. For Pharaoh, it was an affront to his arrogance: the acknowledgment that his continued existence and authority rested not on his own power but on divine permission. For the reader of Romans, it is a declaration of the justice of God: Pharaoh was not destroyed arbitrarily, nor was he manipulated against his will. He was preserved — given more opportunity than any person in that generation to respond to the revelation of God.

This stands as the answer to the allegation that God acted unjustly toward Pharaoh. The justice of God gave Pharaoh extra time, extended the record, multiplied the demonstrations of divine power. Pharaoh used every additional opportunity to reinforce his negative self-determination. The outcome was not divine injustice but the maximally just expression of the consequences of sustained negative volition.

B. The Principle of Psalm 76:10

Psalm 76:10 states: 'The wrath of man shall praise You' — more literally, 'the wraths of man shall praise You' (plural). This principle underlies the entire Pharaoh narrative. God uses the tyranny of man to demonstrate His power and to advance the evangelization of the human race. Pharaoh's rejection of Christ and his subsequent lack of integrity were not obstacles to the plan of God; they were incorporated into that plan and made to serve it. The arrogance of a great dictator became the instrument by which the omnipotence of God was displayed before the watching world.

C. Arrogance, Pettiness, and the Mechanism of Self-Destruction

Pharaoh's fundamental problem was arrogance expressed as pettiness — the inability to tolerate the exaltation of another, particularly the God of a slave people. When the plagues declared the supremacy of Jehovah Elohim over the gods of Egypt, Pharaoh's response was not inquiry but intensified resistance. Each plague that demonstrated divine power was an affront to his sense of sovereign prerogative, and each affront drove him deeper into scar tissue of the soul.

This pattern — greatness of authority combined with pettiness of character producing self-destruction — is a recurring feature of human history. The capacity to acknowledge and appreciate the achievement of others, including the power of God, is one mark of genuine greatness. The inability to do so, expressed in jealousy, vindictiveness, and implacability, destroys the very authority and influence it seeks to protect. Pharaoh, ruler of one of the greatest empires in history, was reduced to the instrument of his own people's liberation by the petty arrogance with which he wielded absolute power.

D. The Deceitfulness of Pharaoh and the Stability of the Believer

Amenhotep II was a man of no integrity. He would agree to release Israel under the pressure of each plague, then countermand the order once the pressure subsided. He was, in the plainest sense, a liar and a promise-breaker. The Scripture does not soften this. The historical record of his repeated reversals is the record of a man whose word meant nothing.

The personal application for the believer is direct. Deceitful people are a constant feature of human experience. The capacity to deal with betrayal, broken trust, and deliberate malice — without vengeance, without counter-attack, without the attempt to vindicate oneself by exposing the offender — is a function of doctrine in the soul. The royal family honor code governs the believer's response: leave vengeance to the Lord (Romans 12:19), maintain composure, and refuse to join the cycle of retaliation. This is not weakness; it is the operational expression of maturity adjustment.

Moses encountered in Pharaoh one of the most consistently deceitful men of his generation. Yet Moses did not function on the basis of personal offense. He operated on the basis of divine commission. The doctrine in his soul gave him the capacity to deal with a pathologically deceitful adversary without losing his own integrity.

E. The Plan of God Cannot Be Frustrated by Negative Volition

A recurring temptation, particularly for the believer who has failed, is the assumption that personal failure frustrates the plan of God. Pharaoh operated on the opposite version of this error: he assumed that his sustained refusal could prevent the plan of God from moving forward. Both errors rest on the same false premise — that human volition, whether negative or positive, can determine the outcome of God's eternal purpose.

The plan of God is not contingent on human cooperation. It incorporates human volition — positive and negative — but is not limited by it. When a believer fails, the plan of God continues. When a tyrant says no, the plan of God continues, and the refusal itself is taken up into the plan as the means of accomplishing something that a compliant response could not have achieved. God could have replaced Pharaoh with a sympathetic ruler who immediately released Israel. But that sympathetic ruler would not have produced the worldwide evangelistic impact that Amenhotep II's intransigence generated.

F. The Omnipotence of God over Human Power and Tyranny

The divine omnipotence demonstrated through the Pharaoh narrative is absolute. There is no concentration of evil — no political tyranny, no ideological system, no military force — that exceeds or even approaches the power of God. First John 4:4 states the principle concisely: 'Greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.' God is not in competition with human power. He preserves human power, uses it, and overrules it without exertion. The preservation of Pharaoh to say no four additional times after the sixth plague was not a near thing for God. It was a deliberate, sovereignly administered extension of grace toward a man who refused it, deployed in such a way that the entire ancient world was exposed to the gospel.

G. Supralapsarianism Rejected

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart does not support supralapsarian double predestination. God did not create evil in Pharaoh. Pharaoh, from his own free will and self-determination, became what he was. God recognized Pharaoh's negative volition in the decrees of divine omniscience — omniscience feeds only actuality, not probability, into the decree — but He did not originate it. Pharaoh rejected divine restraint and resisted doctrine on the basis of his own volitional choices. While God did not make Pharaoh evil, He used Pharaoh's self-made evil to further His own plan. The integrity of God remains the issue throughout: the righteousness of God cannot do wrong, and the justice of God cannot be unfair.

IV. Partial Translation of Romans 9:17

On the basis of the exegesis above, the clause examined in this chapter translates as follows:

Romans 9:17 (partial) “For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, 'For this very purpose I have raised you up...'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For the Scripture says to Pharaoh — quote — 'For this very purpose I have caused you to continue in history...'

The remaining clauses of Romans 9:17 — the statement of divine purpose and the declaration that God's name be celebrated throughout the earth — will be taken up in the following chapter.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Ninety-Three

1. Divine preservation is an act of justice, not favoritism. God did not give Pharaoh less opportunity than any other person; He gave him more. The extension of Pharaoh's life and authority through plagues seven through ten was the justice of God operating at maximum generosity toward a man whose volitional pattern was one of sustained refusal.

2. The verb exegeirō (ἐξεγείρω) corrects a common mistranslation. The Koine sense of the verb is not merely 'to raise up' but 'to cause to appear in history' or 'to preserve in continued existence.' The correct translation — 'I have caused you to continue in history' — makes clear that the issue is God's ongoing preservation of Pharaoh, not some initial act of elevation.

3. The plan of God cannot be frustrated by negative volition. Pharaoh assumed his refusals were hindering the divine purpose. They were in fact serving it. Each 'no' intensified the manifestation of divine power and extended the reach of the evangelistic witness to the surrounding nations.

4. Scar tissue of the soul is the mechanism by which negative volition becomes self-reinforcing. Each refusal added scar tissue to Pharaoh's right lobe, which in turn supplied greater volitional momentum for the next refusal. This is the inner dynamic behind the hardening — not divine manipulation but the compounding consequences of the soul's own choices.

5. God hardened Pharaoh's heart by removing restraint, not by mechanical coercion. The hardening consisted in permitting Pharaoh to express his own negative volition without the degree of divine restraint normally operative in history. This is a correct and just act of divine omniscience and sovereignty.

6. The wrath of man praises God (Psalm 76:10). Arrogance directed against the plan of God ultimately becomes the instrument by which that plan is advanced. Pharaoh's sustained resistance to the release of Israel produced the worldwide evangelistic impact that a cooperative response never could have achieved.

7. Arrogance combined with great authority produces pettiness and self-destruction. Authority without the capacity to appreciate and acknowledge the achievements of others — including the power of God — becomes the engine of its own undoing. Pharaoh's inability to tolerate the exaltation of Jehovah Elohim drove him through ten plagues to the destruction of his army in the Red Sea.

8. The believer's response to deceitful people is governed by the royal family honor code. Vengeance belongs to God (Romans 12:19). The response to betrayal, malice, and broken trust is composure, silence toward the offender, and confidence that the justice of God will address the matter. Counter-attack, gossip, and self-vindication are all violations of the honor code and expressions of reversionism.

9. God's omnipotence is infinitely greater than any human power or concentration of evil. No political authority, ideological system, or military force can compete with the power of God. First John 4:4 states the principle: 'Greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.' The Pharaoh narrative is the Old Testament demonstration of this principle on the largest available stage.

10. Supralapsarian double predestination is excluded by the text. God recognized Pharaoh's negative volition in the decrees of omniscience; He did not create it. Pharaoh's evil was self-generated through his own free will. The integrity of God — the righteousness that cannot do wrong and the justice that cannot be unfair — remains the theological ground of the entire argument in Romans 9.

11. Blessing at maturity adjustment contrasts with maladjustment at the unbeliever level. Moses received imputed blessing in the field of superabundance (the Z-radical) through maximum doctrine in the soul and maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Pharaoh, as an unbeliever reversionist operating in the X-radical, used his great power and lack of integrity to perpetuate tyranny. The contrast of the two men in Romans 9 is the contrast between the two possible outcomes of divine justice operating on human volition.

12. The mixed multitude that departed Egypt with Israel was the fruit of the plague sequence. As Pharaoh intensified his refusals and God intensified the demonstrations of power, Egyptians, Ethiopians, and other peoples reached positive volition toward Jehovah Elohim. When Israel departed, these believers departed with them. The hardening of Pharaoh's right lobe was, paradoxically, the means of their salvation.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
exegeirō ἐξεγείρω exegeirō — to cause to appear in history, to preserve in continued existence Compound verb: ex (out, forth) + egeirō (to raise, to arouse). In classical Attic Greek: to raise up, to bring into being. In Koine: to cause to appear or continue in history. The aorist active indicative in Romans 9:17 is culminative, viewing Pharaoh's entire historical existence as a completed whole whose existing result is the glorification of God.
hoti ὅτι hoti — that; quotation marker Conjunction with multiple functions in Greek. Most commonly introduces a content clause ("that") or a causal clause ("because"). In Romans 9:17 it functions as a quotation marker — equivalent to an opening quotation mark — and need not be translated independently.
eis auto touto εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο eis auto touto — for this very purpose, for this same purpose Prepositional purpose phrase. The preposition eis with the accusative expresses purpose. Autos in its attributive (intensive) use means "same"; combined with the immediate demonstrative touto, the phrase asserts that what follows is the direct and specific intention of the divine act described.
autos (attributive use) αὐτός autos — same (attributive/intensive use) The pronoun autos normally functions as the third-person personal pronoun (he, she, it, him, her) or as an intensive pronoun. In the attributive position — a relatively rare usage — it carries the sense of "same." In Romans 9:17 it modifies the demonstrative touto to produce the phrase "this very/same purpose."
scar tissue of the soul Accumulated hardness in the right lobe of the soul produced by sustained negative volition toward divine revelation. Each refusal of God's word or command adds scar tissue, which in turn increases the capacity and momentum for subsequent refusals. In Pharaoh's case, scar tissue of the soul is the inner mechanism behind the externally described "hardening of the heart."
maladjustment to the justice of God The condition of the unbeliever or carnal believer who has not made the required adjustment — salvation adjustment or rebound — that satisfies divine justice and opens the channel for divine blessing. Pharaoh represents maximum maladjustment: sustained refusal of the salvation adjustment across repeated opportunities, compounded by reversionist living.
maturity adjustment The third and progressive category of adjustment to the justice of God, achieved through daily intake of Bible doctrine over time via the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). Maturity adjustment brings the believer through the maturity barrier and into the stages of supergrace and ultra-supergrace, where imputed blessings are received in the field of superabundance.
supralapsarianism A predestinarian theological position holding that God's decree of election and reprobation logically precedes and causes the fall. In its extreme form it implies that God creates some human beings specifically for damnation. The exegesis of Romans 9:17 rejects this position: God recognized Pharaoh's negative volition in omniscience but did not originate or cause it. Pharaoh's evil was self-generated through free will.
royal family honor code The operational standard governing the conduct of Church Age believers as members of the royal family of God. Key provisions include: no vengeance (Romans 12:19), no counter-attack, no self-vindication through exposure of the offender, composure under pressure, and confidence in the justice of God to address all injustice in His time and manner.

Chapter Five Hundred Ninety-Four

Romans 9:17 — Concluding Exegesis: Divine Purpose, Worldwide Evangelism, and Adjustment to the Justice of God

Romans 9:17 “For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, 'For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: I have caused you to continue in history in order that I might demonstrate my power by means of you, and in order that my person might be proclaimed throughout the entire earth.

Romans 9:17 continues the Apostle Paul's sustained argument, begun in verse 6, that the word of God has not failed with respect to Israel. Having established in the preceding verses the sovereign differentiation between Jacob and Esau, and between Isaac and Ishmael, Paul now turns to the paradigmatic case of Pharaoh — Amenhotep II of the Eighteenth Dynasty — as the supreme Old Testament illustration of negative volition operating within, rather than against, the plan of God. This chapter completes the exegesis of verse 17, working through the Greek purpose clause, the historical background, and the systematic doctrinal implications that Paul draws from the exodus narrative.

I. The Purpose Clause: Greek Exegesis

The corrected translation established in prior sessions reads: 'For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: I have caused you to continue in history.' The verse now introduces a purpose clause that specifies two divine objectives behind Pharaoh's preservation in history.

A. The Conjunction and the Subjunctive Formation

The purpose clause opens with the conjunction hopōs (ὅπως), used to introduce a final clause denoting aim or objective, correctly translated 'that' or 'in order that.' Paired with the subjunctive mood, hopōs marks the construction as a divine purpose clause throughout.

B. First Purpose: The Demonstration of Divine Power

The first verb is the aorist middle subjunctive of endeiknymi (ἐνδείκνυμι), meaning to show, to manifest, to demonstrate. The aorist here is a culminative aorist — it views the demonstration of God's power across all ten confrontations in their entirety, but regards them from the standpoint of their existing results: worldwide evangelism. The middle voice is the indirect middle, emphasizing God as the agent producing the action in a uniquely personal way. The subjunctive mood expresses the potential future reference inherent in the purpose clause.

The phrase rendered 'by means of you' uses the preposition en (ἐν) plus the instrumental dative of the personal pronoun sy (σύ), meaning by means of you. The direct object is the accusative singular of dynamis (δύναμις), power, modified by the possessive genitive of egō (ἐγώ): my power. The corrected translation of this clause reads: in order that I might demonstrate my power by means of you.

C. Second Purpose: Universal Proclamation of the Divine Person

The second purpose clause is introduced by the connective conjunction kai (καί) followed by the repetition of hopōs with the subjunctive, continuing the purpose structure. The subject is the nominative singular of onoma (ὄνομα), which carries the semantic range of name, person, reputation, and fame, with the possessive genitive of egō: my name, my person, my reputation.

The verb is the aorist passive subjunctive of diaggellō (διαγγέλλω), meaning to proclaim far and wide, to announce throughout. The constative aorist contemplates the action of worldwide proclamation in its entirety. The passive voice indicates that the person of Christ — revealed as Jehovah Elohim in the exodus narrative — receives the action of proclamation. The subjunctive mood again forms the purpose clause. Corrected translation: and in order that my person might be proclaimed throughout the entire earth.

D. Complete Corrected Translation of Romans 9:17

For the Scripture says to Pharaoh — quotation from Exodus 9:16 — I have caused you to continue in history in order that I might demonstrate my power by means of you, and in order that my person might be proclaimed throughout the entire earth.

II. Historical Background: Amenhotep II and the Eighteenth Dynasty

The Pharaoh of the Exodus is identified with Amenhotep II, son of Thutmose III, the greatest ruler of the Eighteenth Dynasty and widely regarded as the greatest military Pharaoh in all of Egyptian history. The historical and dynastic context clarifies both the magnitude of Pharaoh's authority and the nature of the confrontation with Moses.

A. The Dynasty and the Palace

Thutmose III was the dominant figure of the Eighteenth Dynasty, ascending through a complex dynastic situation involving Hatshepsut, who served as co-regent and queen. Hatshepsut is the princess who discovered and adopted Moses, calling him the prince out of the water. Her legitimate daughter, Meritre, was the royal heiress. Thutmose III had a secondary son, who would become Amenhotep II. In the palace dynamic, Moses, Thutmose III, and Meritre grew up together. Moses was the step-nephew in the line of adoption, making Amenhotep II — whom Moses confronted in the ten plagues — his nephew by the same reckoning.

Moses was renowned as a multi-gifted figure: a military genius who drove an Ethiopian invasion back to the fourth cataract, an administrative architect of Egyptian governance, a builder of treasure cities, and a musician of distinction. When Moses, in sustained occupation with the invisible God, voluntarily relinquished his position and stepped away from the Egyptian court, he left behind a throne he could have occupied. Thutmose III filled that vacuum by marrying Meritre and consolidating his own reign — a reign that became the greatest in Egyptian history, though it pales in comparison to what Moses accomplished both before and after the exodus.

B. The Character of Amenhotep II

Amenhotep II was characterized by jealousy — of his own father Thutmose III, and particularly of Moses. His arrogance, vindictiveness, instability, pettiness, and deceptive character are woven throughout the exodus narrative. He was also the first Pharaoh to introduce the worship of the Syrian storm god Resheph into Egypt — the religious innovation that would eventually contribute to the dissolution of the Eighteenth Dynasty and the rise of the Nineteenth. The seventh plague, the plague of hail, was a direct confrontation with Resheph, demonstrating that the deity Amenhotep II had chosen to follow was entirely powerless before the God of Israel.

C. The Death of the Firstborn and Secular Attestation

The Cambridge Ancient History, Vol. II, Part 1, page 321, notes concerning Thutmose IV — the son who succeeded Amenhotep II — that he was apparently not his father's heir apparent, but had obtained the throne through what the historians describe as 'an unforeseen turn of fate, such as the premature death of his eldest brother.' This secular attestation, developed independently of the biblical text through archaeological and philological analysis, corroborates the biblical account of the tenth plague: the death of the firstborn. Amenhotep II's heir did not survive to succeed him. His second son, Thutmose IV, inherited instead — a circumstance the Egyptian historical record itself acknowledges as anomalous.

III. The Mechanics of the Hardening of Pharaoh's Heart

The phrase 'God hardened Pharaoh's heart' has been examined at length in prior sessions. The mechanics are summarized here as they bear directly on the exegesis of verse 17.

Through the first six confrontations, the text consistently records that Pharaoh hardened his own heart. Pharaoh's pattern was a cycle of resistance: an initial no, a coerced yes under pressure, followed immediately by a return to no once the pressure was removed. His yes meant no. Beginning with the seventh confrontation — Exodus 9:12 and 9:16 — the text reads that God hardened Pharaoh's heart. This does not mean God created an evil disposition in Pharaoh. It means God removed all restraint on Pharaoh's already-entrenched negative volition and kept him alive, permitting him to continue exercising that volition in confrontations seven through ten. Pharaoh from plague seven onward was operating on borrowed time. He held, in effect, a world record for saying no to God under the greatest possible clarity of divine power.

The parallel with Romans 1:24–28 is exact: just as God turned the Gentile world over to their vile affections and reprobate minds, so God turned Pharaoh over to his own maximum negative volition. In neither case is God the author of the evil. In both cases, God permits the free operation of negative volition to serve the larger purposes of His plan.

Exodus 9:20 provides a significant datum before the onset of the seventh plague: 'The one among the servants of Pharaoh who feared the word of the Lord made his servants and his livestock flee into the houses.' An administrator in Pharaoh's own cabinet had already become a believer. The word rendered fear here carries the sense of respect produced from faith. The evangelization of Egypt was already producing results within the court itself.

IV. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:17

A. Divine Power Revealed Through Opposition

God used Pharaoh's negative volition and arrogant resistance as the occasion for demonstrating His omnipotence. The more Pharaoh resisted, the greater the manifestation of divine power became. Each confrontation escalated the visibility of God's power until the death of the firstborn made the sovereignty of the God of Israel unmistakable across the empire and beyond. Pharaoh in his opposition to God became a monument to the power of God.

The empirical character of the ten plagues is significant. Empiricism cannot see God, but empiricism can register the power of God when it acts within the observable world. Each confrontation was constructed around the deceitfulness, vacillation, instability, and lack of honor in Amenhotep II — qualities that made the contrast between human power at its greatest and divine power at even a measured expression unmistakably clear.

B. Negative Volition Does Not Hinder the Plan of God

Pharaoh's resistance did not frustrate the plan of God. It fulfilled it. His sustained no accelerated the evangelization of Egypt and the entire ancient world. As Psalm 76:10 states, the wrath of man shall praise God. Pharaoh's deceptive character and maximum negative volition served as the vehicle through which the person of Christ was proclaimed throughout the earth. The plan of God cannot be stopped by any act of human or satanic resistance. It does not depend on the cooperation of creatures for its execution.

C. Human Freedom Preserved Within Divine Sovereignty

God's use of Pharaoh's negative volition did not deprive Pharaoh of his freedom. Pharaoh had maximum freedom: absolute political authority as the sovereign of the Eighteenth Dynasty, complete privacy, extensive property, and no external divine coercion on his will. God did not create his negative disposition. God permitted it, sustained his life beyond what Pharaoh had any right to expect, and used the exercise of Pharaoh's free volition as the means of worldwide evangelism. Man is not robbed of self-determination by the omnipotence of God; he is actually provided with greater historical opportunity to express non-meritorious free will.

D. God Permits the Worst So That the Best Can Come From It

The parallel with the fall of Adam is instructive. God did not sponsor Adam's sin, but He permitted it in order that He might present to the world the Redeemer through the work of Christ on the cross. Similarly, God permitted the free operation of Pharaoh's maximum negative volition in order that an entire generation of Egypt, Israel, Ethiopia, and Canaan might receive the gospel and have the opportunity to believe. The plan of God moves forward in periods of historical disaster and historical prosperity alike. Neither negative volition at the individual level nor catastrophic historical events can deflect its course.

The theologian Forbes stated it clearly: all good originates from God, all evil originates from the creature. Election originates in the free grace of God; reprobation originates in the free will of man. To God belongs the whole glory of the salvation of the elect; to God belongs no part of the responsibility for the ruin of the reprobate. The entire glory of eternal salvation belongs to the person, the plan, and the grace of God.

E. No Predestination of Sin, Human Good, or Evil

The omniscience of God knew in eternity past every sin, every act of human good, and every expression of evil that would occur in history. This knowledge was fed into the divine decrees as actuality. But the printouts of the divine decrees — election, foreknowledge, predestination, justification — apply to believers only. Sin, human good, and evil are never objects of predestination or foreordination. The unbeliever is not predestined to the eternal lake of fire; he arrives there through the sustained exercise of his own free will in rejection of Christ. His personal sins do not even condemn him — it is the imputation of Adam's original sin at birth that establishes condemnation. While sin, human good, and evil are permitted within the plan of God, they are constantly being overruled by the sovereign omnipotence and divine integrity of God. Jesus Christ controls both history and the devil's world.

V. Paul's Comparison of Contemporary Israel to Pharaoh

The rhetorical force of the citation of Exodus 9:16 in Romans 9:17 lies in Paul's implicit comparison of the Jews of his own day to Pharaoh. Paul's audience knew the history. They knew that Pharaoh was arrogant, petty, jealous, vindictive, implacable, unstable, deceitful, and dishonorable. They knew he was the great enemy of Israel at the most defining moment in Israel's national history. To be compared to Pharaoh was a profound insult. To be compared to a Gentile — a category the Jews designated with the term — was even worse. Paul's comparison was deliberately provocative: you Jews of my day are not like Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or Moses. You are like Pharaoh.

Just as Amenhotep II hardened his heart through maximum negative volition toward the divine power manifest in the ten plagues, so the legalistic Jews of Paul's generation had hardened their hearts through maximum negative volition toward doctrine — specifically toward the gospel of Jesus Christ, who is Jehovah Elohim, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the Shekinah glory. The hereditary people of God had become heretical in the pattern of Ishmael, Esau, and Pharaoh — the three figures Paul has selected as the paradigm cases of negative volition in this context.

The Jews had violated their magnificent spiritual heritage. The unique origin of the nation through the positive volition of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — men who believed in the Lord and to whom righteousness was credited — should have made the importance of faith in Christ unmistakably clear. The contrast between the positive volition of Moses and the negative volition of Pharaoh was written in their own Torah. They had both the doctrinal record and the historical example. And yet they had failed to understand that their spiritual heritage was constituted by faith in the God of Israel, not by genetic descent from the patriarchs.

VI. The Justice of God and the Imputation Framework

Paul's burden for Israel in chapters 9 through 11 is ultimately a burden about adjustment to the justice of God. The mechanism that determines whether any person — Jew or Gentile — enters into the blessing of the Abrahamic, Palestinian, Davidic, and New Covenants is not ethnicity, not law-keeping, not ritual worship, not asceticism, and not moral achievement. It is the imputation of divine righteousness at the moment of faith in Christ.

Divine justice can only bless divine righteousness. This is axiomatic. The integrity of God — His holiness — is composed of two inseparable attributes: His righteousness and His justice. Justice is the guardian of all divine attributes and the believer's point of contact with God. Righteousness is the home, the target, the recipient of all blessing that justice distributes. God cannot bless sinful humanity directly without violating His own immutability and holiness. To avoid any compromise of His attributes, God designed a mechanism: the imputation of His own perfect righteousness to the believer at the moment of faith in Christ. With that righteousness in residence, the justice of God is free to impute blessing without any compromise of divine integrity.

Every covenant with Israel contains what may be called forever clauses — unconditional promises of blessing extending into eternity. The only way to receive blessing that extends forever is to possess eternal life. The only way to receive eternal life is through the imputation of divine life to the human spirit, which is created by God the Holy Spirit at the moment of salvation. Therefore, to inherit the promises of the Abrahamic, Palestinian, Davidic, and New Covenants, a Jew must possess both the righteousness of God and the life of God. Genetic descent from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — however significant in establishing historical privilege — cannot substitute for these imputations. As the premise of verse 6 states: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel.

A. Categories of Election and Adoption

Only believers are adopted at salvation as the adult sons and heirs of God, regardless of dispensation. Four historical categories of such adoption may be distinguished. First, the election of the Gentile family of God, composed of all believers in the dispensation of the Gentiles from Adam to Abraham. Second, the election of Israel, composed of all Jewish believers in the dispensation of Israel from Abraham to Christ — interrupted for the Church Age and resuming in the Tribulation. Third, the election of the royal family of God, composed of all believers, Jew and Gentile, of the Church Age from approximately AD 30 to the Rapture. Fourth, the election of the millennial population, composed of all believers during the millennial reign of Jesus Christ from the Second Advent through approximately one thousand years. Each of these categories requires adoption. Jews do not inherit from God through natural birth, even as the physical descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. They inherit through adoption as adult sons, and adoption requires faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

B. The Three Adjustments and the Imputation Sequence

The imputation sequence that underlies Paul's argument can be traced as follows. At physical birth, human life is imputed to the human soul, and Adam's original sin is simultaneously imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. This is the state designated as spiritual death. The first judicial imputation of salvation — all personal sins imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there — establishes the basis for salvation adjustment. The second judicial imputation — God's righteousness imputed at the moment of faith in Christ — creates the target for all subsequent divine blessing and establishes the potential for maturity adjustment. Eternal life is also imputed at salvation to the human spirit created by the Holy Spirit.

Maturity adjustment to the justice of God requires maximum doctrine resident in the soul through sustained operation of the Grace Apparatus for Perception. When the maturity barrier is cracked, the justice of God is free to impute experiential blessing — logistical grace, supergrace blessing — to the divine righteousness already resident in the believer. Beyond maturity, the believer who persists through suffering and continues in doctrine momentum accumulates the basis for the seventh imputation: the imputation of eternal reward to the resurrection body at the Judgment Seat of Christ. This is the full trajectory of the plan of God for the individual believer.

Paul's great pastoral concern is that the Jews of his generation remain in spiritual death — in the state prior to salvation adjustment. They possess the genetic heritage of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. They possess the covenants, the oracles, the law, and the historical record of God's dealings with Israel. But they do not possess the righteousness of God or the life of God, because they have refused the salvation adjustment available through faith in Jesus Christ. Without that first plus — faith in the Lord Jesus Christ — no Jew can enter into the true heritage of Israel, no matter how meticulous his law-keeping, how precise his ritual observance, or how impressive his moral achievement.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Ninety-Four

1. Pharaoh becomes a monument to divine power through resistance. The more Amenhotep II resisted God through maximum negative volition, the greater the manifestation of divine omnipotence in each successive confrontation. Opposition to the plan of God does not diminish it; it becomes the occasion for its amplification.

2. The culminative aorist of endeiknymi views all ten confrontations from their results. The aorist of

2. The culminative aorist of endeiknymi views all ten confrontations from their results. The ten plagues are treated as a unified action whose existing result is worldwide evangelism. Each successive no from Pharaoh contributed to the cumulative demonstration of divine power that evangelized Egypt and the ancient world.

3. God hardened Pharaoh's heart by removing all restraint and keeping him alive. Beginning with the seventh plague, the hardening of Pharaoh's heart means God withdrew all restriction on Pharaoh's already-established negative volition and sustained his life beyond what justice demanded, giving him maximum opportunity to exercise his free will in saying no. God created no evil disposition in Pharaoh; He simply permitted and preserved the one already operative.

4. Negative volition does not hinder the plan of God — it serves it. Pharaoh's resistance fulfilled the purpose of God by leading to worldwide proclamation of the divine person. As Psalm 76:10 states, the wrath of man shall praise God. No act of human or satanic opposition can deflect the execution of the divine plan.

5. Human freedom is preserved, not overridden, by divine sovereignty. Pharaoh exercised his freedom at the highest possible level — as absolute sovereign of the greatest empire of his day, with complete privacy and unrestricted property. God provided him with greater historical opportunity to express non-meritorious free will, not less. The omnipotence of God was deployed not to coerce Pharaoh but to sustain his life and multiply his opportunities.

6. Sin, human good, and evil are never objects of predestination. The divine decrees contain the actuality of all events known by divine omniscience in eternity past. The printouts of those decrees — election, predestination, justification — apply exclusively to believers. The unbeliever arrives at eternal judgment through the exercise of his own negative volition, not through any divine foreordination of his condemnation.

7. God permits the worst so that the best can result from it. As He permitted Adam's sin in order to present the Redeemer to the world, God permitted Pharaoh's maximum negative volition in order to evangelize an entire generation. The plan of God advances through historical disaster and historical prosperity alike. The believer in doctrine momentum moves forward regardless of the historical circumstances surrounding him.

8. Paul's comparison of contemporary Israel to Pharaoh is the most provocative argument in this context. To be compared to Pharaoh — arrogant, petty, jealous, vindictive, implacable, deceitful, dishonorable — was an extreme insult to Jewish sensibility. To be compared to a Gentile compounded the offense. Paul's point is precise: the Jews of his day were not continuing in the heritage of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses, but were repeating the pattern of Ishmael, Esau, and Pharaoh through maximum negative volition toward the gospel of Jesus Christ.

9. Divine justice can only bless divine righteousness — the axiomatic principle of the epistle. No system of human merit — law-keeping, ritual observance, moral achievement, asceticism, or religious activity — can serve as the basis for divine blessing. The integrity of God requires that His justice impute blessing only to His own righteousness. That righteousness is received through a single mechanism: faith in the Lord Jesus Christ at the moment of salvation adjustment.

10. The forever clauses of the Israelite covenants require both divine righteousness and eternal life. The Abrahamic, Palestinian, Davidic, and New Covenants contain unconditional promises extending into eternity. To receive eternal blessing, the recipient must possess eternal life, which is imputed to the human spirit at salvation. Genetic descent from the patriarchs establishes historical privilege but cannot substitute for the imputation of divine righteousness and divine life. The physical seed of Abraham inherits only when it becomes the spiritual seed of Abraham through faith in Christ.

11. Paul's burden for Israel is ultimately a burden about the imputation sequence. The Jews remained at the point of spiritual death — in possession of extraordinary historical and doctrinal privilege, but without the righteousness of God or the life of God required for any blessing to be imputed. The first step out of that condition is salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Jesus Christ — the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the Shekinah glory, Jehovah Elohim.

12. Only believers are adopted as adult sons and heirs of God. Natural birth into the Jewish nation does not constitute adoption into the family of God. Adoption requires faith in Christ in every dispensation. The four historical categories — the Gentile family of God from Adam to Abraham, the election of Israel from Abraham to Christ, the royal family of God in the Church Age, and the millennial population — all share this common requirement. The heritage of Israel is accessible only through the adoption that comes with salvation adjustment.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
endeiknymi ἐνδείκνυμι endeiknymi — to show, to manifest, to demonstrate Compound verb: en (in, by means of) + deiknymi (to show). Used in Romans 9:17 for the divine demonstration of omnipotence through the ten confrontations with Pharaoh. The aorist middle subjunctive here is a culminative aorist with indirect middle voice, emphasizing God as the agent acting in a uniquely personal way.
hopōs ὅπως hopōs — in order that, that Conjunction used with the subjunctive mood to introduce a purpose or final clause denoting aim or objective. In Romans 9:17, it introduces the two divine purposes behind Pharaoh's preservation in history: the demonstration of divine power and the worldwide proclamation of the divine person.
dynamis δύναμις dynamis — power, ability, might Noun denoting inherent power or ability. Used in Romans 9:17 in the accusative singular as the direct object of endeiknymi: 'my power.' The reference is to divine omnipotence as demonstrated through the ten plagues of the exodus narrative.
onoma ὄνομα onoma — name, person, reputation, fame Noun with a semantic range extending from the simple proper name to the full concept of person, character, reputation, and fame. In Romans 9:17, used in the context of worldwide proclamation: 'my person might be proclaimed throughout the entire earth,' referring to the revelation of the divine person through the exodus events.
diaggellō διαγγέλλω diaggellō — to proclaim far and wide, to announce throughout Compound verb: dia (through, throughout) + aggellō (to announce, to proclaim). Used in Romans 9:17 in the aorist passive subjunctive for the worldwide proclamation of the divine person as a result of the exodus events. The passive voice indicates that Christ as Jehovah Elohim receives the action of proclamation.
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — the righteousness of God The central organizing concept of the Epistle to the Romans. The righteousness of God is imputed to the believer at the moment of faith in Christ, establishing the only basis on which the justice of God is free to impute blessing. Divine justice can only bless divine righteousness; no human merit, moral achievement, or religious activity can serve as a substitute.
epignōsis ἐπίγνωσις epignōsis — full, exact perception; categorical knowledge Distinguished from simple gnōsis (knowledge) by the prefix epi-, indicating complete or full apprehension. In the doctrinal framework of this commentary, epignōsis designates the category of knowledge required for spiritual growth — Bible doctrine received through the Grace Apparatus for Perception, metabolized by the Holy Spirit, and resident in the right lobe of the soul.
culminative aorist culminative aorist — aorist of existing results A grammatical category of the Greek aorist that views an action in its entirety but regards it from the standpoint of its existing results. Used in Romans 9:17 for endeiknymi: all ten confrontations are viewed as a completed whole, regarded from the perspective of the result — worldwide evangelism.
indirect middle voice indirect middle — middle of special interest or close personal involvement A use of the Greek middle voice emphasizing the agent as uniquely and personally involved in the action of the verb. Used in Romans 9:17 to indicate that God's demonstration of His power through the exodus confrontations was an expression of His own character in a distinctive and non-transferable way.

Chapter Five Hundred Ninety-Five

Romans 9:18 — Divine Mercy and Hardening; The Decrees, Scar Tissue of the Soul, and the Sovereignty of God

Romans 9:18 “So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Consequently therefore he shows mercy on whom he desires; in fact, whom he desires, he hardens.

Romans 9:18 brings the first major section of chapter 9 to its theological apex. Paul has been tracing the historical origin of Israel through the patriarchs and through the confrontation between Moses and Pharaoh, establishing from Exodus 9:16 that God's sovereign administration of history is neither arbitrary nor coercive. Verse 18 draws the conclusion: the same divine omniscience that feeds all historical actuality into the decrees produces both mercy toward positive volition and hardening toward sustained negative volition. The verse divides cleanly into two clauses, each grammatically parallel and doctrinally complementary.

I. The Inferential Conclusion: Grammatical and Logical Force

The verse opens with a double inferential particle combination. The first is

The verse opens with a double inferential particle combination: ἄρα οὖν (ara oun). Each particle alone is inferential, drawing a conclusion from preceding material. Together they signal a major conclusion — one of the strongest inferential constructions in Pauline Greek. The combination is rendered: consequently therefore or so then. This is not a casual transitional phrase; it announces that everything studied about the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in Exodus 9 and in the preceding verses now converges in a single doctrinal statement.

II. First Clause: Mercy on Whom He Desires

A. The Verb eleeo — Morphology and Tense

The first clause uses the present active indicative of ἐλεέω (eleeō), meaning to have mercy, to show compassion, to demonstrate grace-blessing. This is a perfective present — a tense that refers to a fact which has come to be in the past and is now emphasized as a continuing present reality. The mercy of God toward positive volition is not a fresh or reactive decision; it has been established since eternity past, when divine omniscience fed the actuality of human history into the computer of the divine decrees. The active voice indicates that God Himself produces the action; the declarative indicative marks this as an absolute, dogmatic statement of doctrine.

B. The Relative Pronoun — On Whom

The accusative singular relative pronoun ὅς (hos) functions as the direct object: on whom. This pronoun anchors the clause to specific individuals whose volition was already recorded in the divine decrees — not as an infringement on their freedom, but as a perfect reading of what their freedom would in fact produce.

C. The Verb thelō — He Desires

The verb θέλω (thelō) means to will, to desire, to choose, to intend. This is a static present — a doctrine taken for granted as an established fact. God's desire is not arbitrary impulse; it is the expression of His perfect integrity acting in full knowledge of what every human soul has chosen and will choose throughout all of history. The full clause: consequently therefore he shows mercy on whom he desires.

III. The Divine Decrees and the Framework of Mercy

The mercy shown to Moses, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is not capricious favoritism. It is the output of a perfect system. In eternity past — what may be called Alpha Time — the omniscience of God fed only actuality, not mere probability, into the computer of the divine decrees. Every thought, decision, motive, and action of every human being was recorded there simultaneously, before time began. The printout of that process yields several categories:

Election for foreknowledge — the recognition in eternity past of positive volition toward God. Foreordination — the predetermination of roles, positions, and ordination in the plan of God. Justification — the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at the moment of faith, the foundational print out of grace. Adoption — the believer's reception as an adult heir in the family of God. Together these constitute the framework by which God is free to show mercy.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all received this printout because their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ — Jehovah Elohim, the Shekinah of Glory — was fed into the decrees billions of years before they were born. Their subsequent advancement to spiritual maturity then became the basis for the imputation of blessing from the justice of God in time. The unconditional promises of the Abrahamic and Palestinian covenants could be made precisely because God knew in eternity past that Abraham would believe, that imputed divine righteousness would be credited to his account, and that the printout of justification would be his.

IV. The Three Brackets — Potential, Information, and Hope

The structure underlying Paul's argument can be organized into three brackets corresponding to three stages of God's grace provision in history.

A. The First Bracket — Common Grace and Salvation Potential

Every human being born into the world receives two imputations: the imputation of human life at physical birth, and the imputation of Adam's original sin to the genetically transmitted old sin nature. The second imputation is pivotal: it alone establishes the potential of salvation for every member of the human race without exception. There has never been a person born who did not have this potential. The potential becomes actual only with information — the gospel — which activates the first hope: faith in Christ. When that non-meritorious faith is exercised, the result is eternal life. Moses made that adjustment; Pharaoh did not. Jacob made it; Esau did not. Abraham made it in the Sumerian city of Ur of the Chaldees; his brother Nahor did not. Isaac made it; Ishmael did not. In every case, the potential was identical. The difference was volition.

B. The Second Bracket — Blessing in Time and Maturity Potential

At the moment of salvation, the believer receives two judicial imputations: the imputation of all human sin to Christ at the cross, which constitutes the saving work of God's justice, and the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer — the plus-R that becomes the basis of all subsequent blessing. This second judicial imputation sets up the second potential: the imputation of blessing in time, available to the believer who advances through sustained intake of Bible doctrine to maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Without the second imputation there is no access to the grace blessings of time, no maturity barrier to be crossed, and no supergrace qualification. The racial Jew who possesses only the genes of Abraham without the righteousness of God has no standing before divine justice and no legitimate claim to the covenant promises. This is Paul's burden throughout chapter 9: the true Israel is the regenerate seed of Abraham, not the physical seed.

C. The Third Bracket — Eternal Blessing and the Judgment Seat

The imputation of blessing in time establishes a third potential: eternal reward and blessing imputed at the judgment seat of Christ, received in a resurrection body. The information required is sustained doctrinal intake — the Grace Apparatus for Perception functioning over time — and the resulting confidence is absolute: the believer who cracks the maturity barrier and advances to supergrace and ultra-supergrace will stand at the judgment seat having glorified God in time and will receive imputed blessing for eternity. This is the goal of the Protocol Plan of God; this is the content of the mercy God wills to show.

V. Second Clause: In Fact, Whom He Desires, He Hardens

A. The Intensive Conjunction de

The second clause opens with the postpositive conjunctive particle δέ (de). Here the particle is neither transitional nor purely adversative but intensive: it is rendered in fact. The intensification signals that the second clause is not a contrast introduced to qualify the first, but an equally absolute doctrinal statement that stands alongside it.

B. The Verb sklērunō — To Harden, To Calcify

The second clause introduces the present active indicative of σκληρύνω (sklērunō), meaning to harden, to calcify, to make rigid. This is again a perfective present: a fact established in the past, now presented as a continuing present reality. The hardening of Pharaoh is not a past curiosity; it is a present reality intelligible from the completed study of Exodus. The active voice indicates God produces the action; the declarative indicative presents it as an absolute dogmatic fact. The full clause: in fact, whom he desires, he hardens.

VI. What Divine Hardening Actually Means

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart does not mean that God reached into Pharaoh's soul and converted positive volition into negative, then locked it in place. That interpretation is incompatible with every divine attribute and with the entire argument Paul has constructed. The correct understanding emerges from the data of Exodus itself.

Through the first six confrontations — plagues one through six — the text of Exodus consistently states that Pharaoh hardened his own heart: Exodus 7:13, 22; 8:15, 32; 9:34–35. Pharaoh, designated in the historical record as Amenhotep II, was the free agent. He said no repeatedly and from his own volition. By plague seven, the accumulated scar tissue of his soul had reached a level at which, under normal conditions, God would have removed him from life and authority because his divorce from reality made him dangerous to his nation's survival. God did not remove him. He let him live. He sustained his authority. He gave him more opportunities to confront divine omnipotence and to say no. That is what the text means when it says from Exodus 9:12 onward that God hardened Pharaoh's heart. God afforded maximum opportunity for negative volition to express itself — and did so because worldwide evangelism was the result.

The illustration is straightforward: a soldier who walks fifty miles develops calluses. The commanding officer who orders him to walk another fifty — and another, and another — might be said to have hardened his feet. The officer did not reach down and thicken the skin from the outside. He simply provided the conditions in which the soldier's own physical response produced the hardening. God hardened Pharaoh's heart by giving him more miles to walk. Every additional confrontation, every additional opportunity to face the omnipotence of God and refuse, produced more scar tissue than the one before. While Pharaoh said no, thousands of Egyptians, Ethiopians, and Hebrews throughout Egypt said yes. The confrontation that destroyed one man evangelized a generation.

VII. Scar Tissue of the Soul — Doctrinal Analysis

A. The Mechanics of Scar Tissue

The underlying Greek concept is ματαιότης (mataiotēs) — translated emptiness or futility, but functioning in the soul as a vacuum. When a person repeatedly says no to God consciousness, gospel truth, or doctrinal content, that repeated refusal does not leave the soul neutral. It creates negative suction. The vacuum draws in whatever is available — human viewpoint, human good, error, and the full range of satanic thinking — not because the person consciously selects it, but because the vacuum demands content and error is always available. The more truth is refused, the stronger the vacuum; the stronger the vacuum, the more thoroughly error saturates the soul; the more thoroughly error saturates the soul, the more blind the person becomes to any subsequent presentation of truth.

Scar tissue is formed in two ways: by saying no to truth and by saying yes to error. Both produce the same calcification. A believer who attends a congregation where false doctrine is consistently taught builds scar tissue just as certainly as a believer who explicitly rejects sound doctrine. The result in both cases is progressive blindness in the affected area of the soul, increasing arrogance, and progressive divorce from reality.

B. Scar Tissue and Israel — Anticipation of Romans 11

The scar tissue phenomenon explains what Paul will develop fully in Romans 11: blindness in part has happened to Israel. The Jewish people of Paul's day were not uniformly blind. They retained clarity on significant portions of Mosaic legislation — principles of authority, taxation, military function, civil law, and concepts of freedom — because they had accepted those categories of the Word of God. But in precisely the area where the Mosaic writings pointed most directly to the Lord Jesus Christ as Messiah, they had developed maximum scar tissue through sustained rejection. The rejection of Christ at the first advent was not an isolated failure of perception; it was the terminus of a long process of calcification in that specific area of truth.

C. Scar Tissue and Reality — The Arrogance Dynamic

Scar tissue does not remain static. Its defining characteristic is that it grows. Every increment of blindness produces a corresponding increment of arrogance, because the person who is blind to truth has no external reference point by which to evaluate himself. Arrogance fills the space that orientation to reality vacates. As arrogance increases, the divorce from reality deepens; as the divorce deepens, arrogance intensifies further. The cycle is self-reinforcing and, absent divine intervention, self-terminating only at the sin unto death.

Pharaoh is the historical paradigm. His arrogance as ruler of the dominant empire of the ancient Near East provided the initial condition. His repeated refusals of Moses' demands built scar tissue over that arrogance. His scar tissue increased his arrogance. His arrogance prevented any accurate perception of the power arrayed against him. By the time of the tenth plague — the death of his firstborn son — he was so completely divorced from reality that when Israel departed and he chose to pursue them to the Red Sea, he ordered his chariots into the corridor of dry sea floor with walls of water standing on either side. There was no longer any functioning perception of danger. This is what maximum scar tissue produces.

VIII. God's Integrity in the Hardening — No Violation of Justice

A critical concern in this passage — one that drives the debaters' questions of verse 19 — is whether God's hardening of Pharaoh constitutes injustice. The answer is categorically no, for reasons grounded in the divine attributes.

First, Pharaoh's sins were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged at the justice of God. The doctrine of unlimited atonement establishes that no human being is excluded from the saving work of Christ. Pharaoh was not hardened because he was excluded from atonement; he was hardened because he was consistently and freely negative toward the provision of that atonement. Second, God was not willing that Pharaoh should perish — the principle of 2 Peter 3:9 is universal. The decision was Pharaoh's. God's foreknowledge of that decision does not transform it into God's decision. Third, the integrity of God — His perfect righteousness and absolute justice functioning together as divine holiness — remained entirely intact throughout the hardening process. God did not violate His own righteousness. He did not act arbitrarily. He acted in complete compatibility with His perfect character and His perfect plan of grace. He simply gave Pharaoh more of what Pharaoh's own free will was producing.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Ninety-Five

1. God is not arbitrary in the administration of mercy or hardening. He functions in full compatibility with His perfect integrity and His perfect plan of grace. A perfect God can only produce a perfect plan, and a perfect plan can only be administered by a perfect God. Arbitrariness is excluded by definition.

2. Man remains a free agent in history, responsible for his own thoughts, decisions, motivations, and actions. The divine decrees do not coerce human volition; they record it — accurately and in its entirety — from eternity past.

3. God uses the free will of man to accomplish His will and purpose. Pharaoh's negative volition, sustained through ten confrontations, became the instrument of worldwide evangelism in the generation of Moses. God knew billions of years in advance how that volition would function and incorporated it into His plan without overriding it.

4. All scar tissue of the soul originates in the individual's own free will. God never imposes scar tissue. Every increment of calcification is produced by the soul's own decision — either saying no to truth or saying yes to error. Both produce the same result.

5. To the grace-qualified believer there is grace blessing from the justice of God. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were qualified under grace through election for foreknowledge, foreordination, justification, and adoption — all printouts from the divine decrees based on their positive volition known to God in eternity past.

6. The racial Jew has a great spiritual heritage, but that heritage carries no soteriological weight until he is justified. To be a son of Abraham by genetic descent is nothing until a Jew becomes a son of God through faith in Jesus Christ. The true Israel is the regenerate seed of Abraham, not the physical seed.

7. Without the imputation of divine righteousness there is no access to covenant blessing. The unconditional promises made to Abraham, reiterated to Isaac and Jacob, presuppose the presence of plus-R — imputed divine righteousness at justification. Without it, no blessing from the justice of God is possible, in time or in eternity.

8. God hardened Pharaoh's heart by giving him more opportunities to say no in the presence of more and more facts. He sustained Pharaoh's life, authority, and access to the demonstrations of divine omnipotence so that his accumulated negative volition could produce both the maximum expression of scar tissue and the maximum opportunity for others to say yes. Exodus 9:12; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:8.

9. The integrity of God — perfect righteousness and absolute justice — was not violated in the hardening of Pharaoh. Pharaoh's sins were imputed to Christ and judged. God was not willing that he should perish. The decision was Pharaoh's throughout. God's foreknowledge of that decision does not make it God's decision.

10. Scar tissue of the soul produces progressive divorce from reality and progressive expansion of arrogance. The two dynamics reinforce each other: blindness to truth removes external reference points, arrogance fills the vacuum, and the increasing arrogance deepens the blindness. The terminus of this cycle, absent recovery, is the sin unto death.

11. The blindness of Israel anticipated in this passage is nothing more nor less than scar tissue of the soul applied nationally. Blindness in part has happened to Israel — in precisely those areas of the Mosaic writings that pointed most directly to Jesus Christ as Messiah. This will be developed in detail when the commentary reaches Romans 11.

12. The doctrine of the divine decrees links Alpha Time to history and to Omega Time. What was reality in eternity past becomes reality in historical experience and will be reality in eternal future. Bible doctrine is the mechanism that connects these realities in the believer's soul and orients the believer to historical crisis, to divine discipline, and to the purpose of God in any generation.

Divine decrees The eternal, simultaneous, all-inclusive decisions of God in eternity past (Alpha Time) by which He incorporated the full actuality of human history — every thought, decision, motive, and act of every free agent — into His plan.
