Israēl Ἰσραήλ Israēl — Israel Nominative singular proper noun. Transliteration of the Hebrew Yisra'el. In Romans 9:31, refers to racial Israel — the Jewish people as an ethnic and national entity — not to the regenerate remnant. Paul consistently distinguishes the two in Romans 9–11.
Big Blot Out Technical term for the total negative volition of racial Israel toward the first advent of Christ, encompassing rejection of the virgin birth, the hypostatic union, the cross, the resurrection, the ascension, and the session. The big blot out destroys client-nation function by eliminating the pivot of positive volition that sustains national blessing, and produces inversion discipline as its inevitable consequence.
Inversion A divinely administered system of discipline in which a complete reversal of covenantal, soteriological, or circumstantial position occurs as a consequence of arrogance and negative volition. In the dispensational context of Romans 9–11, inversion denotes the transfer of client-nation function and covenant standing from Israel to the Gentile nations for the duration of the church age, with a second reversal back toward Israel at the second advent.
Epignosis ἐπίγνωσις epignōsis — full, exact knowledge The category of knowledge required for genuine spiritual growth. Distinguished from gnōsis (surface or academic knowledge) by its penetration into the right lobe of the soul under the ministry of the Holy Spirit. Epignosis is the material from which the superstructure of the edification complex is built on the foundation of imputed divine righteousness.
Faith-Rest Technique The stabilizing mechanism by which the believer claims specific promises and employs doctrinal rationales under adversity in order to restore the concentration necessary for application of accumulated doctrine. The prerequisite for all doctrinal application under pressure. Without it, even a doctrinally informed believer remains functionally vulnerable at critical moments.

Chapter Six Hundred Forty-Seven

Romans 9:31–32 — The Big Blot Out: Works Righteousness vs. Faith; The Three Codices of the Mosaic Law

Romans 9:31–32 “but Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law. Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone,” (ESV)
Corrected translation: But Israel, who pursued after the law with human self-righteousness, has not accomplished the purpose of the law. Why? Because they did not pursue it by means of faith, but as by means of works.

Romans 9 has traced the sovereign election of God in the history of Israel and demonstrated that God's word has not failed. The preceding verse established that Gentiles attained righteousness through faith while Israel, paradoxically, did not. Verses 31–32 deliver the diagnosis: Israel's failure was not ethnic, covenantal, or arbitrary — it was volitional. They pursued the law as a system of self-righteousness rather than receiving the righteousness God offered through faith in Christ. This chapter examines the three codices of the Mosaic Law, the nature of the Jewish pursuit of works righteousness, and the grammatical force of Paul's indictment in verse 32.

I. The Purpose of the Mosaic Law: Three Codices

Israel's failure cannot be understood apart from a precise understanding of what the Mosaic Law actually is. The Law is not a single undifferentiated code but a tripartite document with three distinct purposes. Israel's error lay in applying two of the three codices as a system of salvation while effectively blotting out the one codex that pointed directly to Christ.

A. Codex One — The Decalogue (The Freedom Code)

The first division of the Mosaic Law is the Decalogue — the Ten Commandments — called commandments in the King James translation. This codex constitutes the freedom code of Israel. Its function is not primarily to define the totality of sin, since sin is far more extensive than ten prohibitions, but to define the conditions necessary for human freedom within a national entity.

Freedom requires privacy, property, authority, and morality. Each commandment addresses one or more of these components. The prohibition of murder preserves the right of self-determination and physical existence. The prohibition of theft upholds the principle of private property. The prohibition of adultery protects the covenant institution of marriage as a form of relational property and covenant fidelity. These are not arbitrary religious rules but the structural prerequisites of a free society.

The connection between morality and freedom is not incidental. National degeneracy — the collapse of integrity in business, personal life, and public institutions — creates the conditions for the expansion of centralized government. Big government grows in proportion to national immorality because a population that will not govern itself through internal moral constraint must be governed externally by bureaucratic compulsion. The result is the progressive destruction of privacy, property, and self-determination — the very freedoms Codex One was designed to protect.

For Israel as a client nation to God, Codex One was the foundation of the freedom required to evangelize, to sustain a priestly mission to the nations, and to function as the vehicle through which divine blessing could flow outward to the Gentile world. A nation in moral collapse cannot sustain a missionary function. This principle operates in every generation.

B. Codex Two — The Ordinances (The Doctrinal and Spiritual Code)

The second division is called the ordinances in the King James translation. This is the doctrinal code — the spiritual heritage of Israel — and it is the codex that points directly and specifically to the Lord Jesus Christ. Codex Two is the heart of the Mosaic Law from the standpoint of salvation, because it contains the entire typological presentation of Christ's person and work.

The Levitical offerings are the primary vehicle of Codex Two. Each offering communicates a specific aspect of Christ's saving work:

The burnt offering taught propitiation — the complete satisfaction of divine justice by the substitutionary death of an innocent victim. The peace offering taught reconciliation — the restoration of a broken relationship between God and man through the mediatorial work of the priest. The grain offering pointed to the first advent of Christ, the necessity of his true humanity as the vehicle through which he could bear human sin. The sin and trespass offerings addressed the problem of individual transgression and the need for a substitute bearing divine judgment.

The articles of furniture in the tabernacle and later the temple carried the same message in spatial and material form: the brazen altar of sacrifice, the laver of rebound and cleansing, the table of showbread representing Christ as the bread of life, the altar of incense representing prayer and intercession, and the ark of the covenant surmounted by the mercy seat — the throne of propitiation — where the blood of atonement was applied annually on the Day of Atonement.

The holy days reinforced the same theology through annual repetition. The Passover proclaimed that Christ, our Passover, is sacrificed for us. The Day of Atonement presented the covering of sin through vicarious substitution. The feast calendar structured Israel's corporate life around the person and work of the coming Messiah.

The great declaration of Israel's monotheistic faith — the Shema — contains within it both the Alpha and Omega glory of Christ. Israel would recite:

Shema Yisra'el, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai Echad — 'Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one.' The name Adonai (אֲדֹנָי) as Eloheinu (אֱלֹהֵינוּ) declares the eternal Alpha glory of Christ as the God of Israel — co-equal with the Father and the Spirit in the divine essence. Adonai Echad — 'the LORD is one' or 'the LORD is unique' — points to the Omega glory: the hypostatic union, the unique God-Man of the first advent. Israel confessed the eternal God but refused to recognize him in his incarnation.

C. Codex Three — The Judgments (The Establishment Code)

The third division is called the judgments in the King James translation. This is the political and functional heritage of Israel — the establishment code governing the operation of the nation as a theocratic client state. It covers the full range of civil and social function: marriage and family, military service and national defense, taxation, diet and sanitation, quarantine and public health, criminal law including apprehension, trial procedure, and proportional punishment, and a systematic taxonomy of sin and human good.

The fundamental principle of Codex Three is limited government. In the theocracy, the Lord Jesus Christ himself was the supreme government. The judgments were designed to circumscribe human authority so that no human institution could aggregate to itself the sovereignty that belongs to God alone. The principle of a flat tax embedded in the tithing legislation illustrates this: a uniform percentage across all income levels maintains proportionality without destroying the incentive structure of free enterprise, and without requiring the administrative apparatus of a graduated system that penalizes productivity.

II. Israel's Misuse of the Law: The Big Blot Out

The tragic irony of Israel's national failure is that they possessed all three codices and misused two of them to eliminate the third. By taking Codex One (the Decalogue) and Codex Three (the judgments) as the instrument of salvation, they effectively blotted out Codex Two — the very codex that presented Christ and his saving work.

This is the pattern Paul has been exposing throughout Romans 9–10. Israel pursued the law as a system of human self-righteousness. They observed commandments, maintained ceremonial purity, and performed religious acts — all of which were Codex One and Codex Three function — while treating Codex Two as mere ritual stripped of its christological content. The Levitical offerings were performed without faith in what they signified. The Passover was kept as a national memorial without personal faith in the one to whom it pointed. The temple service continued without recognition that the one whom the temple existed to honor had appeared in their midst.

The rich young ruler of the Synoptic Gospels is the paradigmatic illustration. He kept Codex One from his youth. He had no awareness that his law-keeping had produced only self-righteousness — a righteousness that cannot satisfy divine justice, cannot produce eternal life, and cannot receive the blessing of God. He walked away from Christ because he was unwilling to exchange his accumulated self-righteousness for the imputed righteousness of God.

This pattern persists in every generation and culture. The human inclination to establish one's own righteousness through moral performance, social action, or religious observance is the universal alternative to the adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ. The specific form varies — law-keeping, philanthropy, social justice activism, religious devotion — but the structure is identical: works righteousness substituted for faith righteousness.

III. The Limitations of the Law

Scripture is explicit about what the Mosaic Law cannot do, regardless of how meticulously it is observed:

The Law cannot justify. Galatians 2:16 states categorically that by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified. Justification — the imputation of divine righteousness — comes only through faith in Christ.

The Law cannot give life. Galatians 3:21 asks whether the law is therefore against the promises of God and answers that if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law — but no such law exists, because the law was never designed as a life-giving instrument.

The Law cannot provide the filling of the Spirit. Galatians 3:2 makes the point by asking whether the Galatian believers received the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith.

The Law cannot solve the problem of the old sin nature. Romans 8:3 states that what the law could not do, weakened as it was by the flesh — that is, the old sin nature — God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.

The Law is not the standard for Church Age spirituality. Romans 6:14 declares that believers are not under law but under grace. Romans 8:2–4 and Galatians 5:18 establish that the filling of the Spirit, not law-keeping, is the operative principle of the Christian life. Certain moral principles embedded in the Mosaic Law have been re-revealed for the Church Age under the framework of the royal family modus operandi, but the Mosaic Law as a covenant institution was given exclusively to Israel (Exodus 19:3; Leviticus 26:46; Romans 3:19; 9:4; Deuteronomy 4:8; Romans 2:12–14) and was never given to the Church. This includes Sabbath observance, which is Mosaic legislation with no Church Age counterpart (Acts 15:5, 24; Romans 6:14; Galatians 2:19).

IV. Exegesis of Romans 9:32 — The Grammatical Diagnosis

Verse 32 opens with what is formally a prepositional phrase functioning as a rhetorical question. The construction is:

διὰ τί (dia ti) — a prepositional idiom using διά (dia, because/on account of) plus the interrogative pronoun τίς (tis, what/why). The combined idiom means 'because why?' or simply 'why?' It is a reinforced interrogative that presses the rhetorical point with maximum force. Paul is not asking because he lacks the answer; the question is designed to bring the hearer to confront his own failure.

The answer follows immediately with the causal conjunction:

ὅτι (hoti) — because. The διὰ τί … ὅτι (dia ti … hoti) construction is a standard Greek idiom for posing and answering a diagnostic question: 'Why? Because.'

A. The Negative: Not by Means of Faith

The negative is οὐκ (ouk) — the strong indicative negative, used here because the following verb is in the indicative mood. The verb to be supplied by ellipsis is the present active indicative of διώκω (diōkō), to pursue, to run after. The subject is Israel; the object, implied from verse 31, is the law understood in terms of its true purpose.

The prepositional phrase qualifying the pursuit is ἐκ πίστεως (ek pisteōs) — ἐκ (ek) plus the ablative of means from πίστις (pistis, faith). The ablative of means (rather than the instrumental case) is used here because the means carries the implication of source or origin — faith as the divinely appointed channel through which righteousness flows. Critically, πίστεως is singular: one act of faith in Christ, one time, produces eternal salvation. The singularity is grammatically significant.

B. The Contrast: But as by Means of Works

The adversative conjunction ἀλλά (alla) introduces a sharp contrast: not by faith, but — emphatic opposition. Following the adversative is the comparative particle ὡς (hōs, as/as if), which characterizes the quality of Israel's pursuit. They pursued as if by works — the ὡς capturing the self-deceived confidence with which they treated law-observance as though it were a legitimate path to righteousness.

The prepositional phrase is ἐξ ἔργων (ex ergōn) — ἐκ plus the ablative plural of ἔργον (ergon, work/deed). The plural is deliberate and theologically pointed. Faith is singular — ἐκ πίστεως, one act of faith in Christ and the transaction is complete, eternal, and irrevocable. Works are plural — ἐξ ἔργων, many works accumulated over a lifetime, and none of them sufficient. The grammatical contrast between singular πίστεως and plural ἔργων is not accidental; it encapsulates the entire argument of Romans regarding the adjustment to the justice of God through faith.

C. The Result: They Stumbled at the Stumbling Stone

The clause concludes with the result of Israel's works-based pursuit: they stumbled at the stumbling stone. The stumbling stone is identified in the following verses (9:33) through a composite citation from Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16. The stone is Christ himself — specifically, Christ presented as the object of faith for salvation. For those who approach him by faith, he is the cornerstone of election and honor. For those who approach him by works, he is a rock of offense — not because he causes the offense, but because works righteousness is inherently incompatible with the grace principle on which salvation rests.

Israel did not stumble because they lacked information. Codex Two gave them everything they needed. They stumbled because they refused the epistemological framework — faith — through which alone the content of Codex Two could be appropriated. Walking by sight, they could observe the commandments and the judgments. Walking by faith, they would have seen Christ in the ordinances. They chose sight over faith and stumbled over the very stone that was meant to be their foundation.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Forty-Seven

1. The Mosaic Law has three distinct codices, each with a distinct purpose. Codex One (the Decalogue) is the freedom code, establishing the moral prerequisites of national liberty. Codex Two (the ordinances) is the doctrinal code, presenting Christ typologically through the Levitical system. Codex Three (the judgments) is the establishment code, governing the political and social life of Israel as a theocratic client nation. Confusion of these three categories is the root of Israel's failure and of every subsequent form of legalism.

2. Israel's failure was volitional, not covenantal. God's word did not fail (Romans 9:6). Israel failed because they chose to pursue righteousness through Codex One and Codex Three while blotting out Codex Two — the codex that presented the Lord Jesus Christ as the sole object of saving faith. The information was available. The choice was made against it.

3. Works righteousness and faith righteousness are mutually exclusive. The grammatical contrast in verse 32 between singular ek pisteōs (by means of faith) and plural ex ergōn (by means of works) encodes the theological argument in the morphology: one act of faith in Christ produces eternal salvation; an infinite accumulation of works produces only self-righteousness. The two systems cannot be combined.

4. The Law cannot accomplish what only grace through faith can accomplish. The Law cannot justify (Galatians 2:16), cannot give life (Galatians 3:21), cannot provide the filling of the Spirit (Galatians 3:2), and cannot solve the problem of the old sin nature (Romans 8:3). These are not deficiencies that greater effort can overcome; they are structural limitations built into the Law's purpose. The Law was designed to demonstrate the need for faith, not to substitute for it.

5. The Mosaic Law was given exclusively to Israel and was never given to the Church. Exodus 19:3, Leviticus 26:46, Deuteronomy 4:8, Romans 2:12–14, and Romans 3:19 establish that the Law was Israel's national covenant. Acts 15:5, 24, Romans 6:14, and Galatians 2:19 confirm that it was never imposed on the Church Age believer. This includes Sabbath observance. Certain moral principles embedded in the Law have been re-revealed for the Church Age, but they derive their authority from their re-revelation in the New Testament, not from their inclusion in the Mosaic code.

6. The Shema contains both the Alpha and Omega glory of Christ. Adonai Eloheinu declares the eternal Alpha glory — the God of Israel co-equal with the Father and the Spirit. Adonai Echad declares the Omega glory — the unique God-Man of the first advent. Israel confessed the formula while rejecting its incarnational content. They believed in God as the eternal sovereign but refused to believe in him as the Lord Jesus Christ, the only Savior.

7. The stumbling stone is not a cause of offense but a revelation of the underlying problem. Christ did not cause Israel to stumble; their prior commitment to works righteousness made stumbling inevitable when they encountered the grace principle. The stone is the same in both cases — what differs is the posture of the one approaching it. Faith receives the cornerstone; works righteousness strikes it and falls.

8. The diagnosis of verse 32 is the universal diagnosis of human religion. Every generation and culture produces its own form of works righteousness — law-keeping, moral performance, social action, religious devotion. The specific content varies; the structure is constant. The adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ is the only exception to this universal human pattern, and it is an exception that must be chosen against the default orientation of the fallen soul.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
dia ti διὰ τί dia ti — because why? / why? A prepositional idiom formed from dia (on account of) and the interrogative pronoun tis (what/who). Functions as a reinforced interrogative meaning 'why?' Used in Romans 9:32 to open Paul's rhetorical diagnosis of Israel's failure.
hoti ὅτι hoti — because, that Causal conjunction. In the dia ti … hoti construction, hoti introduces the answer to the rhetorical question: 'Why? Because.' Standard Greek idiom for diagnostic argument.
pistis πίστις pistis — faith, trust, belief Noun, feminine. Non-meritorious trust in a designated object. In the context of salvation, the object is the Lord Jesus Christ. Appears in the ablative singular ek pisteōs in Romans 9:32, emphasizing that one act of faith in Christ is sufficient and final for eternal life.
ergon ἔργον ergon — work, deed Noun, neuter. In the plural ex ergōn (by means of works), refers to the accumulated acts of law-observance by which Israel sought to establish righteousness before God. Appears in the ablative plural in Romans 9:32, in deliberate grammatical contrast to the singular pistis: many works yield no righteousness; one act of faith yields eternal life.
alla ἀλλά alla — but, however Strong adversative conjunction. Introduces a sharp contrast between what Israel should have done (pursued by faith) and what they actually did (pursued as by works). One of the strongest contrastive particles in Greek.
hōs ὡς hōs — as, as if, just as Comparative particle. In Romans 9:32, hōs qualifies the pursuit of righteousness through works: Israel acted 'as if' works were a legitimate means to righteousness. The particle captures the self-deceived confidence of the works-righteousness pursuit.
diōkō διώκω diōkō — to pursue, to run after, to press toward Verb. Used in Romans 9:30–31 to describe both Gentile pursuit (of righteousness, not sought) and Jewish pursuit (of the law). The irony is that Israel's intense pursuit of the law by the wrong means — works rather than faith — resulted in failure to attain its true purpose.
Shema שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל Shema Yisra'el — Hear, O Israel The foundational confession of Israelite monotheism (Deuteronomy 6:4). 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.' Theologically, the declaration contains both the Alpha glory of Christ (Adonai Eloheinu — the eternal God of Israel) and his Omega glory (Adonai Echad — the unique God-Man of the first advent). Israel confessed the formula while rejecting its incarnational content.
dikaiosynē δικαιοσύνη dikaiosynē — righteousness Noun, feminine. The righteousness of God imputed to the believer at the moment of faith in Christ. Distinguished from human self-righteousness (works righteousness), which Israel pursued through law-keeping. The central term of Romans: the adjustment to the justice of God is the mechanism by which divine righteousness is received.
ek pisteōs ἐκ πίστεως ek pisteōs — by means of faith Prepositional phrase: ek (ablative of means/source) plus pistis in the ablative singular. Singular number is theologically significant: one act of faith in Christ produces eternal righteousness. The ablative of means rather than the instrumental case indicates that faith is not merely the instrument but the divinely appointed channel of origin through which righteousness flows from God to man.
ex ergōn ἐξ ἔργων ex ergōn — by means of works Prepositional phrase: ek (ablative of means) plus ergon in the ablative plural. Plural number is theologically significant in contrast to the singular pistis: an indefinite accumulation of works never produces the righteousness that one act of faith in Christ produces instantaneously and permanently.

Chapter Six Hundred Forty-Eight

Romans 9:32–33 — The Stone of Stumbling; The Big Blot-Out; The Panorama of Israel

Romans 9:32–33 “Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, 'Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Why? Because they did not pursue it by means of faith, but as by means of works. They have tripped over the rock of stumbling, just as it stands written: Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling, even a rock which arouses opposition; nevertheless, he who believes on him will not be disappointed.

Romans 9 concludes with Paul's explanation of why Israel, though possessing every covenantal advantage, failed to attain divine righteousness while Gentiles who possessed none of that heritage did attain it. The answer lies in the mechanism of faith versus works — and in the catastrophic phenomenon Paul's argument has been building toward: the big blot-out. Verses 32 and 33 deliver the verdict and the scriptural documentation for that verdict, drawing on two interwoven quotations from Isaiah. The chapter then closes with an introductory panorama of Israel across the dispensations, setting the stage for Romans 10 and 11.

I. The Verb of Stumbling: Romans 9:32b

The critical verb in verse 32 is the aorist active indicative of proskopto, meaning to stumble against or trip over. The aorist is culminative, viewing the entire history of Jewish legalism in its completed result — the big blot-out — while regarding that result from the standpoint of its existing consequences. The active voice indicates that unbelieving Israel produced this action; it was not imposed upon them from without. The indicative mood is declarative, asserting the historical reality of the blot-out in every generation from Moses to Christ.

The compound verb proskopto (προσκόπτω) carries the sense of seeing something in the path and falling over it regardless. This is the interpretive key: stumbling does not imply ignorance. The Jew who stumbled over the Lord Jesus Christ did so with full visibility — maximum information, maximum negative volition. The Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4, recited from earliest childhood, contained within it the full announcement of the first advent: Adonai Elohenu — Jehovah is our God — expressing his Alpha glory as the eternal second person of the Trinity; Adonai Echad — Jehovah is unique — expressing the uniqueness of the incarnation, the hypostatic union, the God-man. They had the testimony before them from early youth (Deuteronomy 6:7). They tripped over it, rose, and moved on. This is the big blot-out.

The illustration holds a precise shape. A thousand-carat diamond lies in the path. The Jew, running after the law in pursuit of self-righteousness, stumbles over it, curses it, and continues. The Gentile, possessing no Torah, no Navim, no accumulated heritage of written revelation, comes along the same path, sees the stone, picks it up, and carries it off as the most precious thing in the world. This is the great inversion that has structured the entire argument of Romans 9. The Jew preferred minus R — his own self-righteousness — to plus R, the divine righteousness imputed through faith in Christ.

II. The Composite Quotation: Isaiah 8:14 and Isaiah 28:16

Verse 33 introduces the scriptural documentation with the formula kathōs gegraptai — just as it stands written — followed by a carefully constructed composite quotation drawing on two passages from Isaiah. The perfect tense of gegraptai (to write) is the intensive perfect, emphasizing the existing results of the Old Testament canon as a finished product. The passive voice presents the mechanics of inspiration: God the Holy Spirit communicated to the human authors — Isaiah, and now Paul quoting Isaiah — in such a manner that without overriding their human intelligence, literary style, or personal characteristics, the divine message was recorded with perfect accuracy in the original languages, the very words bearing the authority of divine authorship.

A. The Structure of the Composite

Paul does not quote either Isaiah passage in full. He selects phrases and assembles them into a new unit that addresses his specific argument. The structure is as follows:

From Isaiah 28:16, the opening clause: Behold, I lay in Zion. The four intervening lines of that verse — a foundation stone, a rock of testing, a cornerstone of honor, a secure foundation — are not quoted because they are not pertinent to Paul's point at this moment.

From Isaiah 8:14, the insert: a stone of stumbling, even a rock which arouses opposition. In Isaiah's original context, the Lord was to be a sanctuary to the believer and a stone of stumbling to both houses of Israel — the northern and southern kingdoms — that reject him. Paul takes only the stumbling-stone phrase, setting aside the snare-and-trap language that follows.

From Isaiah 28:16, the closing clause: the one who believes on him will not be disappointed. This final line of Isaiah 28:16 returns to complete the unit.

The result is a sandwich: the top slice of bread from Isaiah 28:16 (Behold, I lay in Zion), the filling from Isaiah 8:14 (a stone of stumbling, a rock which arouses opposition), and the bottom slice from Isaiah 28:16 (he who believes on him will not be disappointed). The general subject of both Isaiah passages — Israel's response to her own God — is preserved, while Paul moves the composite into a Greek context to serve his argument about the big blot-out and the great inversion.

B. Behold, I Lay in Zion

The particle idou functions as the aorist middle imperative of horaō — the Hebrew hinneh equivalent — demanding perception and signaling that what follows is of the highest importance. The present active indicative of tithēmi (to lay a foundation) is the perfective present tense: it denotes what was accomplished in the past but emphasizes that past event as a present reality. God the Father, under the title Adonai-Jehovah, produced the action. Zion is named rather than Israel as a whole because Zion was the fortress of David, and David's son is Jesus Christ. The Davidic connection is immediate and unmistakable to any Jewish reader: before there can be the crown, there must be the cross.

C. A Stone of Stumbling, a Rock Which Arouses Opposition

The noun lithos (λίθος) designates a stone — here, the stone over which unbelieving Israel trips. The noun petra (πέτρα) designates bedrock, the great foundational rock. These are two distinct words. The rock of salvation is Jesus Christ himself. The lithos of stumbling and the petra of offense are two aspects of the same person: to the one who believes, he is the bedrock and foundation; to the one who rejects, he is what they fell over. The genitive proskommatos (προσκόμματος) functions as a prophetic title: the stone on which there is stumbling leading to a fall. Paul applies this to the Lord Jesus Christ in his first advent — well known from Isaiah, visible to every generation of Israel, and yet rejected through the mechanism of the big blot-out.

The distinction between petra and petros, familiar from Matthew 16:18, is relevant here. Christ is the petra — the great bedrock. Every believer is petros — a stone in union with that rock, a building stone in the structure being raised upon it. This distinction does not confer any singular authority upon the apostle Peter; if any apostle carried unique apostolic authority in the early church, it was the Apostle Paul, a fact Peter himself acknowledged.

D. Nevertheless, He Who Believes on Him Will Not Be Disappointed

The connective kai here is not additive but emphatic, carrying the force of nevertheless — used to mark a fact as surprising, unexpected, and therefore noteworthy. Even in the midst of the stumbling, one path remains open.

The articular present active participle of pisteuō (πιστεύω) is the eristic present tense, expressing punctiliar action in present time without reference to its progress. The point is that belief is available now — as it was when Isaiah wrote, as it was when Paul wrote, as it is in any generation. One moment taken out of time becomes the present moment of decision. Paul's appeal to the racial Jew guilty of the big blot-out is precisely this: take one moment, believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, cancel the blot-out, become a true member of the house of Israel.

The prepositional phrase is epi (ἐπί) plus the third-person singular pronoun — to believe on him. The preposition epi carries the sense of over as well as on. This is a deliberate paranomasia: you have stumbled over (epi) the rock; now come back and believe on (epi) the rock. The inversion of the stumbling becomes the invitation to faith.

The future passive indicative of kataischynō (καταισχύνω) — to be disgraced, humiliated, disappointed — is negated by the particle ou. The predictive future states that no believer will ever be humiliated at the last judgment. The passive voice plus the negative means the believing Jew will never face condemnation at the great white throne. Faith in Christ eliminates not only condemnation in time but disappointment in eternity. There will be no lake of fire for the Jew who believes in the Lord Jesus Christ.

III. The Big Blot-Out and the Great Inversion: Summary

The big blot-out is the mechanism by which a generation of Jews, possessing maximum information regarding the first advent of Christ — his Virgin birth, his hypostatic union, his impeccability, his redemptive work, his resurrection, ascension, and session — encapsulates that knowledge with deliberate negative volition until it is present but functionally gone. The information does not disappear; it is blotted from the functioning soul. The Shema contains the full announcement. The Mosaic code contains the full announcement. Deuteronomy 6:7 requires that these truths be taught from earliest childhood. The Jew sees the stone, falls over it, rises, and moves on.

The great inversion is the consequence. The Jew, possessing Torah, Navim, the unconditional covenants, the Shekinah glory, the worship of the true God, and the promises — ends the dispensation of Israel with minus R, having pursued self-righteousness through works. The Gentile, possessing none of these things, ends up with plus R through a single non-meritorious act of faith in Christ. The one who had everything has nothing; the one who had nothing has everything. This is the great inversion that structures Romans 9–11 and that Paul now documents from Isaiah.

The big blot-out also explains the historical sufferings of the Jewish people under divine discipline — the Inquisition, the pogroms of 1881, the Holocaust of 1933–1945. These terrible events operate on the principle that the genuine believers among the Jewish people in any generation form a pivot of preservation for that generation. When that pivot is insufficient in number or in maturity, the protective buffer fails and the cycle of national discipline falls with full force. The true Jew — the regenerate Jew, the spiritual seed of Abraham — carries the false Jew in time; this cannot be extended into eternity.

IV. The Panorama of Israel: Introduction to Romans 10–11

Romans 9:32–33 concludes chapter 9 and simultaneously introduces the extended argument of chapters 10 and 11. Before entering that argument, it is necessary to survey the position of Israel across the dispensations. This panorama has four components: the Jews in the past, the Jews in the present, the Jews in the future, and the Jewish problem.

A. The Jews in the Past

First, the origin of the Jewish race is absolutely unique. Abraham was a Gentile for ninety-nine years — a Chaldean, therefore Semitic by natural descent — but he became a Jew after cracking the maturity barrier. Genesis 15:6 records that Abraham believed in the Lord, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. That salvation adjustment set up the great potential for the subsequent imputation of blessing in time. When Abraham reached maturity, the justice of God imputed a specific blessing: the creation of a new race, with circumcision as its sign.

Second, all Gentile races originate from Shem, Ham, and Japheth by physical birth. Israel originates from the same Semitic line, but not by the ordinary mechanism of racial formation. God made Abraham a Jew at age ninety-nine. He was born Chaldean; he became Hebrew. This is the foundational uniqueness of the Jewish race.

Third, the racial line descends through the regenerate progeny of Isaac and Jacob rather than through their unbelieving brothers. The election of the seed operates through the spiritual line, as Romans 9:6–13 has already established.

Fourth, at the Exodus, Moses became the father of the Jewish nation — as Abraham had been the father of the Jewish race. Israel therefore has two fathers: Abraham, father of the race; Moses, father of the nation. The Exodus established the original client nation to God: custodians of written revelation, guardians of the laws of divine establishment, responsible for evangelism, Bible teaching, inculcation of doctrine, and missionary activity.

Fifth, in the dispensation of Israel the Jewish people received the unconditional promises of the Abrahamic, Palestinian, and new covenants.

Sixth, Israel's past failure resulted in the administration of five cycles of discipline. The fifth cycle was administered three times: to the Northern Kingdom by Assyria in 721 BC; to the Southern Kingdom by Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC; and to the united remnant by Rome under Vespasian and Titus in AD 70. This third application of the fifth cycle came only after the death of the Apostle Paul. Until Paul died, nothing of that magnitude would be done to Israel. One man's maturity and his strategic position in the plan of God preserved the client-nation status of Israel for forty years after the church age began. Only after Paul's death did the times of the Gentiles begin in its full expression.

Seventh, the dispensation of Israel was temporarily halted — not terminated — after the resurrection, ascension, and session of Christ. The reason for the halt was the necessity of electing a royal family for the third and highest category of our Lord's royalty. As God, the Son holds the title Son of God; his royal family is the Father and the Holy Spirit. As the son of David, he holds Jewish royalty; his royal family is the Davidic dynasty. But as the victor of the angelic conflict, seated at the right hand of the Father as King of Kings and Lord of Lords, he has a category of royalty for which no royal family yet existed. The church age is the period of calling out that royal family. When the royal family is complete, the resurrection of the church occurs, and the Jewish age resumes.

Eighth, the past failure of the Jews and the big blot-out do not hinder the Jewish people from continuing in history. Divine discipline — including the most severe — does not eliminate the race. There will always be Jews on the earth. The unconditional covenants guarantee their continuation.

B. The Jews in the Present

First, the present of the Jew began on the day of Pentecost, when the baptism of the Holy Spirit occurred for the first time and the body of Christ was formed. At that moment the Jewish age was halted and the dispensation of the royal family began. The Jewish nation continued to exist for forty years under client-nation status, but the age itself — the calling out of Israel's covenantal destiny — was suspended pending the completion of the royal family.

Second, in the present dispensation both Jew and Gentile become royal family at the moment of faith in Christ. The racial distinction between Jew and Gentile is removed within the body of Christ. The unconditional covenants belong to ethnic Israel in the past dispensation and in the millennium; they do not belong to church-age believers, whether Jew or Gentile.

Third, the collective advantages of the dispensation of Israel are set aside during the church age and replaced by the advantages of the royal family. A Jew who believes in Christ in this dispensation enters into those royal-family advantages. A Jew who does not believe in Christ has no covenantal advantage in the present age. The times of the Gentiles — which began with the fifth cycle of discipline to Israel in AD 70 and continues to the second advent — means that no Jewish nation can function as a client nation to God during this period. Only Gentile nations can currently occupy that role.

Fourth, the mechanism for the Jew in the present is adjustment to the justice of God — the same mechanism required in every dispensation. Salvation adjustment through faith in Christ is the entry point. From there, rebound adjustment and maturity adjustment operate as they do for every church-age believer.

C. The Jews in the Future

First, when the royal family of God is complete, the rapture of the church occurs. The living are translated; the dead are resurrected. The entire body of Christ departs the earth in resurrection bodies, and the tribulation begins.

Second, the tribulation is not a separate dispensation. It is the conclusion of the Jewish age. The times of the Gentiles — beginning in AD 70 — extends through the tribulation and terminates only at the second advent of Christ. During the tribulation, though there is no Jewish client nation, individual Jews perform the function of evangelism on a scale without historical precedent. The 144,000 sealed Jews of Revelation 7 and 14 operate as evangelists. Moses and Elijah function as primary witnesses in the latter half of the tribulation.

Third, because of the elect within Israel, the tribulation is shortened. The large number of believing Jews accelerates the completion of that period's purpose.

Fourth, at the second advent, the church returns with Christ in resurrection bodies. The baptism of fire follows: Jewish believers alive at the end of the tribulation enter the millennium as the restored client nation of God. Jewish unbelievers are cast into fire. The same principle applies to Gentiles: believers enter the millennium as citizens under the client nation of Israel; unbelievers face the baptism of fire.

Fifth, at the second advent Christ fulfills the unconditional covenants to Israel. The Abrahamic covenant — divine righteousness imputed to the believing seed — is fulfilled. The Palestinian covenant — the great territorial grant from the Nile to the Euphrates, encompassing the entire Middle East — is fulfilled. The Davidic covenant — Christ the son of David reigning forever — is fulfilled. The new covenant to Israel — a believing, regenerate nation — is fulfilled. These covenants have never been fully fulfilled to this point; they await the second advent for their complete realization.

D. The Jewish Problem and the Satanic Conspiracy

God's plan for the Jew is never hindered or frustrated by Jewish failure. In any dispensation, to become the spiritual seed of Abraham, any Jew need only believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. In the dispensation of Israel, that belief brings the blessings of the unconditional covenants. In the church age, that belief brings the blessings and privileges of the royal family of God forever. In either case, the imputation of divine righteousness establishes the potential for all subsequent blessing, and the imputation of eternal life secures the eternal dimension. Every generation of Jews from Abraham forward has access to this identical mechanism.

The Jewish problem in any generation is therefore not racial or political but spiritual: the big blot-out operating through negative volition toward the Lord Jesus Christ. False Jews are those who carry the genetic line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob but are caught in the blot-out. True Jews are the regenerate seed — those who, like Abraham, believe in the Lord and have righteousness credited to their account.

Anti-Semitism in every form is the satanic conspiracy designed to frustrate the eschatology of Israel. Satan's objective is the elimination of the Jewish people from history, thereby preventing any Jew from being alive at the second advent, living through the tribulation, or entering the millennium. If the eschatological plan requires believing Jews alive at the second advent, then the destruction of the Jewish race would, in Satan's strategy, make the fulfillment of the unconditional covenants impossible. This is the real structure of anti-Semitism, beneath every political or social form it takes. Every believer who understands the plan of God will refuse any participation in anti-Semitism in any form. God's grace toward the Jewish people is never canceled by their failure, and therefore there is hope for Jews in every generation — the same hope available to the Gentile: the Lord Jesus Christ, who is not only Savior but the God of Israel and the Prince-Ruler of the church.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Forty-Eight

1. The aorist active indicative of proskopto identifies the big blot-out as a completed historical fact: in every generation of the dispensation of Israel, unbelieving Jews stumbled over the Lord Jesus Christ with full visibility of who he was. This was not ignorance but willful rejection under maximum negative volition.

2. The great inversion is the consequence of the big blot-out: the Jew who possessed every covenantal advantage ended with minus R, while the Gentile who possessed nothing ended with plus R through faith in Christ. The one who had everything has nothing; the one who had nothing has everything.

3. The composite quotation of Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16 is structurally a sandwich: the opening clause (Behold, I lay in Zion) and the closing clause (he who believes on him will not be disappointed) are both from Isaiah 28:16, with the stumbling-stone phrase from Isaiah 8:14 inserted between them. Paul preserves the general subject of both passages while applying them to his specific argument about the first advent.

4. The particle kathōs gegraptai (just as it stands written) with its intensive perfect tense defines the doctrine of verbal plenary inspiration: God so supernaturally directed the human writers of Scripture that without overriding their human intelligence, literary style, or personal characteristics, a complete and coherent divine message was recorded with perfect accuracy in the original languages.

5. The prepositional paranomasia on epi is deliberate: Israel has stumbled over (epi) the rock; Paul's appeal is to return and believe on (epi) the same rock. The inversion of the stumbling is precisely the mechanism of faith. This rhetorical move reflects the genius of Paul's argumentation, designed to relax the very Jew whom the argument has just shaken.

6. The future passive indicative of kataischynō with the negative ou states the absolute guarantee: the believing Jew will not be humiliated at the last judgment, will not be disappointed in eternity, and will not face the lake of fire. Faith in Christ eliminates condemnation in time and in eternity.

7. Israel has two dispensational fathers: Abraham, father of the Jewish race at age ninety-nine through maturity adjustment; and Moses, father of the Jewish nation through the Exodus. The racial line runs through the regenerate progeny of Isaac and Jacob — the spiritual seed, not merely the physical seed.

8. The dispensation of Israel was halted, not terminated, at Pentecost, for the specific purpose of electing a royal family for the third and highest category of Christ's royalty: King of Kings and Lord of Lords. The church age is the dispensation of the royal family. When that family is complete, the rapture occurs, the Jewish age resumes, and the tribulation — the conclusion of the Jewish age — follows.

9. The times of the Gentiles, beginning with the fifth cycle of discipline to Israel in AD 70, continues through the tribulation and terminates only at the second advent. During this entire period no Jewish nation can function as a client nation to God. The death of the Apostle Paul was the trigger point for the commencement of this period; God preserved Israel's client-nation status for forty years after Pentecost for the sake of one man's strategic position in the plan.

10. Anti-Semitism is the satanic conspiracy to frustrate the eschatology of Israel: to eliminate the Jewish people from history so that no Jew is alive at the second advent and the unconditional covenants cannot be fulfilled. No believer who understands the plan of God will participate in anti-Semitism in any form. Grace toward Israel is never canceled by Jewish failure; there is always hope — in every generation, in every dispensation — through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

11. The true Jew in every dispensation is the regenerate Jew: the one who, like Abraham, believes in the Lord and has righteousness imputed to his account. The physical seed without faith carries the label of Israel but not the substance. To be the spiritual seed of Abraham is to believe in Christ — the identical non-meritorious act that has always been the mechanism of salvation adjustment to the justice of God.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
proskopto προσκόπτω proskopto — to stumble against, to trip over Compound verb: pros (against, toward) + koptō (to strike, cut). To strike against an obstacle, to stumble over or trip over something in one's path. In Romans 9:32 the aorist active indicative (culminative aorist) views the entire history of Jewish rejection of Christ as a completed action with existing results — the big blot-out. The active voice indicates Israel produced this action. The word implies visibility: one stumbles over what one actually sees.
proskomma πρόσκομμα proskomma — stone of stumbling, cause of offense Cognate noun of proskopto. The thing over which one stumbles; the stone or obstacle that causes a fall. Used as a prophetic title for the Lord Jesus Christ in his first advent: the rock of salvation to those who believe, the stone of stumbling to those who reject. From Isaiah 8:14 quoted in Romans 9:33.
lithos λίθος lithos — stone A stone, whether a cut stone or a natural stone. In Romans 9:33 (quoting Isaiah 8:14), used of the Lord Jesus Christ as the stone of stumbling over which unbelieving Israel trips. Distinct from petra (bedrock). The contrast between lithos and petra is theologically significant: Christ is the petra, the great foundational rock; the believer united to him is petros, a stone within the rock.
petra πέτρα petra — bedrock, the great rock Bedrock; a large mass of rock used as a foundation. In Romans 9:33 (quoting Isaiah 8:14), used of Christ as the foundational rock of salvation — the rock of offense to those who reject him. Distinguished from petros (a detached stone or piece of rock). Christ is the petra; believers in union with him are petros.
kataischynō καταισχύνω kataischynō — to disgrace, humiliate, disappoint Compound verb: kata (down, against) + aischynō (to shame). To put to shame, to humiliate, to disappoint in one's expectations. In Romans 9:33 the future passive indicative negated by ou: the believing Jew will never be humiliated at the last judgment, never disappointed in eternity, never face the lake of fire. Same concept as Romans 8:1 — no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.
pisteuō πιστεύω pisteuō — to believe, to trust To believe, to put one's trust in. The articular present active participle in Romans 9:33 is the eristic present, expressing punctiliar action in present time without reference to its progress. The point: belief in Christ is available now, as it was in Isaiah's day and Paul's day. One moment of positive volition — non-meritorious faith in Christ — constitutes salvation adjustment to the justice of God.
gegraptai γέγραπται gegraptai — it stands written Perfect passive indicative of graphō (to write). The intensive perfect tense emphasizes the existing results of the act of writing: the Old Testament canon stands as a finished product with continuing authority. The passive voice reflects the mechanics of inspiration — God the Holy Spirit communicated to the human author so that the divine message was recorded with perfect accuracy in the original language. Used formulaically to introduce Old Testament quotations in the New Testament.
tithēmi τίθημι tithēmi — to lay, to place, to establish To place, set, or lay down. In Romans 9:33 the present active indicative (perfective present tense) denotes what was accomplished in the past — the laying of the foundation in Zion — but emphasizes that past event as a present reality. Used of God the Father under the title Adonai-Jehovah establishing the Lord Jesus Christ as the sole foundation for time and eternity.
idou ἰδού idou — behold, take note Demonstrative particle; aorist middle imperative of horaō used as an interjection. Equivalent to the Hebrew hinneh. Demands perception and signals that what follows is of the highest importance. Used at the opening of the composite Isaiah quotation in Romans 9:33 to arrest attention before the announcement of the foundational stone laid in Zion.
kathōs καθώς kathōs — just as, even as Adverb of analogy derived from kata (according to) + hōs (as). Used to introduce Old Testament quotations that verify or document a theological argument. In Romans 9:33, kathōs gegraptai (just as it stands written) introduces the composite quotation from Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16 that documents the big blot-out and the mechanism of faith.
Echad / Akhad אֶחָד echad — one, unique Hebrew numeral adjective meaning one or unique. The final word of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4): Jehovah our God, Jehovah is one. In the context of the first advent, echad expresses the uniqueness of the incarnate Christ: as the God-man (hypostatic union), he is unique among members of the Trinity in possessing true humanity, and unique among humanity in being God. The Shema therefore contained the full announcement of the incarnation available to every generation of Israel.
